docs.title: port49
docs.text: port49 lets you sign in to network devices with your SSO or a certificate instead of a shared TACACS+ password — no changes to the devices.

docs.title: Why port49
docs.text:
• Nothing to steal. Each login uses a short-lived, single-use token minted for one device. There's no shared password sitting in every config backup.
  • Identity on devices that will never support it. People and machines sign in with a certificate or through your identity provider; the device sees ordinary TACACS+.
  • Policy as reviewed code. port49 policy diff fails a change that widens access until a test or a written acknowledgment accounts for it.
  • Built for a bad day. Failure and break-glass behavior is measured in the lab, platform by platform; each device page says what was measured and what is still open.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• How it fits together: Concepts.
  • Installing it: Install compares the three deployment shapes, which are peers: systemd, containers and Helm.
  • How a person signs in: Signing in.
  • Who may do what: Policy.
  • Contributing: Contributing.

port49 is pre-release. The first beta will be v0.1.0; Versions says what beta promises. The source is at https://github.com/blanketfish/port49, under Apache-2.0. This site is at https://blanketfish.github.io/port49/.

docs.title: Identity providers
docs.text:
A person reaches a device with a certificate the broker issues them. This page covers the three things that can stand behind that issuance:

  • an OIDC provider (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta and the like);
  • a directory (LDAP, Active Directory or Samba AD), which supplies groups and, if you have no provider, passwords;
  • a client certificate you already have.

The concepts are on Identities and Trust domains; what a person types is on Signing in.

docs.title: OIDC issuance
docs.text:
An OIDC human verifier sits under broker.identity.humans. It is paired with issuance, which turns a verified sign-in into a short-lived certificate:

broker:
  identity:
    humans:
      - type: oidc
        issuer: https://idp.example.com/realms/corp
        client_id: port49
        principal_claim: preferred_username
        principal_domains: ["example.com"]
    issuance:
      certificate_lifetime: 12h

issuance: {} turns it on with the defaults. certificate_lifetime is 12h by default and may be 1h to 24h.

The broker's issuing CA is made once, on one broker, with port49-broker init-issuer. It writes issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key into broker.state_dir. Copying it to the other brokers and rotating it are covered on Key rotation and Install.

The config refuses a human oidc verifier with no issuance, unless an x509 humans verifier with per_login_mfa.idp_mfa sits beside it. The reason is the next section.

docs.title: A person's ID token is not a bearer credential
docs.text:
The person's ID token is accepted in exactly two places:

  • POST /v1/certificate, to exchange a fresh sign-in for a certificate. The sign-in must be at most 5 minutes old and bound to the request, or the answer is sign_in_not_fresh, sign_in_not_bound or sign_in_not_certifiable.
  • as the proof of an idp_mfa per-login check (POST /v1/mfa), where the provider's own second factor is the evidence.

Anywhere else, presenting it is refused 401 trust_domain_unresolved, with a message saying that a person's ID token is not accepted there, and /v1/refresh refuses it too. A stolen ID token therefore cannot be replayed at the broker to act as the person.

Even at POST /v1/certificate, the token is bound to the request. The token's nonce must name the public key of the certificate request, and the request must be signed by that key. A thief without the signer's private key gets sign_in_not_bound. A sign-in is also exchanged once; a second exchange gets sign_in_spent.

(max_token_age is 2h by default; clock_skew is 1m.)

docs.title: What a provider may name
docs.text:
• principal_claim is required: preferred_username, email or upn. With email, the provider must say email_verified: true, and the value must be printable ASCII with an @. It is lower-cased into user:<value>.
  • principal_domains is required, and bounds who this provider may name. A provider can only ever speak for the domains you list.

  • The provider's signing keys are fetched from its discovery document, cached in broker.state_dir (oidc-<hash>.json) and refreshed every jwks_refresh_interval (1h).

    If the provider is unreachable, tokens signed by the held keys keep verifying until jwks_max_age (24h by default, up to 720h). After that, every token from it is refused identity_provider_unavailable.

    At 3am, with the provider down, certificate logins and live device sessions are unaffected. If you must accept the held keys longer, raise broker.identity.jwks_max_age and restart. The broker says each state once, for example:

    identity: <issuer>: no key refreshed within broker.identity.jwks_max_age (<jwks_max_age>; the last at <time>); every token from it is refused identity_provider_unavailable until a fetch succeeds; certificate logins and live device sessions are unaffected; to accept the held keys meanwhile, raise broker.identity.jwks_max_age (up to 720h) and restart <process>

  • HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are honoured for the provider's requests, and the start line says how each issuer is fetched.

Unmeasured

Hosted providers, Microsoft Entra ID and Okta, are unmeasured (lab register entry L47, open): whether they send email_verified, what their tokens carry in idtyp and scp, and which aud their v2 tokens use are unknown until a run measures them. Keycloak is the measured provider. Check a hosted provider's token on a test account before relying on it.

docs.title: Back-channel logout
docs.text:
When a person signs out of the provider, or an administrator ends their session there, the provider can tell the broker, and the broker ends the person's port49 sessions. Configure the client in the provider with the logout URL https://<broker>/v1/logout and backchannel logout session required on. The body is form-encoded, at most 16 KiB.

A logout token that carries both sid and sub is handled as two logouts: the one for that sid, then the one for that sub. The consequence is that every session of that sub ends, not just the one that signed out. This was measured: one token revoked by sid and then by sub, and both sessions' ID tokens were refused credential_revoked (cells 6a to 6e of the Arista EOS end-to-end run; the token shapes and the no-retry result are in L45; ruling B, spec decision 39). A logout leaves no standing mark, so the person can sign in again after clock_skew (1m). In the decision log the revoke has origin backchannel_logout <issuer>.

The broker keeps the logout record for max_token_age plus twice clock_skew (on an issuing broker, max(max_token_age, 24h) plus twice clock_skew, since certificates live that long). If it cannot write the record the answer is 503, and the provider is the one to retry. Keycloak does not retry a failed logout.

docs.title: When a logout did not land
docs.text:
The provider's event log shows the 503, and the broker's log carries the recovery, spelled out for the principal. It begins

logout: a logout token from <issuer> could not be applied: the store did not answer; answered 503 so the provider may retry; if it does not, once the store returns: <form>

and goes on with one of two forms. Both are run through your agent (Revocation) and need the revoke_others and lift_revocations rights.

Form 1: the logout wrote its record (a later step failed). The form reads "if the decision log holds" a revoke record with origin backchannel_logout:

if the decision log has a revoke record with origin backchannel_logout for <principal> just before this line, end its contexts with `port49 revoke --principal <principal>`, then `port49 revoke --lift --principal <principal>` so they may log in again; a lift can be lost across a <process> stop, so last check that `port49 revoke --list` shows no mark for <principal>

Form 2: nothing was written, so no logout record refuses the person's held ID token or issued certificate. The revoke is unconditional, and the lift waits for the time the line prints, when that token or certificate has expired (the line's <time> is the record's lifetime from now):

end <principal>'s contexts with `port49 revoke --principal <principal>` (api: revoke_others), and lift it with `port49 revoke --lift --principal <principal>` (api: lift_revocations) only after <time>: no logout record refuses the session's held ID token or issued certificate until then; last check that `port49 revoke --list` shows no mark for <principal>

A token that carries sid and sub can get either form: Form 1 when the logout wrote its record, Form 2 when it wrote nothing. Form 2 is printed once per principal the decision log's mint records name for that sub. Lifting early lets the person's held token mint again.

On an issuing broker the line adds a shorter path:

  1. Revoke each certificate issued to the principal with port49 revoke --cert-issuer <DN> --cert-serial <HEX> (the DN and serial come from each broker's issue records).
  2. Lift the mark after max_token_age plus twice clock_skew, instead of after the printed time.

The shorter path holds only if every broker's issue records can be read. If any cannot, wait out the first time.

For a token that names only a sid, the line first offers port49 revoke --sid <sid> --sid-issuer <issuer> (needs revoke_others and a press of your security key). It ends that one session, as a logout by sid does, and leaves no mark to lift.

docs.title: The directory
docs.text:
A directory supplies groups for group: subjects and the username_attribute for device logins. It is configured under broker.directory; every key is in the port49d reference.

  • bind is one of external (a client certificate), gssapi (Kerberos) or simple.
  • principal_attribute and username_attribute must be writable only by directory administrators, and need a case-insensitive matching rule. Whoever can write them chooses who a person is.
  • A principal is pinned to the entry's immutable id (entryUUID or objectGUID). A rename is followed; two entries claiming one principal are refused identity_ambiguous, and a username that two entries claim username_collision. port49 directory forget <principal> releases a pin.
  • The staleness ceiling is 4h by default, refresh_interval 5m and grace 4h. See Troubleshooting for what a stale cache looks like.
Directory Use Notes OpenLDAP external, mapped by olcAuthzRegexp, with nested_groups: recursive in_chain answers empty there, which fails closed Samba AD simple or gssapi SASL EXTERNAL is refused (LDAP result 1); gssapi needs ldap server require strong auth = allow_sasl_over_tls; in_chain works Windows AD external over ldap:// with start_tls: true ldaps:// gets result 7; result 49 means the certificate is unmapped or that DC's KDC is down; gssapi is refused under LdapEnforceChannelBinding = 2

The Windows row is measured on Windows Server 2025 only (L44); older Windows Server releases are unmeasured. OpenLDAP and Samba are in L42 and L43.

docs.title: Certificate mapping and identity_unmapped
docs.text:
With external on Windows AD, the directory finds a person's entry from the certificate through altSecurityIdentities, so each entry holds the string for its certificate. port49 computes the same string Windows does:

X509:<I>DC=com,DC=corp,CN="corp, ""east"" CA"<SR>11AC0000000012

That is the value for an issuer DC=com, DC=corp, CN=corp, "east" CA: <I> is the issuer's RDNs, most significant first, and <SR> the serial's bytes reversed in upper-case hex. A value is quoted the way Windows' CertNameToStr quotes it: a value is quoted if it is empty, contains any of ,+="<>#; or a newline, or has leading or trailing white space, and an inner " is doubled. A backslash and a slash are not quoted. Of these, a comma, a plus, an inner quote and a leading space were measured; an empty value, trailing white space, =, <, >, #, ;, a newline and white space other than a plain space are unmeasured, so a certificate whose issuer holds one is a case to test.

A multi-valued relative distinguished name in the issuer has no one string, so port49 does not guess one: the mapping is empty and the certificate is refused identity_unmapped. That fails closed.

identity_unmapped is also what you get when no entry holds the string. The broker's detail reads directory: identity_unmapped: no entry under <BaseDN>, and for a certificate from a CA that broker.directory.certificate_mapping.issuers does not pin, the certificate's issuer "<issuer>" is not one broker.directory.certificate_mapping.issuers pins. A certificate with several UPN SANs says the certificate carries <n> UPN SANs; exactly one maps. It does not print the value it searched for. To find the string to look for, compute it as above from the certificate's issuer and serial, or read it from the entry that should hold it.

docs.title: Directory-password sign-in
docs.text:
This is for a site with no provider and no PKI. A person signs in with their directory password and a time-based code from an authenticator app, over POST /v1/sign-in and POST /v1/sign-in/confirm, and the broker issues the same certificate.

The order is deliberate:

  1. The code is checked first, and its step consumed.
  2. Then comes one bind as the person's own entry.
  3. Then the certificate is issued.

A password spray therefore never reaches the directory for someone with a code, and port49 cannot lock an account. Service accounts and workload entries are refused.

The broker refuses a directory_password verifier whose principal_domains overlap an oidc verifier's: a password beside a provider that enforces stronger sign-in is a downgrade an attacker would pick.

docs.title: Enrolling the authenticator
docs.text:
A person with no authenticator enrolls at a sign-in whose password is right, only while a window is open for them:

Window Opens when Default enrollment.open_until a date you set, for the whole fleet (a rollout) none enrollment.new_entries_for after the entry's creation (whenCreated or createTimestamp) 336h enrollment.reopen_for after port49 directory reset-second-factor <principal> 24h

port49 directory reset-second-factor --all opens the reopen window for everyone. Outside every window the answer is 403 enrollment_closed. An entry with no creation time counts as outside its new_entries_for window, so a directory that does not supply one fails closed.

State the weakening plainly: inside a window, the directory password alone lets the first caller enrol their own authenticator. If that password is stolen, the thief enrolls first and the real person later finds a second factor they never set up. Every enrollment is an enroll record you can alert on. Keep windows short, and close open_until when a rollout ends.

The enrollments live in a sealed file in broker.state_dir (or in etcd). Create it once with port49-broker init-enrollments. The broker never creates it, because a store that went missing must not reopen enrollment for everyone.

A missing or unreadable one refuses password sign-in with 503 enrollment_store_lost, and every other path keeps serving. Restore it from backup with port49 directory import, or run reset-second-factor --all. port49-broker export-enrollments writes a copy (backup and restore).

The operator commands are port49 directory forget, unlock and reset-second-factor, run through your agent.

Limits are 5 failures per person and 50 per source in 15 minutes (rate_limits); over them the answer is 429 sign_in_throttled, and port49 directory unlock <principal> clears one person's count at 3am.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
port49 admits a TACACS+ connection by its source address. The inventory says which devices exist, what platform each is, which addresses it connects from and what attributes policy scopes can match. A device that is not in it gets no answer at all (device_unknown), so the inventory is as much an access control as the policy is.

This page covers:

  • the two ways to supply the inventory;
  • what the inventory service's connectors do;
  • the three mechanisms that protect you from a bad source: the removal bound, quarantine, and the refusal to serve an empty list.

The policy is a separate file (Policy); the keys a device is admitted under are in the policy's key_groups: (Key rotation).

docs.title: Two ways to supply it
docs.text:
inventory_file inventory.service What it is one YAML file read by port49d port49-inventory, a service that syncs sources and publishes a signed bundle Sources the file files, NetBox, Nautobot, each at its own interval Use it for a lab, a small fleet, CI, port49 explain against a device that does not exist a fleet whose source of truth is a NetBox or a Nautobot A bad source the previous inventory keeps serving the service keeps publishing the last good bundle, and port49d keeps the one it holds

port49d takes exactly one: inventory_file, or inventory.service with no inventory_file. Naming both is refused at start. Both need a policy: the bundle port49d serves is built from the inventory and the policy together.

docs.title: The inventory file
docs.text:
devices:
  - {name: leaf1, platform: arista_eos, addresses: [192.0.2.1], attributes: {site: east}}
  - {name: edge1, platform: cisco_iosxe, addresses: [192.0.2.21], attributes: {site: west}}

Every key is in the inventory file reference. An unknown key, a second YAML document, a device named twice, a device with no name, or one address given to two devices refuses the whole file.

List every address a device may connect from. TACACS+ is often sourced from a loopback or a management interface, not the primary address. A device that connects from an address the file does not list is device_unknown, and nothing in the message points back at the inventory. Pin the source interface in the device's AAA configuration (ip tacacs source-interface or the platform's equivalent) so the address cannot change under you.

An address written as IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:10.1.1.1) is read as the IPv4 address (10.1.1.1), since that is the source a connection arrives from; listing both forms on two devices is the usual one-address-on-two-devices refusal. A key group cidr written in that mapped form is refused at load: write the IPv4 prefix.

attributes: are the free keys that policy scopes match on, such as site and role. A scope that matches on an attribute the device does not have is decided by the scope's on_missing: (Policy), which is why a connector's map is worth checking before the first sync.

port49d watches the file on the policy watch ticker and re-reads it at SIGHUP. The ticker is broker.policy_watch_interval, or policy.watch_interval on a port49d with no broker: block; 5s by default.

A change loads once two reads in a row agree, so an edit takes effect within two intervals. Write the file atomically (to a new name, then rename), so a half-written file is never read. A file that does not load, or is refused by the removal bound below, leaves the previous inventory serving and sets port49_inventory_file_refused.

The inventory service is different: it re-reads its own configuration only at a restart, and a SIGHUP to it starts a sync.

docs.title: The inventory service
docs.text:
port49-inventory reads one or more sources, checks the result against the policy, and publishes a bundle signed with an Ed25519 key. port49d polls it (inventory.service.poll_interval, 30 seconds by default). It verifies every bundle against inventory.service.verify_key_files, and applies one only when it is newer than the one in force.

The service speaks mutual TLS. readers may fetch the bundle; syncers may also start a sync (port49 inventory sync). Their names are exact: user:<email> in lower case, or a certificate's URI SAN such as spiffe://.... * is not a wildcard.

A source is synced:

  • at its interval (default 10m, 1m to 24h, set on the service or on one source);
  • at the service's start, which refuses to serve with no snapshot at all;
  • when NetBox or Nautobot sends a webhook, if the source names a webhook_secret_ref;
  • on demand, with port49 inventory sync --service URL --ca FILE --cert FILE --key FILE (it waits as long as a sync may take, up to sync_timeout), or by SIGHUP to the service.

Size interval to how long a change may wait. The webhook is the fast path, but no measured NetBox or Nautobot release sends a refused delivery again at its defaults (NetBox, Nautobot). The scheduled sync is the backstop. When a webhook is lost, a newly racked device cannot be admitted for up to one interval. A webhook that arrives while the service is shutting down triggers nothing (the startup sync covers it).

docs.title: A NetBox source
docs.text:
listen: ":8443"
tls_cert_file: /etc/port49-inventory/server.pem
tls_key_file: /etc/port49-inventory/server-key.pem
client_ca_file: /etc/port49-inventory/clients-ca.pem
readers: ["spiffe://example.com/port49d"]
syncers: ["user:alice@example.com"]
signing_key_file: /etc/port49-inventory/signing.key
policy_file: /etc/port49-inventory/policy.yaml
state_dir: /var/lib/port49-inventory
interval: 10m
safety: {max_removed_percent: 10}
sync:
  - name: netbox_prod
    type: netbox
    url: https://netbox.example.com
    ca_file: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
    token_secret_ref: env:PORT49_NETBOX_TOKEN
    filter: {status: [active]}
    map: {site: site.slug, role: role.slug}

Started with PORT49_NETBOX_TOKEN set to a placeholder, the service says what is wrong with that file before a listener opens:

port49-inventory: sync[0] (netbox_prod): map must name platform: the path the device's platform is read from

Add platform: platform.slug to the map. With the token variable unset the service says port49-inventory: sync[0].token_secret_ref the environment variable it names is not set, and every fault of this kind is a refusal at start, never a half-started service. The key list is in the service reference; the token and the webhook secret are secret references, read at start and never printed.

What the connector does that a hand-written file would not:

  • It reads the release first (/api/status/) and picks a mapping profile for it.
    • The accepted releases are NetBox 3.7, NetBox 4.x, Nautobot 1.6, and Nautobot 2.x and 3.x.
    • The lab measured NetBox 3.7 and 4.7 and Nautobot 1.6, 2.4 and 3.2. Another minor of an accepted major is read with that profile and noted as unmeasured.
    • A release outside that list refuses every sync until the source sets profile:, with <product> <version> is a release no lab run measured (spec §15 L27, L30: <measured list>); set profile to read it with a measured release's fields, at your own risk. The last good bundle keeps serving meanwhile, but new devices are not admitted until you act.
    • After a NetBox or Nautobot major upgrade, check that the next sync succeeds. The notes (NetBox, Nautobot) record what each release was measured to do.
  • Removals are confirmed. A device the last read kept and this read lacks is asked for by name before it counts as removed (up to 256 of them; past that the whole list is read a second time and both reads must agree). One that is still there makes the sync fail, so a list that shifts under paging, a rename or a delete at a page boundary, never reads as a removal.
  • GraphQL first, REST as the fallback (api: auto). A GraphQL list is taken only when its length equals REST's count before and after it and no device appears twice, so a server cap or a page lost to a concurrent delete fails the sync instead of looking like devices removed.
  • filter: keeps status: [active] unless you say otherwise, and tags: or has_primary_ip: narrow it. It is applied by the service, to what was read.
  • map: names, per attribute, the path in the product's record it comes from. It must name platform. An attribute a device does not give (a null custom field, or one that is an object or a list) is left unset, never invented; on_missing: in the policy then decides what that means.
  • Addresses are the primary IPs (addresses.primary, default true), plus the interfaces you name (addresses.interfaces) or every interface (all_interfaces). Interface addresses are opt-in because every address listed admits its source, and an address on two devices refuses the sync. A loopback, link-local, multicast or unspecified interface address is left out.
  • Platforms are translated through a built-in alias table (eos, arista-eos, veos, cisco_xe and the netutils drivers Nautobot reports), plus your platform_aliases:. A slug neither knows is kept as the device's platform, and the device is admitted and served by the generic adapter, which has no platform-specific handling. Each publication that changes that set says so, and port49_inventory_generic_platform_devices holds the count. Treat a nonzero count as a mapping to fix, not as a state to live in.

docs.title: Behind an egress proxy
docs.text:
The service honours HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY for each NetBox and Nautobot source. At start it says, per source, how it will fetch:

port49-inventory: source netbox_prod is fetched directly (no HTTPS_PROXY)
port49-inventory: source netbox_prod is fetched through the proxy <scheme>://<host> (with credentials) (HTTPS_PROXY)

The second form is the shape the line takes with a proxy set. It names the proxy's scheme and host and whether it carries credentials, never the credentials.

Two faults are worth knowing:

  • An HTTPS_PROXY that does not parse as a proxy URL fails every sync of that source until it is fixed. Percent-encode #, /, ? and % in its password.
  • A proxy that answers 407 fails the sync with the egress proxy refused HTTPS_PROXY's credentials; the token was not sent. The source's API token is never sent to a proxy that refused.

Set the variable on the service's unit or container. A Compose broker's note says the same for identity providers (the compose README).

docs.title: Pointing port49d at the service
docs.text:
inventory:
  service:
    url: https://port49-inventory.example.com:8443
    ca_file: /etc/port49/inventory-ca.pem
    tls_cert_file: /etc/port49/port49d.pem
    tls_key_file: /etc/port49/port49d-key.pem
    verify_key_files: [/etc/port49/inventory-signing.pub]
    state_dir: /var/lib/port49/inventory

state_dir holds the last bundle port49d applied, so a restart starts from it with no service reachable; mirror_dir is an optional second copy the service writes, read at a cold start when state_dir has none. List two verify_key_files while the service's signing key rotates (Key rotation). Every path under inventory.service is absolute, and state_dir and mirror_dir may not overlap.

If the service is down, nothing fails closed: the fleet keeps authenticating on the bundle in force. The alerts (Troubleshooting) tell you the service is failing, its bundle is refused or its snapshot is stale.

docs.title: The removal bound: max_removed_percent
docs.text:
A partly available source of truth, a mistyped filter or a NetBox that returns a short page would otherwise silently deauthorize the fleet. So every sync, and every inventory reload in port49d, is refused when it takes more than max_removed_percent of the devices in force out of service.

A device is out of service when it:

  • was removed;
  • stays, but is newly refused admission;
  • stays, but lost every address it had.

The default is 10, on the service (safety.max_removed_percent, or a source's own safety:) and in port49d (inventory.max_removed_percent). 0 refuses every removal and 100 turns the bound off.

A refused change keeps the last good snapshot serving and raises an alarm (port49_inventory_sync_refused on the service, port49_inventory_file_refused or port49_inventory_bundle_refused in port49d). An empty inventory, and one the policy admits no device of, are refused whatever the bound says.

port49 inventory diff runs the same check offline, so you can see a refusal before you make one. For a ten-device inventory (old.yaml) and the same file with the last two devices removed (new.yaml), against the policy in force:

port49 inventory diff --policy policy.yaml old.yaml new.yaml

bundle sha256:<digest> → sha256:<digest>: +0 device(s), -2, 0 changed
  device removed edge1 (cisco_iosxe)
  device removed edge2 (cisco_iosxe)
  scope all_devices: edge1 left
  scope all_devices: edge2 left
refused: the new inventory removes 2 of 10 devices and refuses 0 more (20%), more than inventory.max_removed_percent (10%); fix the file, or, if the change is meant, raise inventory.max_removed_percent in port49d.yaml and send SIGHUP, which re-reads it with the reload

The command exits 1 on a refusal. The <digest> placeholders stand for the two bundle hashes, which differ with every input; everything else is the command's output as it was run. With --max-removed-percent 20 the same two files end with ok: port49d would take the new inventory (inventory.max_removed_percent 20%) and exit 0.

docs.title: A deliberate large removal
docs.text:
Decommissioning more than a tenth of the fleet is a planned change, and you raise both bounds, in this order:

  1. If the devices come from the service, raise safety.max_removed_percent (or the source's own) in port49-inventory.yaml and restart the service (a SIGHUP to it starts a sync; it does not re-read the file).
  2. In port49d.yaml, raise inventory.max_removed_percent and send SIGHUP to port49d, which re-reads this key with the reload. The same bound is the only check on the effect of port49d's own policy file on admission, so it applies to a policy edit that newly refuses or quarantines devices as well.
  3. Make the change, watch it apply, and lower both back.

Why the default stays at 10, and why 100 is not the answer. A service's first sync after its state is lost is bounded by nothing, because there is no earlier bundle to compare to. port49d's bound is then the only thing between a partial NetBox page and most of the fleet leaving admission, and those devices then get no answer from port49. Ten percent is large enough that a normal week of racking and decommissioning passes, and small enough that a source failure does not. Do a deliberate removal in daytime, with the source's owner reachable.

docs.title: Quarantine
docs.text:
Some checks need both the policy and the inventory:

  • a privilege level a platform cannot number;
  • a session reply above the grant's ceiling;
  • a role landing above the ceiling;
  • enable: auto on a platform whose enable exchange carries no principal.

A device racked tomorrow with a new platform can fail them against a policy that was valid today. Refusing the whole bundle would block every inventory change fleet-wide. Instead port49 quarantines the device: it is published with admission: quarantined and the reason, and the rest of the fleet moves on.

What the operator sees:

  • port49d's reload line counts them: inventory reloaded (...): ...; N device(s) quarantined now, M before; ..., and each quarantined device is logged with its cause at start and at every reload that loads.
  • port49_devices_quarantined is the count in force now. port49 policy test ends with ... 0 quarantined, 0 projection refusals.
  • A mint for the device is refused device_quarantined, and its connection is closed without a reply, as for device_unknown.

Silence, not FAIL, on purpose. The device sees a dead server and falls to its local method, which is the posture every platform documents for an outage and the one the reference AAA configuration covers. An answer of FAIL would tell the device that AAA is healthy and refuses everyone. Break-glass therefore works on a quarantined device. The close was measured on Arista, Cisco IOS XE, Cisco NX-OS and Juniper images (spec §10; spec §14 for a quarantine through a sync), and how long break-glass takes with single-connection on is per platform, in the device pages.

Quarantine means port49 cannot compute a correct policy for the device, not that the device is suspect. The way out is the change the cause names: a policy edit that the next reload applies, an adapter or platform-set change, or a corrected attribute in the source. The service's next sync reports the device no longer quarantined. Do not clear one by weakening a ceiling to make the check pass; read the cause first.

docs.title: Verifying a change before it lands
docs.text:
• port49 policy test --policy FILE --inventory FILE reports quarantines, admission refusals and projection refusals for the inventory you give it.
  • port49 inventory diff --policy FILE OLD NEW shows the devices a change removes or re-admits, and the bound.
  • port49 inventory export --service URL ... --verify-key FILE writes a verified copy of the bundle the service publishes. Without --from it accepts an older genuine bundle, and its header names the sequence, so read the header before you compare.
  • port49 explain --policy FILE --inventory FILE --subject NAME --device NAME answers what a subject can do on a device, including a device that is only in your candidate inventory.

docs.title: Key rotation
docs.text:
Four things rotate, each on its own schedule and each safe in only one order:

  1. the device keys, the secrets shared with RFC 8907 devices (a policy edit, no restart);
  2. the encryption: key that seals port49's stored records (three config steps, each a restart);
  3. the issuing CA, when the broker issues certificates (rotate-issuer);
  4. the inventory service's signing key, when you run one.

A device on TLS (RFC 9887) has no shared key to rotate. Its credential is its certificate; see TLS. Where the secrets live and which files port49 will read is on Secrets.

docs.title: Device keys
docs.text:
A device's key is a named key set in the policy's keys: block. A set has one current version, any number of accept versions that still admit a device, and retired versions kept so a log line can name the key a device tried. Key groups, the inventory pin and the device's own record decide which set a device is admitted under; the set is where the versions live. Every key and its fields are in the policy reference.

keys:
  core:
    current: {version: 2, secret_ref: "file:/etc/port49/keys/core-v2"}
    accept:
      - {version: 1, secret_ref: "file:/etc/port49/keys/core-v1", retire_after: "2027-01-31"}

docs.title: Add a version with a new file
docs.text:
A version's secret never changes. port49d reads each key file once, when the version comes into force, and holds what it read. So:

  1. Make the new secret as a new file (core-v2) under the key directory, owned and moded as the secret-file rule says. Put the file in place first.
  2. Edit the policy: the new version becomes current; the old one moves to accept with a retire_after date. Run port49 policy test and port49 policy diff in CI. policy test refuses a secret_ref outside key_secret_refs, and diff names any version that now points at a different reference.
  3. port49d reads the policy file on its watch interval and at SIGHUP. A new version is in force for the next packet. Nothing restarts, and no open connection is cut by adding a version.
  4. Put the new key on each device. port49 keys show --policy FILE --inventory FILE DEVICE says which key set a device is admitted under, by which rule, and which version to provision. It never prints the secret.
  5. Watch the old version empty out (below), then remove it.

Never edit a key file in place, and never point an existing version at another reference. port49d refuses a policy that gives a version a different secret_ref than the one it has held since it started.

If a held file is rewritten anyway, or can no longer be read, port49d keeps the bytes it holds, says keys.<name> version N: <path> has changed since port49d read it (or, for an unreadable file, ... can no longer be read (...); port49d keeps the secret it read, but a restart will refuse to start until the file is back or the policy no longer names the version), and sets port49_key_secret_files_changed above 0 (alert port49_key_secret_files_changed). A restart would take the new bytes on that replica alone, so two replicas would then hold two secrets for one version. Put the new bytes in a new file under a new version number.

docs.title: If the file is not there yet
docs.text:
Adding the policy line before the file exists does not take effect, and does no harm to a running port49d: the policy already serving stays in force, and the refusal is tried again every 30 seconds until the file reads or the policy file changes. On Kubernetes this is the normal case for up to a couple of minutes after you add a key to a Secret (the kubelet took 1m34s in the L82 run). A SIGHUP tries at once.

After a restart the same mistake is a refused start, so a pod crash-loops until the file is restored or the policy line is taken out.

To remove a key, take the policy line out first, then the file.

docs.title: Phasing out the old version
docs.text:
retire_after is the last day (UTC) an accept version admits a device. From midnight after it, the version admits none. The device's next packet on it is a struck failure and the connection is reset at once, so its next connections meet the strike backoff (held_refused).

A policy edit that removes a version or moves it to retired resets connections on it at their next packet, with no strike.

An accept version with no retire_after is reported by port49 policy test as an indefinitely accepted version, which is what rotation exists to prevent.

To see who is still on the old version, run port49 keys status against the port49d log and the policy:

port49 keys status --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml /var/log/port49/port49d.log

It infers, from each device's latest validated login, which version the device presented. The same fact is the gauge port49_key_version_devices{key_ref,version} and, for how long is left, port49_key_retirement_seconds; the alerts port49_key_retirement_within_7d and port49_key_retirement_within_1d fire before a device is locked out. The series are in the metrics reference.

A device that cannot log in after a rotation is the usual question. port49d keys-diagnose --device NAME --capture FILE takes a capture of the device's first packet, tries every version port49d holds, retired ones included, and says which one validates. It prints no byte of the packet or of a key.

docs.title: single_device
docs.text:
The key metrics are labelled by key_ref. A name that admits exactly one device would be that device's name in a metric, and port49 puts no device identity in a metric label. So a key held by exactly one device (a pin, or a key group of one) is reported under key_ref="single_device" and version="any". For those, port49_key_version_devices counts the single-device keys on a version that has a retire_after, and port49_key_retirement_seconds is the least time left among them. Which device is on which version is port49 keys status's answer. A key held by two or more devices keeps its own label.

single_device is therefore a reserved name: a policy or an inventory that names it as a key_ref is refused at load. Pick another name for the set.

docs.title: The encryption: key
docs.text:
port49 seals tokens, receipts, contexts, directory memberships and pins, and second-factor records at rest under encryption.current. encryption.previous is an optional second key that records can still be opened with, which is what makes rotation possible.

Always give a new key a new id. The ids label every sealed record. port49 refuses a previous whose id equals current's, but it cannot see a new secret put under an old id: records sealed earlier then fail to open, with no warning at the start.

Both keys are 32 bytes; their fields are in the reference. Every region holds the same set, and the key is the same value in port49d and in the broker.

Rotation is three steps. Finish each step in every region, on every port49d and every port49-broker, before you begin the next. Each step is a configuration change and a restart.

  1. Add the new key as previous everywhere. The old key stays current. Nothing is sealed under the new key yet, but every process can now open what either key seals.
  2. Swap. The new key becomes current and the old key previous, everywhere. New records are sealed under the new key, and a process that has not swapped yet can still open them, because step 1 gave it that key.
  3. Remove previous everywhere, only when the conditions below hold. Keep the old key file as described there.

Why the order cannot be changed. In step 1 no process seals under the new key, so a process that has not restarted yet is never handed a record it cannot open. In step 2 every process already holds both keys, so the swap can happen one process at a time. Step 3 is the only step that makes records unreadable, so it comes last. Run step 3 on one process early and that process opens nothing a not-yet-swapped neighbour still seals under the old key.

docs.title: Before step 3: what must be gone or re-sealed
docs.text: Do not run step 3 until the records sealed under the old key are gone or re-sealed. Each kind of record has its own wait.

docs.title: Second factors
docs.text: With directory password sign-in, second-factor records and the enrollment mark are re-sealed by the broker's scheduled directory pass (every refresh_interval). Wait for a pass to complete after step 2. If the broker says the re-seal could not open N second factors; encryption.previous cannot be retired while they are sealed under it, do not run step 3.

docs.title: Tokens, receipts and contexts
docs.text:
These are short-lived, and the scheduled pass above does not re-seal them. After step 2 has finished everywhere, wait for the largest of:

  • session.max_session_age_default plus session.grace_window (port49d.yaml; 12 hours plus 10 minutes by default, and a policy role can only lower it);
  • receipt_max_age (2 hours by default);
  • session.staleness_ceiling (4 hours by default, the age of the snapshots a stopped process is read from);
  • 20 minutes (a token lives at most 15, and the idempotency records that carry minted tokens are kept under 20);
  • the directory membership lease (24 hours: broker.directory.grace is capped at 24 hours, and the lease is the larger of the two).

The lease is on the list because every verify reads a principal's membership record before it rewrites it. A record sealed under the old key therefore keeps failing, for that principal, until its lease runs out. This holds on a single shared store as well as on a split. Tokens are also purged at every start on etcd.

Records still under the old key after step 3 do not open:

  • a token is dropped from the candidates and counted in port49_crypt_open_failures_total{record="token"};
  • a session's context is denied store_unavailable;
  • a second factor is never treated as "not enrolled". For that second factor an operator runs port49 directory reset-second-factor.

docs.title: Directory pins
docs.text:
Directory pins (on a directory store of its own: a split, or more than one region) are re-sealed by the same scheduled pass. A pin has no expiry, so it never ages out.

What to wait for. After step 2 has finished everywhere, wait for a pass that ended after the last step-2 restart (port49_directory_pins_reseal_last_complete_timestamp_seconds later than that restart) with port49_directory_pins_sealed_previous at 0.

  • Read both on the replica that holds the keyspace (port49_store_keyspace_held 1). A replica that handed the keyspace over keeps the values of its last pass until it restarts. Any region's holder will do, because they all read the one directory store.
  • The gauges are absent until a runner completes its first pass after it starts. They are also absent on a single shared store, where a membership record has a lease (the 24 hours above) and there is no pin to re-seal.

How the pass works. The runner lists every pin with the key it is sealed under, in pages of 500, and opens only the pins not under current. It writes each one still sealed under previous again under current, by a compare on the revision it read. A pin that a port49 directory forget, a re-pin or another region's runner changed in between is left as that writer wrote it, and the next pass reads it again. Each pin is one compare-and-swap, so nothing is left half-written.

The pass has a budget of half refresh_interval, so it never holds off the stamping refresh. A large fleet can take several intervals to finish its first pass.

What it says.

  • A pass that moves pins says directory store: the re-seal sealed N pins under the current key; M are left under encryption.previous.
  • If the directory store stops answering or refuses the broker's identity, the pass says directory store: the re-seal of pins stopped: <error>; the next pass starts again and changes no gauge.
  • A cancel (shutdown, or the keyspace handed over) stops the pass silently and changes no gauge either.
  • A write that fails any other way does not stop the pass. That pin is counted in port49_directory_pins_sealed_previous, it is named once an hour as directory store: <principal>'s pin could not be written under the current key (...), and the pass goes on with the pins after it.
  • A pass that runs out of its budget says directory store: the re-seal of pins ran out of its <budget> budget after sealing N pins (M did not open); the next pass goes on from there once an hour and changes no gauge.

While step 2 is rolling out, expect the re-seal sealed N pins lines in every region, because regions on different current keys move pins back and forth; finish step 2 promptly.

docs.title: A pin that opens under neither key
docs.text:
A pin that opens under neither key is counted in port49_directory_pins_unopenable (alert port49_directory_pins_unopenable, on the keyspace holder). It means a key was retired while it still sealed pins. Reading the pin fails with an unknown-key error (ErrUnknownKey).

What it breaks. Bind, mint and refresh fail for that principal. From the code (not measured), sessions already open are denied context_stale once session.staleness_ceiling has passed. Each pass opens the pin again, so port49_crypt_open_failures_total{record="membership"} rises at least once per pass for each such pin, and more with traffic, because bind, mint and refresh open it too.

What the pass says. The pass never deletes or rewrites such a pin. It says directory store: <principal>'s pin does not open (...) once an hour, for at most 20 principals a pass (the first 20 in sorted order); the count's line says how many more are not named.

  • When the cause is an unknown key, the line says to put the retired key back as previous and restart.
  • For any other open error, it says the record does not match its seal and to run port49 directory forget <principal>, because the record was changed outside port49 and no key helps.

How to recover. Putting the retired key back as previous and restarting deletes nothing, and the next pass re-seals the pin. If that key is gone, port49 directory forget <principal> frees the principal, and the person's next sign-in pins them again. Any admin with forget_principals whose own pin opens can run it, and every pin that opens is on current after a pass. Confirm that the person who signs in is the same person, as on Stores. There is no offline forget on port49-broker.

docs.title: Rotating again
docs.text: There is one previous slot, so a rotation's step 1 drops whatever key previous held. Begin a rotation only after the last one's step 3. The waits above gate that step, so every pin is then under current. Only pins have a gauge. A second factor is under current once a pass has completed without the could not open N second factors line and without sign-in: the re-seal of second factors stopped.

docs.title: Backups and exports need every key that sealed their records
docs.text:
An etcd snapshot and a Velero backup are the raw stores, and each record in them keeps the key that was current when that record was written. An enrollment export (port49-broker export-enrollments) keeps each record's seal too, and seals only its envelope under the key current at export time. So a backup taken between steps 2 and 3 needs both keys, and any backup needs every key that was current while its records were written.

port49 directory import refuses a file sealed under a key the broker does not hold and tells you to set that key as previous.

Keep every old key file, offline, as long as any backup that holds its records is kept. Restoring without it loses the second factors and pins sealed under it, and each enrolled person must then run port49 directory reset-second-factor. Velero also stores the encryption Secret in the bucket, so a Velero restore brings back the key its backup was taken with, and that bucket must be guarded like the key.

docs.title: A process that starts without the key
docs.text:
If a process starts without a key the store was last written under, what you see depends on the store:

  • On a directory store of its own, the start is refused, naming the store and the key id. Fix encryption: and start again.
  • On the session store, the start goes on. port49d (and port49-broker, in its own name) says that the store was last written by a process whose current key it does not hold, the sessions sealed under that key are denied store_unavailable, none is revoked, and port49_crypt_store_key_unknown is 1 (alert). If the key was retired by mistake, set it as previous again and restart.

The recipes that make the key file, with the right owner and mode and without ever overwriting an old one, are in each shape's install page: systemd, container, Helm. See also Stores.

docs.title: The issuing CA
docs.text: This applies only when the broker issues certificates (broker.identity.issuance is set). Every broker on one store must issue from the same CA. The CA is two files in broker.state_dir, issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key, and the store holds a record of the CA's fingerprint, never its key.

docs.title: First install
docs.text:
Run init-issuer once, on one broker, as that broker's user:

sudo -u port49-broker port49-broker init-issuer

(port49d init-issuer does the same under port49d's configuration.) It writes the key first, then the certificate, owner-only. It refuses a configuration without issuance:. Run again where a whole CA already is, it writes nothing and says so; a half CA (a key without the certificate, or the reverse) it refuses, and it never replaces one.

Then copy both files to every other broker's broker.state_dir, keeping them private (0600, the broker's user), and restart each. Never run init-issuer on a second broker: that would make a different CA. The Helm chart's scripts/copy-issuer.sh does the copying and refuses to overwrite a different CA.

Compare the fingerprints. Each broker's start prints a line like issuing as <subject> (sha256:<fingerprint>), valid until <date>. Read that line on every broker; the fingerprints must be identical. The first broker to start on a store writes its fingerprint as the store's record, and every later broker is held to it.

docs.title: The three refusals
docs.text:
A broker whose CA does not match the record refuses to start, and the line names what to do. At 3am there are three, all from issuance: in the broker's journal or kubectl logs:

You see It means Do issuance: this broker's issuing CA (<fingerprint>) is behind a promotion: the store records <fingerprint>, promoted from it by <broker> at <time>. Copy issuing-ca.pem, issuing-ca.key and issuing-ca-previous.pem from that broker into broker.state_dir, then start A rotation was promoted on another broker and this one missed the copy. Copy those three files from the broker named, then start. issuance: this broker's issuing CA (<fingerprint>) is not the one the store records (<fingerprint>, by <broker> at <time>): every broker on one store issues from one CA. Copy issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key from a broker that holds it ... This broker holds a different CA than the store records, usually a second init-issuer or a restored old volume. Copy issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key from a broker that holds the recorded one. Do not run init-issuer. issuance: the store's issuing CA record kept changing under this start; start again Two brokers were writing the record at once. Start again.

Do not reach for forget-issuer for any of these. It is for one case only: every broker lost the CA and no copy exists.

docs.title: forget-issuer
docs.text:
port49-broker forget-issuer --current sha256:<fingerprint>

It removes the store's record of the CA so a new one can be made, then init-issuer on one broker and a copy to the others. It names the fingerprint it forgets, so a record that holds a different CA is kept; and it deletes at the revision it read, so a broker that recorded in the meantime keeps its record. After it, every certificate the old CA issued stops working. Stop every broker on the store before starting one on another CA. The current fingerprint is the one a broker's start line prints.

docs.title: rotate-issuer
docs.text:
rotate-issuer replaces the CA with an overlap, so the certificates already issued stay valid. It is run on one broker, twice, with copies between:

  1. Stage. rotate-issuer makes issuing-ca-next.pem and issuing-ca-next.key. Copy the certificate only (issuing-ca-next.pem) to every other broker and restart each, so every broker trusts it. The key stays on this broker. This broker loads the CA only at its start, so restart it too before it promotes.
  2. Promote. Run rotate-issuer again on the same broker. The current certificate becomes issuing-ca-previous.pem, the staged pair becomes current. Copy issuing-ca.pem, issuing-ca.key and issuing-ca-previous.pem to every other broker, remove the staged issuing-ca-next.pem there, and restart each, and restart this one too, which holds the old CA in memory until it does. Each issues with the new CA and still trusts the previous one.
  3. Retire. After certificate_lifetime has passed since the promotion, remove issuing-ca-previous.pem from every broker and restart each.

Step 1 before step 2 is what keeps anyone out: a broker that trusts the staged certificate can verify a certificate issued under it the moment another broker promotes. A promotion is refused while a previous CA from an earlier rotation is still there, since certificates it issued may still be valid. An interrupted promotion is finished by running it again. An expired CA is recovered the same way: run rotate-issuer twice, restarting every broker after each. The alerts port49_issuing_ca_expiring and port49_issuing_ca_missing say when.

docs.title: The inventory service's signing key
docs.text:
The inventory service signs each bundle with signing_key_file. port49d verifies every bundle against the public keys in inventory.service.verify_key_files: list two while the key rotates, the old key's public key and the new key's, and SIGHUP re-reads the list. The fields are in the service reference and the port49d reference.

A bundle names its signing key by an id, the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 of the public key. A verifier picks the verify key with that id; if two files in the list carry the same id (the same key listed under two paths), the last one listed is the one a document is checked against. List each public key once. A document that does not verify is refused with the document's signature by <id> does not verify, and one signed by a key no file holds with the document is signed by <id>, which no verify key holds.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
The policy file decides who may log in to which devices and what they may run there. It is one YAML document that lives in your repository, so a change to access is a change to a file that someone reviews, tests and diffs before it ships.

port49d reads the file on its watch interval and at SIGHUP, and refuses a file that does not load. The tools that check a change run offline, against the policy and the inventory file, so CI can run them and nothing needs a broker.

This page shows how the pieces of the file fit together, how to write tests for it and how to review a change. Every key is in the policy reference.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
A decision is made in four steps, and each has a block in the file:

  1. A subject says who: a directory group of people (group:), a group of workloads (machine_group:), or a list of literal identities (identity:).
  2. A scope says where: a selector over inventory attributes, such as site or os_version.
  3. A role says what: the command rules it permits and denies, a privilege level, and how long a session may last.
  4. A grant ties a subject to a scope with roles.

Roles and grants have their own page. This is a policy that decides one thing:

platform_set: 1.3.0

keys:
  core:
    current: {version: 1, secret_ref: "file:/run/port49/keys/core-v1"}

key_groups:
  - {match: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/8}, key_ref: core}

scopes:
  - name: dc_fabric
    match: {site: [dc1, dc2], role: [leaf, spine]}
    on_missing: exclude

roles:
  - name: read_only
    privilege: readonly
    permit: ["show **", "terminal length *"]
    max_session_age: 8h

subjects:
  - name: netops
    group: "cn=netops,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
    token_ttl: 300s

grants:
  - {subject: netops, scope: dc_fabric, roles: [read_only]}

tests:
  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "show version", expect: permit}
  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "configure terminal", expect: deny}

The keys: and key_groups: blocks say which shared secret admits which device; they are covered in Key rotation. The tests: block is covered in Writing tests.

An unknown key, or a second document in the file, is refused, and the error names the key or the line.

docs.title: Writing a rule
docs.text:
A rule is a list of terms matched against the command, one term per argument:

Term Matches word that argument, ignoring case * exactly one argument, any value ** any number of arguments; only as the last term @class one argument in a named set of entity names the platform defines /regex/ one argument matching the RE2 expression

A rule matches the whole command. show bgp summary does not match show bgp summary detail unless the rule ends in **.

docs.title: When a permit and a deny both match
docs.text:
When several roles apply, their permits and denies are pooled. A permit wins only if it is more specific than every deny that matches the command, at every word; otherwise the command is denied. Two examples:

  • A permit of show ** does not beat a deny of show running-config **, because the deny names more of the command.
  • A permit of copy ** against a deny of * * /^(tftp|ftp):/: the permit names the command and the deny names the destination. Each wins a different word, neither dominates, and the deny stands.

Prefer literals, * and classes to regexes. A regex is the one term whose reach port49 policy diff cannot enumerate.

A regex in a deny may not turn case-insensitivity off. port49 matches ignoring case, so a case-sensitive deny could be walked past by changing the case of what is typed. A regex in a permit may.

docs.title: Output modifiers
docs.text: Output modifiers after a pipe are judged apart from the command, against the role's pipe: list. The list defaults to include **, exclude **, begin **, section **, json, count and no-more. A role that sets pipe: {permit: []} allows no pipe at all.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A scope selects devices by inventory attribute. match: {site: [dc1, dc2], role: [leaf, spine]} is every device whose site is dc1 or dc2 and whose role is leaf or spine. A scope with no match selects every device, and match: {name: core-sw01} pins one.

A version key takes a comparison, such as os_version: {lt: "4.31.2F"}. The comparison orders vendor version strings token by token, not as semver.

docs.title: on_missing
docs.text:
Sometimes the inventory cannot describe a device: the sync dropped its os_version, or its version string cannot be ordered. The device then has no value for a match key, and on_missing says which way it goes: include puts it in the scope, exclude leaves it out.

The safe direction depends on what the scope does:

  • A scope that delivers a deny is the one a broken sync could silently lift. A missing value should mean the device is affected: on_missing: include.
  • A scope that gives access should leave out a device it cannot describe: on_missing: exclude.

port49 refuses to guess. A scope with a match key that delivers a deny must write on_missing, whether the deny comes through attached_roles or through a grant whose role holds a deny. A file that leaves it out does not load. Any other scope takes on_missing: exclude.

docs.title: The include-scope grant refusal
docs.text:
A grant on an on_missing: include scope is refused at load, whatever its roles carry. The reason: a grant is what lets a login reach a device, even when its roles only deny. On an include scope, a device the inventory cannot describe would get a session from the grant alone. (A scope with no match key, or one pinned by name alone, is the exception; see the end of this section.)

The error reads:

grants[1] (subject netops, scope eos_unpatched): scope "eos_unpatched" is on_missing: include and a grant lets
a login reach a device even when its roles only deny, so a device the inventory cannot describe would get a
session from this grant; put the grant on a separate scope with the same match and on_missing: exclude, and
put a mitigation's deny in the include scope's attached_roles (spec §5.5)

The fix is two scopes with the same match. The deny goes on the include scope, and the grant on the exclude one:

scopes:
  - name: eos_unpatched
    match: {platform: arista_eos, os_version: {lt: "4.31.2F"}}
    on_missing: include
    security_log: true
    attached_roles:
      humans: [no_running_config]   # a role of denies alone
  - name: eos_unpatched_known
    match: {platform: arista_eos, os_version: {lt: "4.31.2F"}}
    on_missing: exclude             # a grant is earned by data

roles:
  - name: no_running_config
    deny: ["show running-config **"]

An include scope may attach only roles that cannot widen access: no permit, no privilege, no attributes. A role that carries one is refused at load, and the error says to put it on an exclude scope.

The exception, for both the grant refusal and the attached-roles rule, is a scope with no match key, or one pinned by name alone. It has no attribute a device could be missing, so it has nothing to include.

docs.title: security_log
docs.text:
Whoever can edit os_version can lift a mitigation without touching the policy, and the inventory is often written by a discovery tool rather than a person. security_log makes a device joining or leaving a scope a security record in the log.

It defaults to true for a scope that delivers a deny, so the log says when a device left the mitigation. A scope with per_login_mfa and a match key other than name must say security_log: true outright.

Writing security_log: false on a deny-bearing scope is allowed, because the file chose it, and port49 policy test reports it:

report: deny_scope_unlogged: scope "eos_unpatched" delivers a deny and says security_log: false: an edit of
os_version or platform that lifts the deny leaves no record (spec §5.5)

The report does not fail the run. Remove the line, or write true, unless you have a reason to want the silence.

docs.title: Writing tests
docs.text:
Tests are the policy's own statement of what it should decide. They do two jobs:

  • port49 policy test runs every test and fails when one does not hold, so a change that breaks an intended decision fails CI.
  • port49 policy diff reads the passing tests in the new file as the author's evidence that a widening of access is intended. A widening no test (or acknowledge: entry) accounts for fails the diff.

Tests go in the top-level tests: list. There are two kinds:

  • A command test has a command:. It asks: would this subject be permitted this command on this device?
  • A session test has no command:. It asserts what a login to the device gets: its privilege level, its ceiling, its reply attributes, the subject's API rights or its per-login MFA requirement.

docs.title: Who and where
docs.text:
Every test names who it runs as and the device it runs against:

Key What it says Example subject the subject the test runs as subject: netops principal a principal identity, in any form identity: takes; the test runs as whichever subject it resolves to principal: "user:alice@example.com" device an inventory device; required device: leaf1

Give subject or principal, exactly one. A device the inventory does not name fails the test.

A test is answered in the order the broker answers a mint, as port49 explain does:

  • a subject with no grant on the device is a deny, no_grants_matched;
  • a device with no platform is refused, device_unconfigured;
  • any subject on a quarantined device is a deny, device_quarantined;
  • a mint the broker would refuse permits nothing.

docs.title: Command tests
Session tests
docs.text:
A session test takes no expect or reason. It names at least one of these keys, and passes where the subject would be minted a token on the device with every value it names:

Key What it asserts Example level the privilege level the subject is minted a token at level: operator max_privilege the ceiling the token carries, a level or none max_privilege: none priv_lvl the priv-lvl number (0 to 15) the reply carries, or none; 015 reads as 15 priv_lvl: 15 enable the subject's enable mode: none, auto or token enable: none reply the exact session reply, in order; an empty list asserts an empty reply reply: ["priv-lvl=1", "roles=network-operator"] api the subject's broker API rights, the whole list, in any order api: [explain_others] per_login_mfa the effective per-login requirement, none or a mapping of accept and reuse_for per_login_mfa: none

A session test fails where no token would be minted, for example where the subject has no grant on the device. The one exception is a test that asserts api and nothing else: API rights belong to the subject, not to a session, so that test passes on any device.

docs.title: How a test clears a policy diff label
docs.text:
Each label in the policy diff table is cleared by a different kind of test. The test must be in the new file and must pass.

Label The test that clears it EXPANDS a command test with expect: permit on a command the change frees, on a device of that group. One test clears every command shape of the same deny and permit; in the example below, one test clears three lines. RAISES a session test asserting the new value. The diff prints the test to add. REGEX-CONSTRAINED a passing command test with expect: permit on a command the changed rule decides, or, for a deny, on a command it used to refuse. A wider deny whose freed commands you cannot name takes an acknowledge: entry. API a session test whose api: lists the subject's whole new list. The diff prints the test to add. PRINCIPAL, USERNAME a session test naming the principal (principal:); a test that asserts only api does not count. A USERNAME change is cleared by a test naming any one of the subject's principals. A PRINCIPAL change whose new subject gains API rights also needs api: with the subject's whole list. per_login_mfa_weakened a session test with per_login_mfa: asserting the new requirement, which is new or changed against the old file. A test carried over unchanged does not count. SUBJECT a session test naming the subject.

A test that expects deny never clears a widening, since it cannot tell a deny rewritten narrower from one rewritten wider. ADAPTER, QUARANTINES, REFUSED and UNRESOLVED are not cleared by tests.

Once a test clears a label, the diff still prints the change, in lowercase and marked, and passes: EXPANDS: becomes expands (a policy test exercises it):, and RAISES: becomes raises (a session test asserts it):.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
The read_only role from the policy above gains a deny, and a test pins it:

roles:
  - name: read_only
    privilege: readonly
    permit: ["show **", "terminal length *"]
    deny: ["show running-config **"]
    max_session_age: 8h

tests:
  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "show version", expect: permit}
  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "configure terminal", expect: deny}
  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "show running-config", expect: deny, reason: no_permit_dominates_deny}

That is the version on main. A pull request now deletes the deny: line, which lets netops read the running configuration. The first thing to fail is the test that pinned the deny. port49 policy test on the new file prints:

FAIL netops on leaf1: "show running-config" -> permit permit_dominates, want deny no_permit_dominates_deny
3 tests, 1 failed; 0 shadowed denies, 0 unacknowledged; 0 quarantined, 0 projection refusals

and exits 1. port49 policy diff --old main-policy.yaml --new policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml shows the widening, one line per command shape the deny used to cover, and exits 1:

EXPANDS: netops on leaf1: "show running-config" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
EXPANDS: netops on leaf1: "show running-config <any other argument>" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
EXPANDS: netops on leaf1: "show running-config <any other argument> <any other argument>" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
3 commands changed: 3 widen, 0 narrow; 3 unacknowledged expansions past a deny; 0 unacknowledged privilege raises; 0 unacknowledged per_login_mfa weakenings; 0 unacknowledged regex-constrained widenings; 0 unacknowledged principal or username changes; 0 devices newly quarantined, 0 released; 0 mints newly refused; 0 unresolved; 0 unacknowledged adapter edits; 0 projection refusals; 0 devices newly refused admission

If the change is intended, say so with a test. Turn the old test around:

  - {subject: netops, device: leaf1, command: "show running-config", expect: permit}

Now port49 policy test prints PASS netops on leaf1: "show running-config" -> permit permit_dominates and exits 0, and port49 policy diff prints the same three changes as cleared and exits 0:

expands (a policy test exercises it): netops on leaf1: "show running-config" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
expands (a policy test exercises it): netops on leaf1: "show running-config <any other argument>" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
expands (a policy test exercises it): netops on leaf1: "show running-config <any other argument> <any other argument>" was denied by "show running-config **" (read_only), now permitted by "show **" (read_only)
3 commands changed: 3 widen, 0 narrow; 0 unacknowledged expansions past a deny; 0 unacknowledged privilege raises; 0 unacknowledged per_login_mfa weakenings; 0 unacknowledged regex-constrained widenings; 0 unacknowledged principal or username changes; 0 devices newly quarantined, 0 released; 0 mints newly refused; 0 unresolved; 0 unacknowledged adapter edits; 0 projection refusals; 0 devices newly refused admission

The reviewer sees one changed test line beside the removed deny: the widening is written down and tested. In CI, the job in Run the checks in CI blocks the first version of the pull request and passes the second.

A privilege raise works the same way, with a session test. If the same pull request had changed read_only's privilege: readonly to privilege: operator, the diff would print the test it needs:

RAISES: netops on leaf1: level readonly -> operator, max_privilege none -> none, priv_lvl 1 -> 15, enable none -> none, reply ["priv-lvl=1", "roles=network-operator"] -> ["priv-lvl=15", "roles=network-operator"]; no session test asserts it: add {subject: netops, device: leaf1, priv_lvl: 15, level: operator}

Paste {subject: netops, device: leaf1, priv_lvl: 15, level: operator} under tests:, and the line becomes raises (a session test asserts it): ... and passes.

docs.title: Checking a change
docs.text: Four commands read the policy: port49 policy test, port49 policy diff, port49 policy replay and port49 explain. They take --policy FILE --inventory FILE (policy diff takes --old and --new with one --inventory). They never read a secret, and with the files given they never ask a broker. Every rule and command they print is redacted as the daemon's records are.

docs.title: port49 policy test
docs.text:
port49 policy test --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml [--config port49d.yaml]

It loads the policy against the inventory as port49d does, so every load error is a failure here. Then it prints, in order: the platform set, the key check, the reports, the shadowed-deny report, one line per test, and a summary. For the policy above, against an inventory whose leaf1 is an arista_eos device with site: dc1 and role: leaf, it prints:

platform_set: 1.3.0
keys: checked against the default key_secret_refs (env: variables starting PORT49_KEY_, file: under /run/port49/keys); pass --config to check port49d.yaml's
report: group_subject: subject "netops" is a group: subject: it mints only with broker.directory configured, through which the broker matches a person to the group; explain and policy tests evaluate it by name
PASS netops on leaf1: "show version" -> permit permit_dominates
PASS netops on leaf1: "configure terminal" -> deny no_rule_matched
2 tests, 0 failed; 0 shadowed denies, 0 unacknowledged; 0 quarantined, 0 projection refusals

It exits 1 when any of these holds:

  • the policy does not load;
  • a test fails;
  • a deny is shadowed by a more specific permit and no test exercises it;
  • a device is quarantined, now or at a later grant expiry;
  • a composition gets a projection's fail-closed reply;
  • admission refuses a device;
  • a key problem exists: no keys: block, a key_ref the block does not define, or a secret_ref outside key_secret_refs.

Pass --config to check against your port49d.yaml's key_secret_refs, which is the only key it reads from that file. Without it, the default allowance is used and the output says so.

Lines that begin report: are lint findings. They are review questions, not failures. They include deny_scope_unlogged above, no_tests for a file with no tests, grantless_subject, api_rights for each subject that holds an api: list, group_subject, acknowledge_stale, dead_rule, fallback_exposure and the projection reports. Read them; they are what a reviewer would ask.

docs.title: port49 policy diff
docs.text:
port49 policy diff --old main-policy.yaml --new policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml

Run it in CI on every pull request that touches the policy (Run the checks in CI). It compares the two files for every subject on every device, over every command shape the rules distinguish, now and at every later grant expiry. It prints each change, and exits 1 on a widening that no test or acknowledgment accounts for.

These labels fail the run. Writing tests shows the test that clears each one.

Label The change What clears it EXPANDS a command the old version refused with a deny, at a pipeline stage or on a quarantined device, that the new one permits a passing test with expect: permit on that command, on a device of that group RAISES a privilege level, priv_lvl, max_privilege ceiling or enable mechanism that went up, or a reply that changed a session test (no command:) asserting the new value REGEX-CONSTRAINED a permit with a regex or class term added, or a deny with one removed or rewritten a passing permit test on a command that rule decides, or an acknowledge: entry for a deny API api: rights added to a subject a session test with api: listing the subject's whole list PRINCIPAL, USERNAME an identity that now resolves to another subject, or a username: that changed a session test naming the principal per_login_mfa_weakened a per_login_mfa requirement removed or loosened on a device a session test asserting the new requirement that is new or changed against the old file; a test carried over unchanged does not count SUBJECT a subject's group: or machine_group: changed, or a new group subject was added a session test naming the subject ADAPTER an edit to a platform adapter key that changes what port49 decides an acknowledge: entry (below) QUARANTINES, REFUSED, UNRESOLVED a device newly quarantined, a mint or admission newly refused, a composition the diff could not compare fix the cause; no test clears these

A test that expects deny never acknowledges a widening. The last line of the output counts each kind. A lowering, such as a narrower permit or a dropped right, prints and passes.

docs.title: acknowledge:
docs.text:
Some widenings have no command to flip. A deny rewritten wider, such as /^(wri|rel)/ ** as /^wri/ **, frees commands the diff cannot list. An adapter edit changes what port49 reads. The author acknowledges these in writing, in a top-level block that review reads beside the change:

acknowledge:
  - {role: guard, rule: "/^(wri|rel)/ **", reason: "rewritten as /^wri/: rel* commands are allowed on purpose"}
  - {platform: juniper_junos, field: rpc_entry_denies, sha256: <sha256>, reason: "moved to set 1.2.0"}

There are two kinds of entry:

  • A role and rule entry names the exact removed or rewritten rule.
  • A platform, field and sha256 entry names the digest policy diff prints for the key's new value, so it covers that edit and no later one.

reason is required in both. An entry that matches nothing is reported as acknowledge_stale and acknowledges nothing; delete it. Do not use acknowledge: for an ordinary expansion: a literal deny removed is cleared by a test, and an entry for it is reported stale.

docs.title: The ceiling line
docs.text:
session ceiling: netops on 1 devices: 8h0m0s or the default, whichever is less -> 24h0m0s (may lengthen: depends on session.max_session_age_default)

The session ceiling: line says that a subject's max_session_age changed: the least of its roles' values, on how many devices, from what to what. It prints and does not fail the run, because a longer session is not a wider permission. It is what you read when a change touches max_session_age.

A lengthened ceiling reaches live sessions only when they refresh. This line is not the max_privilege ceiling: a raise of that is a RAISES and fails.

docs.title: A new grant is a reviewer's call: the gate does not see it
docs.text:
The gate judges commands that a deny, a pipeline stage or a quarantine used to refuse. A new grant is none of those. A subject that had no grant on a device and now has one gets a single line,

access: netops gains every grant on leaf1, leaf2

and the diff exits 0. A new role on a device the subject already reaches is a widens: line per command shape (widens: netops on leaf1: "ping length" was no_rule_matched, now permitted by "ping *" (extra)), and that exits 0 too. No test is demanded for either.

Who gets access to what is a decision for the person reviewing the pull request. Read every access: and widens: line, and run port49 access review --policy FILE --inventory FILE --subject NAME to see one subject's grants, how many devices each reaches and when each expires.

Only a grant to an existing, unchanged subject is ungated. The gate still catches:
