  • a new group: or machine_group: subject, whatever its grants: it exits 1 on a SUBJECT: NAME's none -> group ... line until a session test names the subject (a new identity: subject is a PRINCIPAL);
  • a grant that adds api: rights;
  • a new identity for an existing subject, or a changed group;
  • a per_login_mfa weakening that no new or changed session test asserts;
  • a privilege raise on a device the subject already reached.

docs.title: Run the checks in CI
docs.text:
Run both checks in the CI of the repository that holds your policy, so a failed check blocks the merge:

  • port49 policy test on every change.
  • port49 policy diff on every pull request, with --old taken from the branch the pull request merges into (git show origin/main:policy.yaml > /tmp/old-policy.yaml) and --new the pull request's file.

Both exit 1 on a failure (and 2 on a usage error), so any nonzero exit fails the job. Neither reads a secret or asks a broker, so the job needs no credentials. Here is a GitHub Actions job; any CI that can run a shell works the same way:

name: policy
on: pull_request
jobs:
  policy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
      - name: Install port49
        env:
          PORT49_VERSION: "0.1.0"
        run: |
          base="https://github.com/blanketfish/port49/releases/download/v${PORT49_VERSION}"
          cd "$RUNNER_TEMP"
          curl -fsSLO "${base}/port49_${PORT49_VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
          curl -fsSLO "${base}/SHA256SUMS"
          sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
          tar -xzf "port49_${PORT49_VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" port49
          echo "$RUNNER_TEMP" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
          "$RUNNER_TEMP/port49" --version
      - name: port49 policy test
        run: port49 policy test --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml
      - name: port49 policy diff
        run: |
          git fetch --depth=1 origin "$GITHUB_BASE_REF"
          git show FETCH_HEAD:policy.yaml > "$RUNNER_TEMP/old-policy.yaml"
          port49 policy diff --old "$RUNNER_TEMP/old-policy.yaml" --new policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml

The install step pins a release and checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS; raise PORT49_VERSION when you upgrade. Install the clients has the same steps for a workstation. In the worked example, this job fails the pull request that deletes the deny at its policy test step, and passes once the test is turned around.

docs.title: port49 policy replay
docs.text:
port49 policy replay [--line N] [--policy FILE --inventory FILE] decisions.jsonl

It re-runs the decisions in a decision log against the policy blob each record carries. Use it to check that this build still decides as the build that wrote the record did, or to audit a past decision.

It prints each record that diverged and a summary, replayed N records: A agree, D diverge, U unverifiable; S not replayed, and exits 1 if any diverged or could not be verified. A record denied before policy ran is counted and not replayed.

  • With --policy and --inventory, it rebuilds a blob a redacted record hid.
  • With --line N, it replays one record and prints it either way.
  • Give - instead of a file to read the log from standard input.

docs.title: port49 explain
docs.text:
explain answers one hypothetical question: what would port49 decide for this subject, on this device, for this command?

port49 explain --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml --subject netops --device leaf1 \
  --command "configure terminal"

deny no_rule_matched
  subject     netops
  device      leaf1 (arista_eos)
  grants      dc_fabric [read_only]
  roles       read_only
  level       readonly; max_privilege none
  session     max_session_age 8h0m0s (the least of its roles')
  per_login_mfa none
  command     configure terminal
  rule        no permit matches
  permitted by none
note: arista_eos does not declare config_commands: whether a command typed in configuration mode is sent to port49 at all is unmeasured, so if this is a configuration-mode command the device may apply it whatever this answer says (spec §9, §12)

It prints exactly one reason from the reason codes, and, for a denial, names the role that would permit the command. It exits 0 whether the answer is permit or deny; a nonzero exit means a policy or a name did not load.

Leave out --command to see the session instead, and add --show-attributes to see each session attribute and where it came from.

explain also tells you when the platform cannot enforce the control you asked about, rather than reporting a decision the device will not honor. On a platform that authorizes sessions only, the note says that a session ceiling, a revocation, a username change and the session-ceiling warning act at the next authorization request:

  • On Junos (juniper_junos), the device makes one after login only if authorization-time-interval is set. With it set, Junos asked again once an interval after login, a revoked principal was denied there, and the denial did not end the session (L36-juniper_vjunos-router.md, L36-juniper_vsrx.md). On a projected Junos the note also names what ends an idle session: the class idle-timeout that port49 platform export --classes renders from max_session_age.
  • On any other session-only platform, the device is not known to make one after login, and the note says not to rely on these controls there.

Unmeasured: a second re-authorization

Whether Junos re-authorizes an open session more than once, so whether a control made after the first ever reaches it, is unknown (L40, open). Do not rely on these controls to end a live Junos session.

With neither --policy nor --inventory, explain asks the broker through your agent, from the policy in force: port49 explain --device leaf1 --command "show version". Explaining another person with --principal needs api: [explain_others]. The broker's explain records carry hypothetical verdicts, so a dashboard of denials should filter event!="explain".

docs.title: Platform sets
docs.text:
The shipped adapters say what each platform's reply looks like, which commands it sends and how its privilege is rendered. They come in numbered platform sets, and your policy pins one with platform_set:.

A policy that pins none renders with 1.0.0 on every later binary, so upgrading port49 never changes what a policy renders. port49 platform list and show print the newest set unless you pass --set or the policy.

Only juniper_junos differs between the sets; the other shipped adapters are the same in every one.

Set What it adds 1.0.0 The first set. Junos is session-only and no level is rendered. 1.1.0 Junos renders your command rules into the session reply (command_projection: junos_regex): permission bits with each bit's reach, carve-outs and the smallest bits a grant needs. 1.2.0 rpc_entry_denies: ["junoscript **", "op **"] on Junos. Where a deny is the only guard beneath a sent bit, the reply adds these denies, which close the CLI's xml-mode and op url routes into a native RPC and that session's NETCONF. 1.3.0 deny_reach_bits: [view-configuration] on Junos. A reply may send the view-configuration bit where the grant permits a carve-out of it, with the rest of the bit's reach denied on the wire. It is read only where rpc_entry_denies is kept.

The routes rpc_entry_denies closes, and the bits deny_reach_bits covers, were measured on the two Junos images the Junos page lists, and the evidence table there links each note.

Unmeasured

Whether the junoscript deny also closes REST, the XML API, outbound-ssh and scp is unknown (L59, open), and so is what these replies do on a Junos release or hardware family the lab did not run. Test a policy on the device before you rely on it there.

docs.title: port49 platform upgrade
docs.text:
A moved pin changes what the policy renders, so moving it is a reviewed change. Do not edit platform_set by hand; run:

port49 platform upgrade --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml --to 1.3.0

It prints exactly what the move changes:

  • each adapter key that differs on a platform your inventory has, and how many devices and subjects it reaches;
  • the acknowledge: entry each gated key needs, ready to paste;
  • each key a platforms: block keeps its own value for while the built-in under it changes;
  • what the move would quarantine or fail closed.

For a policy pinned to 1.1.0 and an inventory with one Junos device, the move to 1.3.0 prints:

platform_set 1.1.0 -> 1.3.0
  platforms.juniper_junos.rpc_entry_denies
    null -> ["junoscript **","op **"]
    affects 1 devices, 0 subjects
    gated: add {platform: juniper_junos, field: rpc_entry_denies, sha256: <sha256>, reason: "..."} under acknowledge:
  platforms.juniper_junos.deny_reach_bits
    null -> ["view-configuration"]
    affects 1 devices, 0 subjects
    gated: add {platform: juniper_junos, field: deny_reach_bits, sha256: <sha256>, reason: "..."} under acknowledge:
  port49 policy diff fails on the move until every gated entry above is under acknowledge: (spec §12); it also shows the replies the move changes

(The <sha256> placeholders stand for the 64-character digests the tool prints; copy them from your own run.)

It writes nothing unless you add --write, which rewrites the pin in the file and nothing else. Then:

  1. Commit the policy.
  2. Let port49 policy diff show the replies the move changes.
  3. Add the acknowledge: entries it asks for, each with a reason a reviewer can read.

The diff fails on the move until each gated key is acknowledged.

docs.title: Revoking access
docs.text: Revocation explains what happens, in order, and what it cannot do. This page is the runbook: the commands, what each one needs, how to read the answer, and the broker settings that check your CA's revocation lists.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
port49 revoke talks to the broker through your own agent, so run port49 login first. It needs your subject to declare the right in the policy's api: list:

  • revoke_others to revoke another principal, a certificate, a (device, username) key or an OIDC session, and to list what is in force;
  • lift_revocations to lift a revocation, and to list.

Every write but --mine also asks for a press of your security key, bound to that one request. Without the right the call is refused before any key press, and the refusal is logged. Your own sessions, with port49 revoke --mine, need neither a right nor a touch.

docs.title: Revoking
docs.text:
You want to stop Run Leaves a standing mark a person or workload, everywhere port49 revoke --principal user:alice@example.com yes one certificate port49 revoke --cert alice.pem yes whoever holds one device login port49 revoke --device leaf1 --username alice no one OIDC session port49 revoke --sid <sid> --sid-issuer <issuer> no your own sessions port49 revoke --mine no

On a terminal, --principal asks revoke <principal> everywhere? ... [y/N] first. --yes skips the question, and a script with no terminal is not asked.

The answer begins with a target: line naming the policy subject the principal belongs to. If it says no subject in the policy in force names it, check the spelling. The mark is written anyway, so a typo of a real colleague's address is a revocation of nobody. The broker spells principals this way:

  • a certificate's principal: user:<lower-case email>;
  • a workload's: its SPIFFE ID, verbatim;
  • a service account's: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

port49 revoke --list shows what is in force, each with its origin (api <who> for an operator, crl <name> or ocsp <responder> for a CA's revocation). A --mine, --device or --sid revocation leaves no mark, so it is not listed; the decision log's revoke record names each, with revocation.by of self, key or a logout.

A revocation does not expire. The agent reconnects with the same key on its own, so only a lift undoes it.

docs.title: --cert over --cert-serial
docs.text:
Name a certificate by file:

port49 revoke --cert alice.pem

port49 revoke reads the issuer and serial out of the file, and prints them before anything is sent, so you see whose certificate it is:

port49 revoke: alice.pem: subject "CN=alice,O=Example", issuer "CN=Example Issuing CA,O=Example", serial 0x2a

The file must hold one certificate, PEM or DER. One that holds a private key, more than one certificate (a chain would revoke the CA's serial and say it did) or more than 1 MiB is refused. The command never prints a key or a block.

The by-hand form is --cert-issuer DN --cert-serial HEX, both required, and it is the one to avoid. Use --cert-serial only when you have no file, for instance a serial copied from your CA's issuance log. Two things go wrong with it:

  • The issuer must be spelled as Go prints it (RFC 2253, CN=Example Issuing CA,O=Example). A differently spelled issuer matches nothing, and the report says so (nothing was found under this certificate; ... use --cert FILE).
  • The serial is hexadecimal. Colons, a 0x and leading zeros are dropped and a leading - is kept. A serial of digits alone is read as hex, though openssl prints a small serial in decimal first (4096 (0x1000)). The report warns when that may have happened: revoke again with --cert FILE, then lift the wrong one.

--cert sends the serial as explicit hex and cannot make that mistake.

A certificate revocation closes that certificate's held connections, deletes unspent tokens and marks its live contexts. It leaves the principal's other certificates working, with one exception: unspent tokens are deleted by (device, username), so the other certificates lose theirs on those devices and can mint again.

A workload renews its certificate under a new serial the mark does not name. For a workload, revoke the principal too, and revoke the certificate at your CA so it cannot renew.

docs.title: A stolen laptop
docs.text:
Revoke in this order:

  1. port49 revoke --principal user:alice@example.com now. It stops every mint, closes the person's held connections and refuses the agent's next request.

  2. Close the device sessions. TACACS+ cannot disconnect a device's session, so a revocation takes effect at the next authorization request. A platform that asks port49 only at login never asks again, so the revocation reaches a context nobody reads. The report names those sessions:

    not reached, on a platform that never asks port49 about a command (close these on the device): leaf1 (alice), srx2 (alice)

    Close each on the device with the device's own tools, and see Junos for what it does on its own. 3. When your CA has issued the person a new certificate, revoke the old one by --cert (or revoke it at the CA, below) and lift the principal.

Close a stranger's session too. --mine and --device/--username leave no mark, so the owner's next login on that device re-admits every session still open there under that username. The report says so.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Exit Meaning 0 done; --list printed 1 nothing was revoked, or it is unknown. Refused or unreachable: no agent, the right missing, the touch refused or not given, a declined confirmation (nothing was revoked), an unreadable or refused --cert file, or a broker refusal that says nothing was done. Unknown whether it ran: the broker did not answer (the broker did not answer ...), it answered with no revocation named (the broker's answer named no revocation; it may be in force), it answered 503 revocation_unconfirmed (the broker could not confirm it: ...), or a revoke got 503 store_unavailable (the broker says: ...). The first two say to run port49 revoke --list and look at the decision log before you retry; for the last two, read the broker's words 2 the flags are wrong: no target, two targets, or a flag that does not go with the form 3 the revocation is in force but incomplete, or not saved to the revocations file, or a lift step did not finish: run the same command again, which repeats every step

Exit 1 is two different things, so read the line. A refusal that says nothing was done means nothing happened; it may be in force means it may have. Two broker answers look like refusals and are not:

  • the broker could not confirm it (503 revocation_unconfirmed): the revocation may have gone through, and so may a lift made meanwhile. Run port49 revoke --list to see what is in force, then repeat the command if the mark is not what you wanted.
  • the broker says: ... on a revoke that got 503 store_unavailable: the mark went nowhere but that one broker's own process, so the credential is revoked on that broker and not, yet, on the others. Do what the broker's words say to make the mark everywhere, and run the revoke again once the store is back.

Exit 3 is never a failure to revoke: the mark stands and refuses every new mint, but until a run finishes, unspent tokens may still log in (up to their TTL) and unmarked contexts keep authorizing. port49 revoke --lift takes the same codes; an answer with no text exits 1 with it may have run.

docs.title: Lifting
docs.text:
port49 revoke --lift --principal user:alice@example.com
port49 revoke --lift --cert alice.pem

A lift needs lift_revocations and a touch. It restores nothing: contexts the revocation marked stay revoked until a login with a token minted after the lift joins them. --lift --principal on a principal that is not revoked answers no such revocation is in force.

Lifting a mark a CA made. A mark whose origin is crl <name> or ocsp <responder> was written because the CA revoked the certificate. The person is told the certificate was revoked at its CA and to request a new one; no lift is offered. You can still run --lift --cert, but it is no fix: the next connection checks the CA again and is refused, or, with the list gone stale, answered certificate_status_unavailable, or admitted under on_unavailable: allow. Lift such a mark only after the CA has unrevoked the certificate, and expect it to be marked again if the CA's list still names it. A certificateHold entry is never marked.

docs.title: Where marks are kept
docs.text:
A standing mark is in the session store and is read by every broker. How it survives a restart depends on the shape:

  • A broker on etcd (the normal split) keeps each mark in the store, and each broker keeps a copy in broker.state_dir, which is what puts a mark back after a store restore. Back that directory up and follow Backup and restore; it also covers port49-broker revoke --offline for revoking with every broker down.
  • A single-process port49d on the memory store also writes every mark to broker.revocations_file. port49d never creates that file, so run port49d init-revocations once at install, as port49d's user (see Install); a missing file refuses every start.

When a revocation was made but the file could not be written, the report says NOT saved to broker.revocations_file, port49 revoke exits 3, and port49_revocations_file_failed is 1. Run the revoke again once the disk is fixed, and see Revocations file failed.

docs.title: Checking your CA's revocation lists
docs.text:
A revocation made at your CA reaches port49 only if the broker is told where to look.

certificate_status is required wherever a client certificate verifier is configured: in the broker block, and in the tls_listener block for devices on RFC 9887 TLS. Leaving it out refuses the config, so skipping the check is always a choice you wrote down.

The device side is on TLS. The broker side, which covers the certificates people and workloads sign in with, looks like this:

broker:
  certificate_status:
    crls:
      - name: corp_ca
        url: http://crl.example.com/corp-ca.crl
        issuer_file: /etc/port49/corp-ca.pem
    # ocsp: {use_aia: true}
    refresh_interval: 10m
    on_unavailable: refuse

To check nothing, write it out:

broker:
  certificate_status:
    disabled: true

disabled: true takes no other key, and port49d says so at every start: certificate status checking is disabled (broker.certificate_status.disabled): a certificate revoked at its CA keeps minting untilport49 revoke --cert`. With it, onlyport49 revoke` ends a certificate.

Otherwise name at least one crls entry or an ocsp block. A CRL is a file or an http(s) url (exactly one), a unique name (lowercase letters, digits and _), and an issuer_file. The lists are fetched or re-read every refresh_interval (10 minutes by default, 1 minute to 24 hours). An OCSP block takes a fixed responder or use_aia: true, and hash: sha1 for a responder that knows no SHA-256 CertID. All keys are in the port49d reference.

docs.title: issuer_file rules
docs.text:
issuer_file is required on every CRL, and it is the CA certificate that signs that list. A list is trusted for the issuer it names, so port49d checks the file at start and refuses to start, naming the source, unless:

  • it holds exactly one PEM block, a certificate, and nothing else;
  • it is a CA certificate, since only a CA signs a list;
  • it is the trust anchor (client_ca_file, or the x509 trust anchor of a workload verifier) or a certificate that anchor signed, since a list for an issuer the broker does not already trust would vouch for certificates it never trusted.

A list is then used only if it verifies against that certificate: signed by it, with an issuer name encoded exactly as the certificate's subject is, an authority key identifier that matches, not dated in the future and not signed with a weak algorithm. A delta CRL, a list with a critical extension port49 does not understand, or one scoped in a way its certificates do not name is refused, and counted at port49_crl_loads_total{outcome="refused"}; the log says why.

An intermediate CA needs the root's list too. Name the root's CRL (issuer_file is your client_ca_file anchor), or every certificate under the intermediate is refused: port49d checks each CA in the chain, and nothing else says whether the intermediate itself was revoked. An OCSP responder the root signs for covers it as well. At start port49d says which CA nothing covers, as certificates issued by <CA> will be refused ...: nothing covers <CA> itself; name the root CA's CRL, and never refuses to start over it. That is the on_unavailable: refuse line; under allow it reads certificates issued by <CA> will be admitted with their revocation status unchecked (on_unavailable: allow): nothing covers <CA> itself; name the root CA's CRL, and those certificates are let in.

Each verified list is kept as crl-<name>.der in broker.state_dir (beside broker.revocations_file for a single-process port49d), so a restart during a publisher outage keeps serving it until its next update. Back these up with the rest of the state.

docs.title: on_unavailable: refuse
docs.text:
When a certificate's status cannot be established, because a CRL is past its next update or an OCSP responder is down, on_unavailable decides:

  • refuse (the default): the broker answers 503 certificate_status_unavailable with Retry-After: 60, the reason trust_domain_unresolved. The agent is told to try again, and nothing is minted for that certificate until the status is known.
  • allow (fail-open): the connection is admitted and the broker says so (admitting a certificate whose revocation status cannot be established). It keeps logins working through an outage, and lets a certificate revoked during the outage in until the list returns. It is the reviewed escape, not a setting to leave on.

An uncovered status, with no CRL or OCSP source for that issuer, follows the same setting. Under refuse it is refused too, and it holds until a source covers it, so retrying does not help; add the CRL. Under allow, a certificate from an issuer nothing covers is admitted with its revocation status unchecked, like any other unavailable status: that is a fail-open case, and the start line quoted under the issuer_file rules is the warning.

What the broker refuses and what it marks:

  • A certificate a CRL or OCSP lists as revoked, or one under a revoked issuing CA, is refused with credential_revoked at login and at every mint.
  • If the certificate holds anything (a connection, a device session, an unspent token), port49d also marks it as port49 revoke --cert would, with origin crl <name> or ocsp <responder>, so its live contexts are revoked and its tokens deleted. A revoked issuing CA is refused and not marked.
  • Freshness follows the broker's clock, so an NTP step forward can make a fresh list stale. Keep time synchronized on every broker host.

Watch port49_crl_next_update_timestamp_seconds (an hour before a list passes its next update, at time() - port49_crl_next_update_timestamp_seconds > -3600), port49_cert_status_unavailable_total and port49_crl_loads_total; they carry a component label of broker or tls_listener. They are in the metrics reference, and the TLS alerts on the alerts reference.

docs.title: Roles and grants
docs.text:
Three blocks of the policy file decide who gets what:

  • A role is what may be done: command rules, a privilege level, optional attributes, a session length and an optional per-login proof.
  • A subject is who.
  • A grant gives a subject some roles in a scope.

The whole vocabulary is in the policy reference. How rules are written, how to test them and how a change is reviewed is on Policy.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
roles:
  - name: read_only
    privilege: readonly
    permit: ["show **", "terminal length *"]
    max_session_age: 8h
  - name: bgp_operator
    privilege: operator
    permit: ["show bgp **", "clear bgp neighbor **"]
    deny: ["clear bgp all"]
    per_login_mfa: {accept: [hardware_key_touch]}
  • privilege names a level from privilege_levels:. readonly, operator and admin always exist and keep that order. You may add levels with a parent:: the level a platform renders the new one as where it has no rendering of its own.
  • baseline, reach_deny and rpc_entry are port49's own rule names, so a role may not be called any of them. A policy that does is refused at load; rename the role.
  • A role's permit and deny lists follow the rules on Policy.
  • attributes: adds attribute strings to the reply, per platform or under all. A grant may add its own.

docs.title: max_session_age
docs.text:
max_session_age is how long a person's session on a device may last: a duration of at least 1m, or never. It is set per role, and a session's ceiling is the least of the roles that compose on that device.

  • A role that says nothing takes session.max_session_age_default from port49d.yaml (12 hours unless you set it).
  • A max_session_age: with no value is refused.
  • If every role says never, so does the session.

port49 explain prints the result for a subject and device:

Line Meaning max_session_age 8h0m0s (the least of its roles') every role names a duration; this is the least max_session_age the lesser of 8h0m0s and session.max_session_age_default one role names no value max_session_age session.max_session_age_default (no role names a finite one) the default decides max_session_age never (every role says never) no ceiling

Shortening a role reaches live sessions at the next policy refresh. Lengthening it, or choosing never, reaches a person's sessions only when they run port49 refresh or log in again. port49 policy diff prints a session ceiling: line for the change; see Policy.

docs.title: Subjects
docs.text:
A subject is exactly one of three things, and never a mix:

Form Who it names Needs group: a directory group of people, by name or DN broker.directory configured machine_group: a group of workloads, by name or DN a workload certificate verifier whose directory maps the workload to an entry identity: one or more literal principals: user:<email>, a SPIFFE ID, system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, or app:<client_id> nothing 
subjects:
  - name: netops
    group: "cn=netops,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
    token_ttl: 300s
  - name: ci_runners
    machine_group: "cn=ci-runners,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
    token_ttl: 120s
  - name: svc_backup
    identity: ["system:serviceaccount:netops:backup"]
    username: svc-config-backup
    token_ttl: 60s

A subject that has both group: and machine_group:, or either one with identity:, is refused. A subject is one trust domain, so a person and a workload each get their own:

  • a person never matches a machine_group: subject;
  • a workload never matches a group: subject;
  • attached_roles.machines reaches the machine domain alone.

token_ttl (30 to 900 seconds) is required on any subject a grant names.

docs.title: machine_group:
docs.text:
A machine_group: is the machine-side twin of group:: it names a group in the directory, but its members are workloads. The broker resolves a workload through the verifier's directory mapping (broker.identity.machines[].directory) and matches it to the subjects whose group it is in. With no mapping configured, a machine_group: subject mints for no one, and port49d's start says so.

A machine_group: subject declares no username:, and one that does is refused: one name for many workloads would put them all in one device login. Its members take the username their own entry gives, or the one an identity: subject listing the same SPIFFE ID declares. See Workloads.

docs.title: Usernames
docs.text:
The device sees a username, not a principal.

  • For a person, the directory supplies it. A group: subject, and an identity: subject for a user: principal, declare none when broker.directory is on.
  • For a machine, a literal identity declares one (username: svc-config-backup above): lowercase and printable ASCII, and never remote, a p49- name or a platform's system user.
  • A subject whose identities are all SPIFFE IDs may leave it out where the directory mapping supplies one. An offline run cannot know whether it does, so port49 policy test reports it as workload_no_username.

docs.title: api: rights
docs.text:
A principal may always mint for itself, end its own sessions (port49 revoke --mine) and explain its own decisions. Acting on other people is a right the subject declares:

subjects:
  - name: netops_oncall
    group: "cn=netops-oncall,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
    token_ttl: 300s
    api: [revoke_others, explain_others]
Right Lets the subject Needs a key press revoke_others revoke another principal, a certificate, a (device, username) key or an OIDC session; list the revocations yes, except the list lift_revocations lift a revocation by principal or certificate; list the revocations yes, except the list explain_others port49 explain --principal another person no forget_principals forget a principal's directory pin yes reset_second_factor reset one principal's second factor, or everyone's yes unlock_sign_in unlock a locked sign-in yes import_enrollments import the enrollment store yes sync, keys_show, replay nothing yet: reserved, declared and reported, granting nothing until an endpoint exists n/a

An admin-level right also needs a press of the person's security key, bound to that one call. An exposed certificate or agent session alone therefore authorizes nothing admin-level. On a broker with no attestation roots loaded, every admin call is refused; see Hardware keys. A right withdrawn by a policy reload is gone at the next call.

An api: list reads like a grant of authority over other people's sessions, and CI treats it as one:

  • port49 policy test prints a report: api_rights line per subject and names the admin-level ones.
  • port49 policy diff fails on a subject that gains a right until a session test asserts the subject's whole list (see Writing tests):
tests:
  - {subject: netops_oncall, device: leaf1, api: [revoke_others, explain_others]}

A right the subject loses passes. A principal moved to a subject with more rights needs that assertion in a test that names the principal.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
grants:
  - {subject: netops, scope: dc_fabric, roles: [read_only]}
  - {subject: netops_oncall, scope: dc_fabric, roles: [bgp_operator], max_privilege: admin, expires: "2026-12-01"}

A grant names a declared subject and scope and at least one role, each listed once. Two grants with the same subject, scope and roles are refused, so merge them.

  • expires is a date (the start of that day, UTC) or an RFC 3339 time, after which the grant stops matching. port49 policy diff and policy test read the policy at every later expiry as well as now.
  • max_privilege is a ceiling on the level a token from the grant may carry, which is how far enable may take the session. With no enable on the subject, nothing escalates to it. The subject's enable is none (the default), auto or token.

A grant on a scope that is on_missing: include is refused (a scope with no match key, or pinned by name alone, is the exception); see Policy.

When one person matches several subjects, the grants of all of them compose:

What How it composes roles the union level the highest of the roles ceiling (max_privilege) the highest across the grants max_session_age the least

Reordering grants never changes a decision.

docs.title: per_login_mfa
docs.text:
A policy may ask for a second factor at each login to the devices it marks. This is a proof at the device login, not the daily sign-in. Write it as per_login_mfa: on defaults:, a role or a scope:

defaults:
  per_login_mfa: {accept: [hardware_key_touch, idp_mfa], reuse_for: 15m}
scopes:
  - name: core
    match: {tier: core}
    on_missing: include             # the requirement holds on a device the inventory cannot describe
    security_log: true
    per_login_mfa: {accept: [hardware_key_touch], reuse_for: 5m}
  - name: core_access
    match: {tier: core}
    on_missing: exclude             # the grant is earned by data

The scope that carries the requirement is include, so a device whose tier is missing is still held to it. A grant on an include scope is refused at load, so the grant goes on core_access, a second scope with the same match (grants: [{subject: netops, scope: core_access, roles: [read_only]}]). For a policy with those two scopes and a device core1 with tier: core, port49 policy test prints, with nothing about per_login_mfa:

platform_set: 1.0.0
keys: checked against the default key_secret_refs (env: variables starting PORT49_KEY_, file: under /run/port49/keys); pass --config to check port49d.yaml's
report: group_subject: subject "netops" is a group: subject: it mints only with broker.directory configured, through which the broker matches a person to the group; explain and policy tests evaluate it by name
PASS netops on core1: "show version" -> permit permit_dominates
1 tests, 0 failed; 0 shadowed denies, 0 unacknowledged; 0 quarantined, 0 projection refusals

port49 explain on core1 still prints the requirement, per_login_mfa accept hardware_key_touch (defaults ∩ scope core); reuse_for 5m (scope core); applies to humans.

Do not put the requirement on an on_missing: exclude scope to be able to grant on it. port49 policy test reports that shape as per_login_mfa_on_missing_exclude: a sync that drops tier lifts the per-login proof from the device.

docs.title: The keys
docs.text:
• accept is a list of hardware_key_touch (a touch on the token holding the session key), idp_mfa (a fresh identity-provider sign-in showing a second factor) or both. Leaving the block out means no requirement; there is no none.
  • reuse_for is how long one proof covers later logins, from 0m (a proof at every login) to 8h, and 15m when left out.

docs.title: When several levels set it
docs.text:
The levels stack and the strictest wins. On a device the requirement is the intersection of the accept lists of every level that applies, with the least reuse_for. A lower level never weakens a higher one, and an empty intersection is a load error naming both levels.

A scope that selects by an attribute other than name must declare on_missing and security_log: true, since whoever edits the attribute can lift the requirement. port49 policy test also reports per_login_mfa_on_missing_exclude where an exclude scope could lose it. A scope pinned by name needs neither.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: A machine principal is exempt except under a level that sets applies_to_machines: true. A workload proves with hardware_key_touch alone, from a key and touch slot on one token.

docs.title: What a login sees
docs.text:
• A mint under an unmet requirement is answered deny with the reason per_login_mfa_required and a challenge.
  • A requirement that no method this broker can verify satisfies is per_login_mfa_unavailable for that device.
  • A requirement gates logins and refreshes, never a live session: adding one revokes nothing.

docs.title: Reviewing a change
docs.text:
port49 policy diff fails, as per_login_mfa_weakened, on a weakening that no session test asserts. The test must be new or changed against the old file; one carried over unchanged does not count. Widening the scope above to accept: [hardware_key_touch, idp_mfa] prints this and exits 1:

per_login_mfa_weakened: netops on core1: accept [hardware_key_touch] reuse_for 5m (defaults ∩ scope core) -> accept [hardware_key_touch, idp_mfa] reuse_for 5m (defaults ∩ scope core); no session test asserts it: add {subject: netops, device: core1, per_login_mfa: {accept: [hardware_key_touch, idp_mfa], reuse_for: 5m}}

The line ends with the session test to add; Writing tests covers the keys.

docs.title: Reading why a grant applied
docs.text:
Offline, port49 explain shows the subject, the grants that matched, the roles (and which scope attached each), the level, the ceiling, the session age and the per_login_mfa requirement for one device, with the reason a command was permitted or denied:

port49 explain --policy policy.yaml --inventory inventory.yaml --subject netops --device leaf1

Signed in, port49 identity prints whom the broker resolves you to (your subject, grants, api: rights) and port49 explain --device NAME asks the broker the same question from the policy in force. The per_login_mfa line reads, for example, per_login_mfa accept hardware_key_touch (defaults ∩ scope core); reuse_for 5m (scope core); applies to humans, or per_login_mfa none: the default is never invisible.

For a review, port49 access review --policy FILE --inventory FILE --subject NAME prints one subject's grant table, with the roles, ceiling, expiry and device count per row.

To offboard a machine subject or a literal identity, use port49 grants remove --subject NAME:

  • by itself, it prints the policy without the subject's grants and its block;
  • --write replaces the file;
  • --pr opens the pull request that carries the removal.

The result must load against the inventory before anything is written. People in a directory group are offboarded in the directory.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text:
A workload is a program that logs in to devices without a person: a configuration backup, a compliance check, a deployment job. It needs an identity of its own so that its access is granted, logged and revoked on its own, not borrowed from a person's. port49 knows two kinds:

Identity Proof Principal Use it when A workload certificate an x509 certificate with a SPIFFE ID in a URI SAN, from a CA you run spiffe://<trust domain>/<path> the job runs on a host you manage, such as a cron job or a backup server A Kubernetes service account token the pod's projected token, checked against the cluster's published keys system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> the job runs in a cluster, and you want no CA and no secret at rest

Either is a peer of the other, and neither is required. The concepts are on Identities and Trust domains; how a workload becomes a subject, and why it gets its own device login, is on Roles and grants.

The workload anchor and the people's anchor must be in unrelated hierarchies, so that nothing a workload CA signs can be read as a person.

docs.title: Workload certificates and step-ca
docs.text:
The worked example is Oxidized, the configuration backup tool, with step-ca as the workload CA. The same shape fits any job on a host: the host holds a certificate valid for a few hours, a renewal timer replaces it, and the broker verifies it against the CA you name.

Four rules carry the design:

  1. The workload CA is the trust root, and it is yours. The broker's broker.identity.machines entry names the CA's certificate (trust_anchor_file) and the SPIFFE trust domains it may speak for (spiffe_trust_domains). Anyone who can get that CA to sign a certificate with a SPIFFE ID inside those domains is that workload.
  2. Give each host its own provisioner, with the SPIFFE ID fixed in the provisioner's template (uris), so a host can only ever obtain its own name. A shared provisioner lets any enrolled host ask for another's.

  3. The certificate must name the CA's CRL. port49 applies step-ca's CRL, which carries a critical issuing distribution point, only to a certificate whose CRL distribution points name it exactly. A certificate without that name is undecided, and the broker refuses it with 503 certificate_status_unavailable (under broker.certificate_status.on_unavailable: refuse, the default; allow would admit it and say so).

    The template below adds the extension. Replace its URL with the name your CA's CRL carries (crl.idpURL when set, otherwise https://<the first of ca.json's dnsNames>/1.0/crl) and check it with step crl inspect. This was measured on step-ca (L48).

  4. For an immediate stop, use port49 revoke (Revocation) rather than waiting for the CA's CRL to be republished and read.

The provisioner's template, step-ca-workload.tpl, is step's default leaf with clientAuth alone and the one addition:

{{- /*
  step-ca x509 template for workload certificates (the provisioner's
  options.x509.templateFile). It is step's default leaf, with clientAuth alone
  and one addition: a CRL distribution point naming the CA's CRL.

  step-ca's CRL names its own distribution point in a critical issuing
  distribution point extension, and port49 applies that CRL only to a
  certificate whose CRL distribution points name it, byte for byte (RFC 5280
  §5.2.5; L48). A certificate without the name is undecided, and the broker
  refuses it (503 certificate_status_unavailable).

  Replace the URL below with the name in your CA's CRL: crl.idpURL when it is
  set, otherwise https://<the first of ca.json's dnsNames>/1.0/crl. Check it
  with `step crl inspect` (Issuing Distribution Point, Full Name).
*/ -}}
{
    "subject": {{ toJson .Subject }},
    "sans": {{ toJson .SANs }},
{{- if typeIs "*rsa.PublicKey" .Insecure.CR.PublicKey }}
    "keyUsage": ["keyEncipherment", "digitalSignature"],
{{- else }}
    "keyUsage": ["digitalSignature"],
{{- end }}
    "extKeyUsage": ["clientAuth"],
    "crlDistributionPoints": ["https://ca.corp.example.com/1.0/crl"]
}

The broker side is the verifier below; its keys are in the port49d reference. Nothing about the broker's TLS is special: workloads reach it over the same listener as everyone (TLS).

broker:
  identity:
    machines:
      - type: x509
        trust_anchor_file: /etc/port49/workload-ca.pem
        spiffe_trust_domains: ["example.com"]

Enrolling, renewing, the broker policy snippet, what port49 policy test says about it and what to do on a bad day are in the Oxidized guide at the end of this page. Its section 7a covers host keys: they are OpenSSH's job, and the guide uses accept-new and known_hosts.

docs.title: The workload directory
docs.text:
By default a workload's groups come only from the policy: a subject names the SPIFFE ID in identity: and the grant follows. At fleet scale you may want the other thing, a directory group of workloads, so that adding a host to cn=ci-runners grants it what the group has, with no policy edit. That is the machine_group: subject:

subjects:
  - name: ci_runners
    machine_group: "cn=ci-runners,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
  - name: svc_backup
    identity: ["spiffe://example.com/host/backup-01"]
    username: svc-backup

A machine_group: subject matches workloads only. It takes no username: (the name comes from the entry), and it never sits beside group: or identity: in one subject. port49 policy test says so when you write one (output re-run for the policy above, with a third subject, svc_mapped, that names a SPIFFE ID and no username):

report: group_subject: subject "ci_runners" is a machine_group: subject: it mints only with broker.identity.machines[].directory configured (a workload certificate's directory mapping), through which the broker matches a workload to the group; explain and policy tests evaluate it by name
report: workload_no_username: subject "svc_mapped" declares no username: it mints only under broker.identity.machines[].directory, where its entry's username_attribute names it

docs.title: Opting in
docs.text:
The broker finds a workload's entry through a directory: block on the machine verifier. It is off until you write it, and all four keys are required:

broker:
  identity:
    machines:
      - type: x509
        trust_anchor_file: /etc/port49/workload-ca.pem
        spiffe_trust_domains: ["example.com"]
        directory:
          kind: spiffe_id
          attribute: uid
          allow_weak: true
          issuers: ["CN=Example Workload CA,O=Example"]
  • kind: spiffe_id is the only kind. The entry holds the workload's SPIFFE ID in attribute.
  • attribute has no default, and it must not be the attribute broker.directory uses for username_attribute or principal_attribute: the config refuses it. Use uid or description. Never wWWHomePage or url on Active Directory: the entry itself can write those whatever the OU's ACL says, so a workload could put another workload's SPIFFE ID on itself. This was measured on a service account's entry (L50), and port49d says it at start if you choose one of them.
  • allow_weak: true acknowledges what the mapping is: a SPIFFE ID is matched by a lookup, not a signature, so it is only as strong as who can write attribute. It is required, with issuers, the RFC 4514 DNs of the CAs whose certificates this mapping accepts.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Every workload this verifier accepts then needs exactly one entry, those whose subject names them in identity: included. port49d prints it at start:

directory: workload certificates map by spiffe_id (weak, pinned to <issuers>) through <attribute> under <filter>; every workload this verifier accepts must have exactly one entry holding its SPIFFE ID: none is refused identity_unmapped, two or more identity_ambiguous, and while the directory is down past grace it is refused directory_unavailable

(Shortened here: the line goes on to name where the username comes from.) In the operator's terms:

Situation The workload sees What to do No entry holds its SPIFFE ID refused identity_unmapped add the entry, or the value to it Two entries hold it refused identity_ambiguous remove one The directory is down past grace refused directory_unavailable, and port49 workload exits 75 restore the directory; pre-warm keeps recently mapped workloads working until then The directory is down longer than session.staleness_ceiling live device sessions deny context_stale the same

Keep pre-warm on, since it is what lets a mapped workload mint through a short directory outage. A workload whose entry changed identity (a host rebuilt with a new directory entry, say) is released from its pin with port49 directory forget spiffe://example.com/host/backup-01. It is run through your agent and needs the forget_principals right and a press of your security key.

The workload's login name comes from the subject that lists its SPIFFE ID (username:), else from the entry's username_attribute. The entry needs a unique canonical one either way.

docs.title: Whoever writes attribute chooses the groups
docs.text:
Anyone who can write attribute on an entry decides which workload takes that entry's group memberships. So it must be writable only by directory administrators, and you should alert on writes to it: Windows event 5136 or 4662, and on Samba dsdb_json_audit at level 5. port49 prescribes no deny ACL; the measured behaviour is in the L50 note for Samba.

A person's entry is never a workload. An entry that holds a SPIFFE ID in attribute is refused as a person, and the reverse.

There is one window. Writing a SPIFFE ID onto a person's entry takes effect at the next directory refresh, whereas port49 revoke --principal user:<email> is immediate, so until the refresh the entry could serve both domains. Only a directory administrator can open that window, and that is the same person who could add the user to any group. If it happens, revoke the person, then fix the entry (Revocation).

The directory itself is configured under broker.directory; see Identity providers.

docs.title: Kubernetes service accounts
docs.text:
Nothing here makes a cluster necessary or preferred: it is the path for a job that already runs in one. The pod's projected token is the identity, with no CA to run and no secret at rest. The kubelet writes and rotates the token, and the broker verifies it against the cluster's published keys.

Unmeasured

Managed Kubernetes services (GKE, EKS, AKS) are unmeasured: whether their token issuers, discovery and key endpoints behave as the kind cluster did is unknown until they are measured (lab register entry L70, open). The Kubernetes guide below is measured on kind only; read each claim for the cell that backs it.

docs.title: The guides in full
docs.text:
Everything from here to the end of the page is two example READMEs verbatim, the Oxidized one first and the Kubernetes one after it. Each numbers its own sections from 1, so the second "1." below is the Kubernetes guide's "What it is". Section headings of the Oxidized guide run from "What runs where" to "What L49 measured, and what it did not".

Oxidized backs up network devices over SSH with a username and password. port49 gives it a short-lived token per device as that password, so no standing credential exists on the Oxidized host. Three files fit together:

  • port49-oxidized-run runs port49 workload token, writes Oxidized's router.db, and asks Oxidized to back each node up now.
  • config is Oxidized's configuration. It reads router.db, and its own interval is set a week out so that its schedule tries as few nodes as possible with an expired token. A try with a spent token cost one authentication, refused token_spent, on each of the five platforms (L49, phase B); how often Oxidized's own schedule still tries is not measured.
  • policy.yaml is the port49 policy: a config_backup role that confines the Oxidized host to show commands where port49 authorizes commands (see §5a).

docs.title: 1. What runs where
docs.text:
Oxidized and port49-oxidized-run run on one host, under one user. The workload certificate and its key are that user's files. Cron runs the wrapper once per backup window:

17 2 * * *  PORT49_BROKER=https://port49-broker.example.com:8443 PORT49_BROKER_CA=... \
            PORT49_CERT=... PORT49_KEY=... /usr/local/bin/port49-oxidized-run

The wrapper's environment is documented at the top of the script. OXIDIZED_NODES is a file of device names, one a line. PORT49_SCOPE names a policy scope in its place: the wrapper then asks port49 for every device the scope selects that this host holds a grant on, page by page, and reads no nodes file (policy engine spec §13 decision 42). A scope that selects nothing for this host, and a scope name that does not exist, both exit 77 with one message. L49 ran with a nodes file; a sweep was not part of it.

docs.title: 2. Enrollment, once
docs.text: Get a certificate whose one URI SAN is the host's SPIFFE ID (for example spiffe://corp.example.com/host/oxidized-01) from your workload CA. step-ca 0.30.2 is one such CA: a certificate requested with --san spiffe://… carries that ID as its one URI SAN, and a renewal keeps the ID and the key (L48, cells 1 and 2). Any CA that puts one URI SAN on a client certificate works. Its key is readable by the Oxidized user alone. On step-ca, issue it under step-ca-workload.tpl (§3 and §5).

docs.title: 3. The workload CA is the trust root
docs.text:
Whoever can get the workload CA to issue a certificate naming a SPIFFE ID is that workload to port49. spiffe_trust_domains does not stop one workload impersonating another within a domain. Restrict each provisioner to the host's own ID. On step-ca 0.30.2 a name policy cannot do it (L48, cell 6):

  • an x509 allow on a URI in the provisioner's options was ignored: another trust domain's ID was issued as asked;
  • the authority's x509 allow takes a URI domain, not an ID: given the full SPIFFE ID, step-ca refused to start ("contains scheme (not supported yet)").

What does pin it is a provisioner x509 template with the ID fixed in uris in place of the requested sans. It does not refuse another request: it issues the pinned ID instead. So give each host its own provisioner, whose copy of step-ca-workload.tpl replaces the sans line with "uris": ["spiffe://corp.example.com/host/oxidized-01"], and keep the provisioner's credential the host's alone. L48 measured the fixed uris in a template without the CRL distribution point; the two in one template are not measured.

docs.title: 4. Renewal
docs.text: Renewal is your CA's renewer's job (step's step ca renew --daemon, or its systemd timer; step ca renew --daemon renewed a 15m certificate at 0.66 of its lifetime, L48 cell 3). port49 needs nothing at a renewal. With the CA down, once under a quarter of the lifetime is left the broker logs "its renewal is late" and port49 workload warns (first seen at 0.79 of it, polling every 30s), and minting stops at expiry with exit 77 (L48 cell 4). A late one shows in cron mail and in port49_workload_certificates_renewal_late_total, which each broker replica counts once per certificate a day. Alert on its increase.

docs.title: 5. The broker
docs.text:
broker:
  identity:
    machines:
      - type: x509
        trust_anchor_file: /etc/port49/workload-ca.pem
        spiffe_trust_domains: [corp.example.com]

The anchor is the CA that issues the workload certificates (on step-ca, its intermediate, L48).

  • Its hierarchy. The workload anchor and the human anchor must be in unrelated hierarchies. The start refuses one that signs the other directly. One further down is refused at every request whose chain shows it.
  • Its status. certificate_status must cover it: name the CA's CRL in crls. An https CRL endpoint under a private root needs that root in the broker's trust store (SSL_CERT_FILE, L48), or sync the CRL to a file: source. With no source, every certificate is refused, and port49 workload exits 77, not 75. Turning status checking off for everyone is not the fix.
  • step-ca's CRL names a distribution point. Its issuing distribution point names the CRL's own URL (in the lab, https://<the CA's first DNS name>/1.0/crl; step crl inspect shows yours), and port49 applies such a list only to a certificate whose CRL distribution points name that URL (spec, "Certificate status, as built"). step-ca's default leaf names none, so with the CRL configured it is refused 503 certificate_status_unavailable and port49 workload exits 77, the detail saying which name it lacks. Issue workload certificates under step-ca-workload.tpl, with its crlDistributionPoints set to the name step crl inspect shows. Measured: a default leaf was refused; a templated one minted, and was refused credential_revoked 1m after step ca revoke (L48 cell 5).

docs.title: 5a. What port49 policy test says about this snippet
docs.text:
Merged as shipped, port49 policy test prints two reports. Neither fails the run, and both are true.

  • fallback_exposure on arista_eos and cisco_nxos. config_backup is at admin, which those platforms render as network-admin. port49's rules confine the session to the permits in policy.yaml. But if port49 stops answering while a session is open, and the device's command method list falls back to local, the device authorizes that session by its role alone. L22 measured that such a session could change the configuration on vEOS and the N9Kv (tests/lab/results/L22-arista_eos.md, L22-cisco_nxos.md). admin is the level spec §2 gives a backup account so show running-config is reachable. Whether a lower level serves each Oxidized model is unmeasured: L49 ran at admin. Until it is, the exposure belongs to whoever holds a session opened with this run's tokens. Keep router.db and the workload key the Oxidized user's alone, and keep PORT49_TTL to one sweep.
  • unenforced_rules on juniper_junos. A policy that pins no platform_set renders with set 1.0.0. Under 1.0.0, Junos neither asks port49 about a command nor receives the role's rules in its session reply, so on Junos the permits above decide nothing: the session gets what the device's own login class gives the port49 username. Set 1.1.0 renders them into the session reply (spec §8), but the permits here name no Junos command. L49 measured it on vJunos-router 23.4R2-S2.1 and vSRX: a full backup under set 1.0.0 sent port49 no command at all, so the device's login class for svc-oxidized is what limits a Junos backup. Which permits a Junos backup would need under set 1.1.0 is not measured.

docs.title: 6. Check before cron
docs.text:
port49 workload identity --broker https://port49-broker.example.com:8443 \
  --broker-ca ca.pem --cert w.pem --key w-key.pem

prints the SPIFFE ID, the subject and the grants.

docs.title: 7. Under cron
docs.text:
Always --out, as the wrapper does: cron mails a job's stdout, tokens included. The wrapper gives --out a fresh file each run, so a run that could not write it leaves the last router.db alone. Size PORT49_TTL to the whole sweep, since the wrapper queues every node at once. A fleet larger than one sweep's TTL mints in waves.

The wrapper never prints a token. If you edit it, do not add set -x or an echo of one.

docs.title: 7a. Host keys
docs.text:
Oxidized runs with secure: true and never secure: false. It has no accept-new of its own, and the one setting it reads, secure, is a boolean (lab L90, vEOS 4.31.2F, Oxidized 0.37.0): with secure: true and no known_hosts entry it raises Net::SSH::HostKeyUnknown and sends no token; with a changed key, HostKeyMismatch and no token; any other value of secure, accept_new included, turns verification off, so a changed key is accepted. An entry OpenSSH's accept-new wrote, hashed or not, is read and the backup runs.

So the wrapper saves a key for each node absent from known_hosts (~/.ssh/known_hosts of the user Oxidized runs as; OXIDIZED_KNOWN_HOSTS moves it), once, with the line L90 measured: ssh -F /dev/null -o UserKnownHostsFile=<known_hosts> -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o BatchMode=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=none -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o IdentityAgent=none -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 -- <address> exit. The key is saved at key exchange, before authentication, and the flags stop every method that would sign or send, so no credential leaves the host. -F /dev/null means the sweep does not read your ssh configuration: a device reached only through a jump host or a ProxyCommand, or one saved under a HostKeyAlias, is not reached by it. Add that device's key with your own tooling (ssh-keyscan, or ssh with your config); the wrapper then finds it listed and leaves it alone. Only IP literals are visited.

  • A listed node is never visited. A changed key stays refused until you remove its line (ssh-keygen -R <address>) after checking the change. The wrapper stays green for it: the symptom is one node whose backups stop, and Oxidized's log says Net::SSH::HostKeyMismatch for it. Look there.
  • The sweep is bounded. The visits run OXIDIZED_HOSTKEY_JOBS at a time (default 32) and none starts after OXIDIZED_HOSTKEY_BUDGET seconds (default 600), nor runs past it. A node not reached is named on stderr, the run exits 1, and the node is tried again at the next window; this window its backup fails at the host key, with no token sent, and every node with a known key is backed up. A node whose key could not be saved (unreachable, blackholed) is named the same way and costs up to the budget each window until it is fixed.
  • Tokens do not age through it. The addresses come from the mint, so the sweep follows a first mint and a run that visited any node mints again after it: the tokens Oxidized gets are minted after the sweep. A window with nothing to visit mints once. The first mint's tokens are never used and lapse at their TTL. A node that stays unreachable makes every window mint the whole fleet twice, which doubles the broker's mint load and audit records for that window: fix or remove the node. A node that first appears in the second mint is visited too.
  • Concurrency is unmeasured. L90 swept one device; up to 32 visits append to known_hosts at once, which OpenSSH does with one small append each. A lost line fails closed: the node is named and tried again at the next window.
  • Needs ssh, ssh-keygen and timeout on the wrapper's host. A missing one is named and the run exits 2 with router.db untouched.
  • Measured on vEOS only (Oxidized 0.37.0). That Oxidized reads what OpenSSH saved for the host-key type it negotiated is unmeasured on NX-OS, IOS-XE and Junos.

docs.title: 8. On a bad day
docs.text:
• Exit 75: the broker or its store did not answer within the deadline, or the broker could not establish the certificate's revocation status (a CRL past its next update, an OCSP responder down: look at the CA, not the broker), the output could not be written, files could not be made beside router.db, another run holds the lock (router.db.lock), or Oxidized refused a request. The nodes minted before it are queued; with none, Oxidized kept its last router.db and was not reloaded. Try the next window.

    • A partial run replaces router.db with the minted nodes alone, so the unminted nodes are absent from Oxidized's list until a later run mints them. Their backup history in git is untouched.
    • Oxidized refusing (each request has a 10 second limit): a failed node prints its name and the rest are still queued. A failed reload prints that router.db was replaced but Oxidized was not reloaded.

    • Just after a broker start: a port49-broker's first start, or a start after a policy edit, refuses every mint with a retryable 503 store_unavailable until its runner's takeover is done.

      How long that takes: up to the session store's etcd.hold_ttl/3 (stores.session.etcd.hold_ttl, or stores.directory.etcd.hold_ttl when stores.session is omitted), which is 5s at the default 15s and 20s at 60s. Add the takeover itself, plus up to hold_ttl more when the last run's lease must expire first (a crash or a SIGKILL of the only broker: 80s or more at 60s).

      The takeover purges every unspent token, so the broker holds the mint rather than hand out a token that is about to be deleted. The cause is this start gate, not a store fault, so do not chase etcd.

      • port49 workload retries it within its deadline, so a run normally just takes longer; exit 75 means the window outlasted the deadline.
      • port49 token, through the agent, does not retry: it exits saying to retry in 5s, and running it again is the answer.

      The broker's stderr says mints wait for a takeover to judge bundle ... and then mints open: ..., and port49_broker_mint_gate_closed reads 1 meanwhile. /readyz stays 200. A rolling restart on the same policy is never held.

      A replica whose policy file differs from the runner's stays held until the files agree (its port49_policy_bundle_matches_runner is 0). When the runner's takeover could not judge every context (the directory or the IdP unreachable), the runner says N live context(s) left unjudged at the takeover. Its own broker mints, and the other replicas stay held until its settle pass records the bundle. - Exit 77: nothing was minted and running again will not change it: an expired certificate (said before anything connects), a revoked principal, every node denied, a certificate status nothing covers, or a TLS trust failure (the broker's certificate is not under --broker-ca, or the broker refused the workload's certificate: wrong CA, a clock off). Oxidized kept its last router.db. The stderr line says which. - Exit 1: a node was not permitted, was not minted after a final refusal, or was left out because its output line would hold a control character. Its line on stderr says why; the rest are queued. A node whose platform has no Oxidized model in the script, or whose name is outside A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -, is skipped with a line and exits 1 the same way. A run that has both a node of this kind (1) and a failed queue or reload (75) exits 75: 75 takes precedence over 1, and the stderr lines name every node either way. - To stop the workload: port49 revoke --principal spiffe://..., and revoke the certificate at the CA.

The config sets auth_methods with keyboard-interactive for the eos model alone (models: eos: vars). Arista EOS offers only publickey and keyboard-interactive over SSH, and Oxidized's default list does not include the second, so without this line Oxidized never sends the token to an EOS device (L49, L49-oxidized-arista_eos.md). Do not change the EOS side to suit it. It is not global: on NX-OS and IOS-XE, which also offer password, an L49 run with it global (at 0a6d546, superseded and not kept as a note) measured a stale token costing two authentications (both denied as spent) instead of one, so those models keep Oxidized's default. After a refused token net-ssh's keyboard-interactive asks a tty for a second password; under a daemon or cron Oxidized logs Errno::ENOTTY for it (measured in the L49 lab, which has no tty). Run from a terminal in the foreground, it may stop at a password prompt instead; not measured.

docs.title: 9. What L49 measured, and what it did not
docs.text:
Measured on all five platforms (tests/lab/results/L49-oxidized-<platform>.md):

  • the wrapper's REST calls answered 200, and the models eos, ios, nxos and junos loaded their nodes and backed them up;
  • one authentication per run, and a stale token refused in one (retries: 0);
  • the commands each model sends: policy.yaml permits every one port49 was asked about (show vtp status on IOS-XE and show inventory all on NX-OS were added from it);
  • no token in Oxidized's log.

Not measured: whether a lower level than admin serves each model (§5a), how often Oxidized's own schedule tries a node with an expired token, and models other than these four.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text: The pod's projected service account token is the workload's identity. No CA, no secret at rest: the kubelet writes and rotates the token, the broker verifies its signature against the cluster's published keys.

docs.title: 2. The cluster
docs.text:
• Set --service-account-issuer per cluster. kubeadm's default is the same everywhere, and port49 refuses one issuer twice. This is the main onboarding cost for a self-managed fleet.

    The safe sequence when changing an issuer is below. It is not measured: it is reasoned from decision 49 of the policy engine spec (rulings 3 and 4), and the two-verifier config is unit-tested. No L69 cell changed a real cluster's issuer; cell (d) rotated a signing key under one issuer.

    1. Add the new issuer as the first --service-account-issuer flag, and keep the old one as a second. The API server signs with the first and accepts both.
    2. In port49, list both issuers as two k8s verifiers on the same jwks: two verifiers with one jwks and different issuers are how one cluster's issuer migration is written.
    3. Roll the pods.
    4. After the longest expirationSeconds in use has passed, remove the old flag and the old verifier.

  • Apply issuer-discovery.yaml. Measured on kind (L69 (c)); managed clusters are unmeasured (L70).

    Know what it exposes. The binding is to system:unauthenticated, so anyone who can reach the API server's address can read the issuer discovery document and the JWKS without authenticating. They are public keys only, no secret, and the binding grants no other anonymous access.

    Where that reach is too wide, use a narrower route instead of the binding:

    • The API server's structured authentication configuration (1.32+), with AuthenticationConfiguration's anonymous.conditions limited to the two discovery paths, /.well-known/openid-configuration and /openid/v1/jwks. The exact form is not measured: L69 (c) measured the binding alone.
    • Publish a mirror of the keys and point jwks at it, with no binding at all (see the jwks item).

    Issuer discovery needs --anonymous-auth on (not measured; kind's default had it on). A CIS-hardened cluster turns it off.

  • jwks is the API server's own address, not the issuer's host. Discovery's jwks_uri names the issuer's host, which nothing outside the cluster may resolve. That is why decision 49 ruling 2 reads jwks directly:

    echo "$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')/openid/v1/jwks"

    It may be any https mirror of the keys (a bucket, a reverse proxy) for a cluster whose API server the broker must not reach.

  • The cluster CA for ca_file:

    kubectl config view --raw --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d

docs.title: 3. The broker
docs.text:
port49d-identity.yaml is a fragment for port49-broker.yaml. Per verifier:

Key Meaning type: k8s a machine verifier; a cluster's service accounts are workloads, not humans cluster port49's name for the cluster, in records and log lines; the cluster's manifests do not change issuer the cluster's --service-account-issuer, as its tokens carry it in iss jwks where the broker reads the keys (section 2) ca_file the CA the broker trusts for jwks audience what the pods' token volume asks for (port49 here) namespaces the namespaces whose service accounts this cluster may name

One verifier per cluster, each with its own cluster name.

Several clusters may list one namespace. The same CronJob deployed to every region is then one identity, system:serviceaccount:netops:oxidized, and one policy subject, with no per-cluster namespace or overlay.

  • Each record's auth.k8s.cluster says which region minted.
  • The start's line identity: k8s namespaces: netops: eu_west, us_east says which clusters vouch for each namespace. Check it after adding a cluster.
  • Where a namespace means different tenants in different clusters, list different namespaces per verifier.

The overlap is allowed because a compromised cluster already holds a genuine token for its own copy of the workload. Refusing the overlap would buy nothing.

docs.title: 4. The workload
docs.text:
backup-cronjob.yaml:

  • automountServiceAccountToken: false, on the ServiceAccount and the pod. The default API token's aud is the API server's and port49 refuses it (measured on kind, L69 (h)); only the projected volume is mounted.
  • expirationSeconds: 3600. The kubelet refreshes a projected token at about 80% of its lifetime (measured on kind, L69 (b)), and the broker refuses a token issued longer ago than broker.identity.max_token_age (2h by default), so keep it at or under 3600.
  • Least privilege: the pod sets runAsNonRoot: true (the image runs as 65532) and seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault; the container sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (/work is the writable emptyDir) and drops all capabilities.
  • --token-file is read at every request, so a rotated token is picked up without a restart.
  • The example stops at the mint. /work/tokens.tsv is on an emptyDir; the consumer (your backup tool) runs in the same pod after this container, sharing the work volume. It is not shown.
  • The image is the repository's Dockerfile target port49: docker build --target port49 -t port49:local .. The broker address and CA in the manifest, and the port49-backup ConfigMap (devices, broker-ca.pem), are placeholders for your own.

docs.title: 5. The policy
docs.text: policy.yaml maps the principal system:serviceaccount:netops:oxidized to the subject svc_backup. username: is required: a service account has no login name of its own. Check a policy offline with port49 policy test --policy policy.yaml --inventory <file>.

docs.title: 6. 3am
docs.text:
What the operator sees. <cluster> is the verifier's cluster name with its issuer.

Case The workload's stderr The broker's log and metric First start, JWKS unreachable 503 identity_provider_unavailable; retries within --deadline, exits 75 identity: <cluster>: no keys fetched yet (<error>)…; port49_oidc_keys_fetch_failures_total{issuer} climbs; record deny trust_domain_unresolved JWKS unreachable later mints go on with the keys held for jwks_max_age (24h); then as above keys not refreshed since <t>…, hourly; alert on time() - port49_oidc_keys_last_success_timestamp_seconds > jwks_max_age/2 Key rotated at the cluster none: one refetch finds the new key (measured on kind, L69 (d)) none; rotated wrongly: 401 "no one key of matches its key id", exit 77 Clock skew 401 "issued at , ahead of the broker's clock by more than clock_skew" fix the broker host's clock Token from an unlisted cluster 401 "no configured verifier accepts its issuer", exit 77 metric under issuer="unknown" Unlisted namespace 401 identity_unmapped "its namespace is not one lists" record auth.method: k8s Wrong audience, or the default API token 401 "its aud is not exactly [port49]", exit 77 fix the volume's audience (L69 (g), (h)) Token past max_token_age 401 "issued ago, past broker.identity.max_token_age" the kubelet stopped rotating, or expirationSeconds is too long Discovery names another issuer each token refused until issuer matches identity: <cluster>: the cluster's discovery … names issuer <X>, once

A deleted service account or pod is not a refusal: see section 7.

docs.title: 7. Stopping a workload
docs.text:
port49 revoke --principal system:serviceaccount:netops:oxidized

Deleting the service account alone is not immediate. The broker does not call the cluster's TokenReview: doing so would put every cluster's API server on the mint path, and needs a broker credential on each cluster. A token already in hand mints until its exp or iat plus max_token_age, at most 2h. L69 (e) measured that TokenReview answers unauthenticated after the pod and then the service account are deleted and port49 still mints, and that revoke then refuses at once (the 2h bound is the configured limit, not measured). revoke closes the window at once; the mark also stands for a service account re-created under that name until port49 revoke --lift.

docs.title: 8. What is not measured
docs.text:
• Managed clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS): L70, open.
  • A CronJob run in a cluster against a broker outside it: not measured.
  • Changing a real cluster's --service-account-issuer (section 2): not measured.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
port49 serves unmodified network devices, so what a device does when port49 answers, refuses, errors or goes dark is the device's own behavior, and the lab is where it was measured. One page per platform says what the lab measured, what bites, and what nobody measured. The reference configurations here are the starting point for every one of them.

Platform Page Arista EOS Arista EOS Cisco IOS XE (and IOL-XE) Cisco IOS XE Cisco IOS XR Cisco IOS XR Cisco NX-OS Cisco NX-OS Juniper Junos Juniper Junos Nokia SR Linux Nokia SR Linux Anything else Other platforms

docs.title: How to read a device page
docs.text:
Every device page has the same sections, in this order:

  1. The lead is the one thing that bites on that platform, with the lab note that measured it linked.
  2. Reference configuration links the files under deploy/device-aaa/ for the platform and quotes the lines that matter. Replace the placeholders (the table below) and load the file.
  3. What the lab measured lists what a lab run observed, each item linked to the results note that records it, with the image and the date in the note.
  4. Traps are the things an operator gets wrong, each linked the same way.
  5. Unmeasured holds everything that is not measured, one yellow box per item. A claim is measured when a linked note shows it, and unmeasured when it appears only in a yellow "Unmeasured" box. Where a box says a device is "reported" to do something, a person saw it and the lab did not measure it: treat it as an expectation, not a limit.
  6. Lab evidence is the table of every results note for the platform, with its image and date, generated from the notes. Each row names the lab register entry the note belongs to and its status: (closed) means the register row is measured and closed, and (open) means that row is still open, so the note is evidence for part of it and a claim that rests on the row alone is unmeasured.

A result written for one image is not a result for a release or a hardware family the page does not name. A platform that is not here was not tested.

docs.title: Qualified platforms
docs.text:
This page is generated by make qualified-platforms from the committed device profiles, their goldens and the lab results notes they cite. It lists what the lab measured, not what port49 claims: a platform that is not here was not tested, and a row says only what its golden shows port49 answering.
