docs.text: If you have Use a PKI and hardware keys an x509 client certificate an identity provider and no PKI OIDC (port49 login --oidc) neither a directory password and TOTP (port49 login --directory) automation in Kubernetes a service account token automation on static hosts a workload certificate automation with a client at your identity provider a machine OIDC client

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text: A token can be short because expiry does most of the work. Revocation is for the other case: a stolen laptop, an offboarding, a certificate that must stop now. port49 revokes through the broker's API, so it needs no access to the store.

docs.title: What an operator runs
docs.text:
port49 revoke takes one target:

You want to stop Run Leaves a standing mark a person or workload, everywhere port49 revoke --principal <principal> yes one certificate port49 revoke --cert <file> (or --cert-issuer with --cert-serial) yes one OIDC session port49 revoke --sid <sid> --sid-issuer <issuer> no whoever holds one device login port49 revoke --device <name> --username <user> no your own sessions port49 revoke --mine no

port49 revoke --list shows the marks in force, and port49 revoke --lift removes one. Revoking another principal needs the revoke_others right and a press of the operator's security key; lifting needs lift_revocations and a touch (both are rights in the policy reference). Without the right the call is refused and the refusal is logged. port49 revoke --help lists every flag, and Administer: revocation is the runbook.

A standing mark is a revocation that stays in force until someone lifts it. It is kept in the store (with a copy in broker.state_dir), or, on the memory store, in broker.revocations_file, so a restart forgets nothing.

A mark does not expire. The agent reconnects with the same key by itself, so a mark that a fresh handshake could outlive would be undone without anyone acting.

docs.title: What happens, in order
docs.text:
1. The mark is written first.
  2. The broker closes the held connections it names.
  3. Unspent tokens for the principal or certificate are deleted.
  4. Every live login context under it is marked revoked, and its receipts are deleted.
  5. The contexts are read and marked a second time, to catch a redemption that was in flight.

The next mint by that principal is refused credential_revoked. A person's agent sees that at its next request, which ends its session. A login that arrives with a token minted before the revocation is refused credential_revoked too, and its token is spent. Because the receipt was deleted, a device's retransmission of an earlier login is answered token_not_found rather than replayed.

Each revocation is one revoke record in the decision log. It names what it reached and which live contexts it could not.

docs.title: Other things that revoke
docs.text:
Revocation is not only an operator's act. Each of these marks the live context revoked, and its next authorization is denied credential_revoked:

  • a certificate appearing on a CRL or OCSP response;
  • an OIDC back-channel logout, by sid or sub;
  • the broker's periodic refresh finding that the principal now has no grant on the device (for example, a policy change withdrew them);
  • the refresh finding that the directory no longer maps the principal: the entry is gone, ambiguous, or renamed to a username another entry holds;
  • a subject's username changing, since the principal can no longer mint under the name the context is keyed by.

The refresh record before the denial says which of these it was.

A certificate that cannot be checked at all, such as a stale CRL, is not revocation: it is trust_domain_unresolved at mint, and the broker setting broker.certificate_status.on_unavailable decides whether that refuses.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text: A workload certificate renews under the same SPIFFE ID, so a mark on one certificate does not follow the renewal. To stop a workload, revoke its principal (port49 revoke --principal spiffe://…), and revoke the certificate at its CA so it cannot renew. port49 revoke says so when it sees the workload anchor as the issuer.

docs.title: What revocation cannot do
docs.text:
port49 denies; it cannot disconnect

TACACS+ has no way for a server to close a device's session. Revocation takes effect at the next authorization request. The TCP session stays up, a candidate configuration stays intact, and an in-progress commit is untouched: the operator is told no, not cut off.

A platform that asks port49 only at login asks nothing afterwards, so a revocation reaches a context nobody reads and the session lasts until the device ends it. Junos asks only at login unless its authorization-time-interval is set. With it set, Junos re-authorizes the open session at the interval (one re-authorization was measured), and a revoked principal is denied credential_revoked there. Measured on vJunos-router 23.4R2-S2.1 and vSRX3 21.4R3.15 with an interval of 15 minutes (L36, closed: vJunos-router, vSRX). The denial does not end the session: it stayed open, and its next command printed an error.

The decision log's revoke record lists the live contexts port49 could not reach, Junos contexts included, so you know which devices still need a manual disconnect. port49 policy test says so when a test names a platform that never asks about a command.

Unmeasured

Whether Junos re-authorizes more than once, so whether a revocation made after the first re-authorization ever reaches the session, is unknown (L40, open). Do not rely on a revocation reaching a Junos session before its device ends it.

Two other limits are worth knowing.

  • --mine and --device leave no mark. If anyone else used your token, your next login on that device re-admits their session too. Close such a session on the device, or have an operator revoke the principal.
  • A key revocation is by principal or certificate only. There is no finer cut, so deleting unspent tokens by certificate also deletes the same principal's tokens from other certificates under the same device and username. The error is toward denying.

Who may revoke is policy: see Policy.

docs.title: Tokens, receipts and contexts
docs.text:
A device login touches three stored records. Each exists to answer one question.

Record Question it answers Written by Lives Token May this one login on this one device proceed? the broker, at mint until spent or its token_ttl ends Receipt Is this a retransmission of a login already accepted? port49d, at redemption a sliding window, with a hard cap Login context Who is logged in here, and what may they do? port49d, at redemption until the session ends, is revoked or goes idle

docs.title: Two credentials, two lifetimes
docs.text:
A login uses two credentials:

  • The person's session is the held connection described in Concepts. It lasts hours, is held by the agent, and is never sent to a device.
  • The device token is minted from the session automatically. It lasts between 30 and 900 seconds and is used once.

Why two? A single long-lived credential pasted into devices would be a password with an expiry date. A session with no per-device token would need a certificate interaction for every device. Two credentials avoid both.

docs.title: The token
docs.text:
A token is an opaque handle: exactly 30 letters and digits, with no prefix and no separator, like xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx (a stand-in, not a value). It carries no claims. The identity, the groups resolved from the directory at mint time and the device it is valid for all live in the store, which is why deleting a token ends it at once.

  • One device. The token is stored under (nas, username): the device (the NAS, in TACACS+ terms) and the device-facing username. A token presented at another device is simply not there. The first six characters are a keyed tag of the device, so port49d can tell a token cut for another device from one that expired. That is device_mismatch, and it does not occur in normal operation, so it is worth alerting on.
  • One use. Redemption is an atomic match-and-delete inside the set of tokens for that key. The set holds only unspent, unexpired tokens, usually one. A cap on the set (candidate_cap_reached) refuses a mint, never a redemption, so a runaway client is told to stop while every token it already holds still works.
  • Short TTL, per subject. token_ttl is a subject's setting in policy (policy reference), not a global. An interactive login needs about a minute; a batch job walking thousands of devices needs a window matching its run. A longer TTL widens replay only for an unspent token. But it also keeps that many recoverable secrets in the store for that long, so size it to the sweep.
  • Encrypted at rest. CHAP makes port49d recompute a digest from the plaintext token, so the store must hold it recoverably. Tokens and contexts are therefore sealed with a key held by the broker and port49d, not by the store. A store dump alone yields no credential. See Secrets for where the key lives.
  • Expiry is the record's, read on port49d's clock. The broker writes the token with its expiry (its own time of minting plus the TTL), and port49d honours a token only before that time on its own clock; the store's leases only clean up later. On etcd the broker's clock and port49d's therefore decide a login together: a broker 20 seconds behind turns a 30-second token into a 10-second one, and one 30 seconds behind mints tokens that are dead on arrival and fail token_not_found. A broker ahead lengthens each token by the skew, until its lease reclaims it: at most lease_grace (5 minutes) plus two minutes past token_ttl. Skew never admits a token minted for another device or one already spent; it widens an unspent token's window only up to that bound. Keep every broker host and every port49d host on NTP, so they disagree by far less than the shortest token_ttl. A broker clock that runs ahead is counted (port49_token_minted_ahead_total) and raises the port49_token_clock_skew ticket. The memory store is one process and has one clock.

An enable login has no principal to type a name for, so the broker mints a pair: a login token and an enable token, both bound to the device, both single use, sharing a TTL. Tools that already have an enable or secret field take the pair unchanged.

docs.title: The receipt
docs.text:
Devices retry. A TCP reset between port49d's read and its reply, or a slow store, makes the device send the same login again. If redeeming deleted the token and nothing else, the retry would find nothing and the login would fail intermittently.

So when port49d redeems a token it leaves a receipt: the decision it made and the context it created, keyed by (nas, username, credential_sha256). The key holds a hash of what was presented. For PAP and ASCII that is the token; for CHAP it is the exchange, which proves possession without carrying it. A byte-identical retransmission finds its own receipt and gets the stored decision (receipt_replayed) and the same context, not a second one. A different password for the same user finds nothing and is judged on its own merits.

A receipt is a sliding window, not a fixed one. Each presentation it answers extends it by receipt_idle_ttl (default 15 minutes), up to receipt_max_age (default 2 hours) from the first redemption. A presentation past either bound is a plain FAIL on the wire, exactly as a wrong password is, and the log says token_spent. Interactive logins present once and never slide; a client that re-presents the same credential does, with no flag to set. The keys are in the port49d configuration reference.

How many times a client library authenticates differs between libraries. On EOS, pyeapi authenticated once per task (10 authorize_session records for ten tasks, the arista_eos note). On NX-OS, NAPALM's nxos driver made 23 for ten tasks, all in one context (the cisco_nxos note).

Unmeasured

Whether any other client library, or any other platform, authenticates more or fewer times per task is unknown (L15, open). Do not size receipt_idle_ttl on a count you have not measured for your own client.

token_spent also covers a receipt whose context no longer exists (it was replaced or reclaimed), and a token brought back by a store restore. The device simply prompts again. See Reason codes for each meaning.

The receipt key does not include the line (the device's port), so a spent token replays on that device over any transport until the window ends. receipt_idle_ttl and receipt_max_age are therefore the bound on a leaked spent token. Keep them as short as your automation allows.

docs.title: The login context
docs.text:
A context is "this principal's authorization on this device". port49d creates it only on a successful redemption, keyed (nas, username). A session port49 did not authenticate has no context, so it is denied: there is nothing to authorize it on.

The context records the principal, the groups, the privilege, the compiled policy for this device, the credential that authorized it (certificate fingerprint, issuer and serial, or the OIDC sid and sub), the session clock and a revocation mark. Authorization requests carry only user, port, rem_addr and the privilege level; the device never sends the credential, so the context is the only place port49d can learn who it is talking to.

  • Keyed on the username, not the line. port and rem_addr are recorded for the log and for accounting and are part of no key, because a device does not present the same port at login and at authorization. A second login by the same principal under the same username on the same device joins the live context rather than replacing it: it keeps the context, raises privilege only, and never shortens a window already granted.
  • Another principal's login replaces it, and the replace is logged.
  • It ends when its session ceiling (a role's max_session_age, counted from the person's authentication) passes, when it sits idle past context_idle_ttl, or when it is revoked. See Revocation. If the broker is unreachable past session.staleness_ceiling, port49d denies context_stale and keeps the context, so recovery resumes it.
  • It is sealed. Every field the authorizer trusts is encrypted and bound to its (nas, username) key, so a store write cannot raise a privilege, lift a revocation or move a record to another device. What a writer to the store can still do is put back a record port49 sealed earlier. The design document lists that residual replay exactly; treat store write access as a privilege to protect.

Session control stops at the device

TACACS+ has no server-to-device disconnect. Everything above stops port49 from authorizing; it does not close a connection. A platform that asks port49 only at login never asks again, so a ceiling or a revocation reaches a context nobody reads there. Junos is one, unless its authorization-time-interval is set. Revocation has what was measured.

docs.title: Trust domains
docs.text: A person and a workload must never be confusable. A workload that could present as a person, or inherit a person's grants, would turn a leaked service credential into an operator's access. port49 makes the difference structural rather than checking a name.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
A principal's trust domain is whichever verifier validated its credential. Configuration declares the verifiers in two lists, broker.identity.humans and broker.identity.machines (port49d reference), and nothing else classifies. A claim inside a token, a naming convention or a group never decides.

broker:
  identity:
    issuance: {}   # an OIDC person's ID token is taken to issue a certificate
    humans:
      - type: x509
        trust_anchor_file: <people-ca.pem>
      - type: oidc
        issuer: https://login.example.com
        client_id: <client_id>
        principal_claim: email
        principal_domains: [example.com]
    machines:
      - type: x509
        trust_anchor_file: <workload-ca.pem>
        spiffe_trust_domains: [example.org]
      - type: k8s
        issuer: https://kube.example.com
        cluster: us_east
        jwks: https://kube.example.com/openid/v1/jwks
        audience: port49
        namespaces: [netops]

The values are placeholders; the full key list is in the reference.

issuance: {} turns on certificate issuance with its defaults. The broker refuses an OIDC human verifier without it. The one exception is an OIDC verifier that sits beside an x509 human verifier and serves only as a per-login MFA proof.

docs.title: What follows from the rule
docs.text:
• A credential no verifier accepts is refused at mint. The reason is trust_domain_unresolved. The same reason covers a certificate whose revocation status cannot be established when broker.certificate_status.on_unavailable is refuse. See Reason codes for the full meaning.
  • A credential two verifiers accept is refused. There is no tie-break. A person's delegated token is never a machine's, and two issuers never give one principal.
  • principal_domains bounds who a provider may name. An OIDC human verifier lists the domains whose people it may name (user:<name>@<domain>), and has no default. Another provider cannot name someone in your domains, even with a claim that looks right. principal_claim likewise has no default: set it to a claim only your provider's administrators can write.
  • The same issuer may serve both lists with a different audience. An identity provider that issues tokens to people and to applications uses one issuer for both. client_id names the public client whose ID token a person presents; audience names the API in the access token a service obtains. Both are checks on aud, and the list the token matched decides the domain.
  • Certificate anchors may not overlap. The handshake verifies against both anchors, and the one the chain ends at is the domain. A chain that ends at both is refused at the TLS handshake. That leaves a line in the broker's log and a count of identity_refused handshake failures, not a decision record. Put the two anchors in unrelated hierarchies. The broker refuses to start if one anchor directly signs the other, and refuses at a request whose chain shows a deeper overlap.
  • A workload never authenticates with a directory password. The password sign-in refuses a workload's entry, and the verifier's filter keeps a person-shaped service account out.
  • Directory groups reach a workload only as a machine group. A workload can be mapped to a directory entry for membership, opt in per verifier, and the membership reaches only a machine_group: subject, never a person's. So a workload cannot inherit a person's grants by any route.

docs.title: What is trusted, and what is not
docs.text:
Inside the domain Outside it the verifier's trust anchor, or the provider's published keys any other CA or provider, even if it names the same user the principal that verifier derived (a certificate's mapped entry, an OIDC principal claim, a SPIFFE ID, a service account name) a group or role asserted by the credential a directory entry the principal maps to exactly once a name that matches more than one entry, which denies

Policy identity strings carry the domain in their form, so a policy test can check the distinction in CI without any credential in hand. See Policy.

docs.title: Your own trust domain
docs.text: port49 is a relying party, not a certificate authority, with one exception: the short-lived certificate it issues a person after an OIDC or directory-password sign-in. That is port49's own trust domain. Only the broker that issued it reads it, no device ever sees it, and its CA lives in the broker's state directory and rotates with overlap.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: port49 is a TACACS+ server in Go (Apache-2.0). This page is what a contributor needs before the first change: how to build and test, the one-time hook setup, and the rule that decides what the docs may say about a device.

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
You need Go 1.26 or later. The module is github.com/blanketfish/port49, and the build is static, with no cgo.

make build
make test && make vet
  • make test runs the lab harness's unit tests (no device), the Python client and Ansible collection tests (Python 3.10 or later), and the whole Go suite (go test ./... -count=1). A full run takes about 20 minutes.
  • make vet fails on any file gofmt would change, then runs go vet. A change is not ready until both commands pass, and you should report their real output in the pull request.
  • Anything that needs a device image, a container runtime or the lab is a separate make lab-* target and is never part of make test. A pull request does not need the lab. Leave those targets to a maintainer with the lab; see Qualification.

docs.title: Once per clone: the hooks
docs.text:
make hooks

make hooks points this clone's core.hooksPath at .githooks. That enables two checks on every commit: a secret scan of the staged changes (gitleaks), and a check that the commit message carries no session link or trailer. The setting lives in the clone's git configuration, which its worktrees share, so run it once per clone. Never bypass a finding with --no-verify; fix it.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Branches and commits. Branch from main as feature/<slug> or fix/<slug> and open a pull request. Commit with Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, docs:, chore:, refactor:, test:). Keep commits small and atomic.
  • snake_case wherever it is data. YAML keys, JSON log keys, configuration keys and metric names.
  • Reason codes are a closed list. A decision's reason comes from the table in spec §5.7 and internal/decision/reasons.go. To add one, add it to the spec table first.
  • The log never holds a secret. No token, password, challenge or response, ever. A credential appears only as credential_sha256, and a body that has not been validated is never logged.
  • No device identity in a metric label.

docs.title: The lab register
docs.text:
Every claim about how a device behaves has an entry, L<N>, in the lab register: the table in spec §15. The register, not memory or a vendor manual, is the source of truth for device behavior. Four rules:

  1. A claim cited to an open entry is unmeasured. Do not "fix" a doc to assert it.
  2. A decision marked provisional on L<N> stays provisional until that row closes.

  3. Closing an entry means all of these:

    • the lab test passed;
    • tests/lab/results/L<N>-<platform>.md exists, with the platform, the image version, the observation and a capture pointer;
    • the row's Status in spec §15 is edited to closed — measured <date>; tests/lab/results/L<N>-<platform>.md;
    • the change is committed as docs: close lab register entries ....

    A row with one platform measured and others open stays open. 4. If a lab result contradicts a doc, the doc is wrong. Fix the doc, cite the results note, and say so in the commit message. A results note wins over a doc.

On this site, a device claim links its results note, or it sits in an "Unmeasured" box worded as unknown.

docs.title: Where the design lives
docs.text:
• The architecture and the policy engine spec (§13 records decisions, §15 is the register).
  • docs/superpowers/plans/: one implementation plan per build step, and its README.md is the roadmap.
  • tests/lab/: the lab harness, and tests/lab/results/ for the notes the register cites.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
• Qualification: vetting a firmware, adding a platform, and the lab regression run.
  • Releasing: how a release is cut and published.

docs.title: Qualification
docs.text:
A platform is qualified when the lab has run a real firmware image against port49 and the measured behavior is recorded. Two tiers use that record:

  • The mock tier (make qual) replays each vetted firmware's measured behavior against a real in-process port49d. It needs no image, no lab and no special runner, so it runs on every pull request.
  • The lab tier boots the real image. It is make lab-qualify, and make qual-vet wraps it for the vetting procedure below. It needs the lab, so only a maintainer with the lab runs it.

The commands you will use:

Command What it does make qual The mock tier: the device-mock packages, tests/qual, and the port49d qualification tests. make qual-vet P=<selector> Vets one firmware in the lab and generates its mock for review. It commits nothing. make qual-update Rewrites the goldens after a deliberate change to port49's decisions. Review the diff. make qual-fleet Linux only: many mock devices, each from its own loopback address, against one port49d. make qualified-platforms Regenerates docs/qualified-platforms.md from the profiles, goldens and notes.

Vendor images are never hosted

port49 does not host, mirror or redistribute a vendor's device image, and no pull request adds one. You obtain an image from the vendor under your own license and keep it on your own lab host. What the repository holds is the measured behavior: the notes, the profiles and the goldens.

docs.title: The procedures
docs.text:
The rest of this section is the contributor guide from tests/qual/README.md, included as it stands. engine_gaps are the behaviors of a device that port49's engine cannot yet express; each one needs Go in internal/devicemock and a test.

The mock tier (make qual) replays each vetted firmware's measured behavior against a real in-process port49d: no images, no lab, any runner. A mock exists only for a firmware the lab has run. The lab run is make lab-qualify; make qual-vet wraps it. Details of the run itself are in tests/lab/README.md, "Qualification".

Layout: profiles/<platform>/<slug>.yaml (the mock), golden/<platform>/<slug>.json (the expected port49 decisions), qual-policy.yaml and qual-daemon.yaml (what every run is played under). docs/qualified-platforms.md is generated from these (make qualified-platforms).

docs.title: Vet a new firmware and add its mock
docs.text:
1. Put the image where the lab host keeps its images (for example /mnt/images).
  2. Add its platforms row in tests/lab/harness_test.go: selector, topology, image, version (as the device reports it) and a measured boot.

  3. Run make qual-vet P=<sel>, for example make qual-vet P=nxos106.

    It refuses when any of these holds:

    • /tmp/port49-STOP-LAB exists
    • the lab is occupied
    • tests/qual, tests/lab/results, tests/lab/evidence or docs/qualified-platforms.md has uncommitted changes

    It then runs make lab-qualify, genprofile, make qual and make qualified-platforms, and commits nothing. If any step fails, it lists the paths the run left changed. Restore them before committing anything, or a failed run's note or evidence goes in with the next commit.

  4. Review the profile against the note. genprofile prints a checklist. Before you commit, confirm every line of it against tests/lab/results/QUAL-<slug>-<lp>.md:

    • each reaction it pre-filled as measured
    • each acceptance rule and its status
    • the review-left defaults, client_chain and server_identity
    • each engine gap id
    • each device fact

    A claim is measured only when a note for this firmware measured it (decision 52, ruling 4).

    On Junos the command cells are not_applicable (L18: tests/lab/results/L18-juniper_vjunos-router.md). So genprofile records the engine gap command_authorization_not_sent; that is expected, not a failure.

    TLS is played in two modes. The TLS login is played the way the device defaults, per-request (tls_token_login), and again with single-connection on (tls_single_connection). Each verdict line names its mode. The harness never turns single-connection on to make a per-request cell pass.

    Where per-request TLS sends port49 no command authorization (NX-OS 10.6(2)F, L73 cell a):

    • genprofile records the device fact tls_per_request_no_command_authorization.
    • The mock plays that login with no command step.
    • The list's "command authorization over TLS" column reads "no" or "single-connection only".
    • The tls_denied_command cell then types the denied command alone over per-request TLS and writes tests/lab/results/L80-<lp>.md (spec §15 L80). Its verdict is observed, never pass. genprofile records its outcome as the device fact tls_per_request_denied_command_runs or ..._refused, citing that note.
    • The list's TLS column then reads "no: over per-request TLS, a command port49 denies runs (L80)" or "no command authorization over per-request TLS; denied commands refused locally (L80)".

    Single-connect offered over TLS. port49 offers single-connect over TLS to some platforms (platform.TLSServerSingleConnect; today cisco_nxos). For those:

    • run.json's tls_server_single_connect_offered is true.
    • The run waits until no connection is open before and at tls_token_login's capture (tls_capture_started_clean).
    • genprofile grades tls_token_login from its header-only *.tls.json and port49's records. It writes tls_server_single_connect_honored when a connection carried a session after a completed one that was not accounting, and tls_server_single_connect_ignored when every connection carried one session.
    • It writes nothing if the capture did not start clean, any two of the cell's connections overlap, or a record falls in no connection.

    Neither is written where port49 never offered: absent is no claim. The mock reuses an offered connection where the profile says honored. The drift test (tests/qual/drift_test.go) fails when the table and the profiles disagree either way. So a firmware that ignores the offer fails before a release ships the table entry for it.

  5. Commit the evidence, the note, the profile, the golden and the list.

No mock is added for an image the lab has not run (ruling 8).

docs.title: Add a platform
docs.text:
1. Add a platforms row and a topology.
  2. Write a startup config with break-glass and the port49 TACACS+ server group.
  3. For TLS, add an l73Dialects row, written help first.
  4. Give it a port49 inventory platform: built in, or generic (which logs platform_unknown).
  5. Vet it as above.

Any engine gap it needs becomes an engine_gaps entry, plus Go in internal/devicemock with a test.

docs.title: When a mock fails on a PR
docs.text:
• A gate (an acceptance rule). The device would reject port49's reply. Fix port49, or, if the rule is wrong, re-measure it in the lab.
  • A golden difference. If port49 changed on purpose, run make qual-update and review the diff. The list shows re-vet pending until the next lab run.
  • A missing reaction. The vetter adds it from the notes.

docs.title: The release-tag gate
docs.text:
1. make lab-regress.
  2. make qual-vet for every profile whose golden is pending.
  3. Commit.

docs.title: The lab regression run
docs.text:
make lab-regress reruns every closed entry in tests/lab/regress.yaml and rewrites its results notes. Each entry's measured_minutes is its wall time in a full run (the first, commit 2c680dbf, 2026-10-19/20, then the L35, L37, L66, L79, L80 and L90 entries, and XRd's L73): the manifest sums to 745.7 minutes. A clean full run is about 12 h plus NX-OS boot hangs (below), so routine use needs a subset: make lab-regress LAB_REGRESS_ARGS=-only=L35,L37. The slowest are L34 (103 min), L36 (67) and L22 (44).

Runs before the 2026-10-20 rebase name the rebased twin of the commit they ran (2c680dbf for the first full run); the tree differs by PR #29's client and spec changes only. The vJunos 23.4R2-S2.1 QUAL run names 73f7a5df, the commit its amended-away original became: the code is identical, and only two stray pcaps were dropped.

The first run passed 58 of 66 entries. Of the 8 that failed, all are resolved:

  • L35, L37: the test expected an older release's circuit-open line; port49d now goes dark on its store health checks (about 5 s). The verdict was fixed and both passed on the rerun.
  • L66 (five entries): the lookup failed for a name outside the inventory; fixed by PR #29, and L66 passed on the rerun.
  • L29-reload on vjunos: no connection open across the change was reset in the refused/rekeyed phase. Junos sends nothing on a held connection, so the phase can fail its premise; a device flake, so retry the entry.

L80 (L80-nxos106) is a regress entry: it re-measures a security fact (a command port49 denies runs over NX-OS 10.6's per-request TLS), and a run that observes nothing is INVALID. A flipped outcome shows as changed lines in the note diff, and a run that observes nothing writes no L80 note. lab-regress reports note changes and does not fail on them. It does fail an entry whose listed note the run did not rewrite (its mtime is before the entry started): notediff masks the header lines a rerun changes, so an untouched note would otherwise read "unchanged".

NX-OS boot hang. 11 of 39 NX-OS deployments never booted: the container log stops after feature netconf and port49d sees no packet within 8 min. The cause is not yet known; the device appears to hang while the launcher applies its startup config. Retry the entry. Each deploy now logs lab: <platform>: boot: and host: lines, for example lab: cisco_nxos: boot: phase=ssh_auth at=2026-11-07T01:04:10Z since_deploy=2m7s and lab: cisco_nxos: host: phase=failed mem_total_kb=32768000 mem_available_kb=900000 swap_total_kb=8388608 swap_free_kb=100000 load1=9.50 load5=7.25 load15=5.00 procs_running=6 procs_total=812. Read a hang from them: ssh_auth with no tacacs_seen is the config apply, and mem_available_kb at failed against deploy_start shows host pressure. Do not raise the timeout without them.

What a run needs beyond the base setup:

  • PORT49_LAB_ETCD_BIN names a directory holding etcd, etcdctl and etcdutl, all v3.6.15 (for example /mnt/images/etcd-v3.6.15 on the lab host). L35-restore needs etcdutl.
  • L66 needs tests/lab/l66/.collections, which is git-ignored, so a fresh worktree lacks it. Create it with <venv>/bin/ansible-galaxy collection install -p tests/lab/l66/.collections <collections>; the L66 preflight prints the exact command with the collection names.

docs.title: Working around the NX-OS boot hang
docs.text:
make lab-regress passes LAB_REGRESS_ARGS to the runner, whose -only= flag takes a comma-separated list of entry ids and runs just those. Use it to retry an entry whose NX-OS device never booted, instead of rerunning the whole manifest:

make lab-regress LAB_REGRESS_ARGS=-only=<entry_id>,<entry_id>

-dry-run lists the entries and their last measured minutes without running anything. Each deploy logs boot: and host: lines; read the hang from them before you raise a timeout.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
This page is RELEASING.md from the repository, included as it stands. Only a maintainer cuts a release.

A release is a v* tag on a commit that is on main. The release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) does the rest: it checks the tag against every version file, builds the packages, image, chart, Python package and Galaxy collection, and publishes each from a job that only downloads. The GitHub release stays a draft until every publisher has finished.

Nothing publishes until a tag is pushed. Do the one-time setup below first; it is what makes a tag without approval harmless.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: port49 uses SemVer. v0.1.0 is the beta. In 0.x, configuration may break between releases, and every such change gets a loud release note. 1.0.0 is the compatibility promise. There is one version across every artifact (packages, image, chart, Python package, Galaxy collection), and bumps come from Conventional Commits. Tags are pushed by hand and carry no pre-release suffix unless it maps to a valid PEP 440 version. The docs site states the same on its Versions page.

docs.title: One-time setup, before the first tag
docs.text:
1. PyPI trusted publisher. Project port49, repository blanketfish/port49, workflow release.yml, environment pypi.
  2. Environments (Settings, Environments):
  3. release (the goreleaser, image and chart jobs): the maintainer as the required reviewer, so no tag publishes without approval.
  4. pypi and galaxy: created beside it.
  5. Each of release, pypi and galaxy: deployment branches and tags restricted to the v* tag pattern.
  6. GALAXY_API_KEY is an environment secret on galaxy only: never a repository or organization secret, so no other job can read it.
  7. Tag ruleset. A repository ruleset protecting v* tags (restrict creation, updates and deletion to the maintainers).
  8. Fork pull-request workflows. Settings, Actions, General, "Fork pull request workflows from outside collaborators": Require approval for all outside collaborators.
  9. Public packages. When the repository goes public, make the GHCR package port49 and the chart package public.
  10. Docs site. Settings, Pages, source Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, folder / (root). docs.yml runs mike, which keeps one built copy of the site per version on that branch, and GitHub's own pages-build-deployment publishes it: there is no github-pages environment and no Pages token. The deploy is two jobs, and only on a public repository. The docs toolchain runs in the deploy job, which has no write token (contents: read): it fetches gh-pages and then the tags, decides the version and aliases itself, builds with mike, commits locally and uploads the branch as a git bundle. The push-pages job runs only git on a verified bundle: it has no checkout and runs no repository code, and it pushes gh-pages, never forced. Outside release.yml, the push-pages job is the only workflow job with contents: write. A main run deploys only if its commit is still the tip of main: when two merges land close together, the older run either decides there is nothing to publish ("a newer main push deploys") or, if its push is rejected after the newer run's, ends green with "superseded by a newer main push; nothing to do". Either way the newer run deploys. Any other rejected push (a tag's, or the newest main run's losing to a tag's) fails red with "another deploy moved gh-pages; re-run all jobs of this run": re-run all jobs, not just the failed one, which would push the same stale bundle. A re-run is safe for both refs: a tag re-run deploys only the highest patch of its line, and a main re-run deploys nothing once a newer main commit exists. There is no automatic retry. Keep the main ruleset off gh-pages, or the bot's push is refused. The deploy also commits a root 404.html that sends an old /port49/<page> link to /port49/latest/<page>, and a root llms.txt copied from latest.
  11. Required check. Add docs (the build job in docs.yml, named docs) to the required status checks of the main ruleset. What deploys: every push to main replaces /dev/; a final vX.Y.Z tag on main replaces /X.Y/ if it is the highest patch of that line, and moves /latest/ (the alias the site root redirects to) if it is also the highest final tag. Only final tags that are on main count, so a stray tag elsewhere takes nothing. Before the first final tag, /latest/ is an alias of /dev/. A lower patch pushed late deploys nothing.
  12. Link check. At go-public, run one external link check over the built site (for example lychee on site/) and fix what it finds.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
1. Set the same version in clients/python/pyproject.toml, the collection's galaxy.yml, and the chart and app versions; go run ./tests/ci/cmd/versioncheck -tag vX.Y.Z must pass.
  2. Merge to main. The tag must be on main; the workflow refuses it otherwise.
  3. The maintainer pushes the tag; nobody else, and no automation, does. The maintainer approves the release environment when the run asks.
  4. Check the draft release's assets and provenance attestations, then let the last job publish it.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text: Read the first section before you need it. A restore is the one routine operation that can admit a person you revoked, so its steps run in a fixed order and each safety step has a check.

docs.title: What a restore does
docs.text:
A restore puts the store back to the moment of its snapshot. Two things follow, and the rest of this page exists to undo them:

  • Revocations made since the snapshot are gone, and lifts made since are undone. A revoked principal or certificate is admitted again until the revocation is put back.
  • Every single-use token redeemed since the snapshot is back, unspent. Redeemable again until it expires (a token lives at most 15 minutes).

port49 defends against both on its own, and still asks you for steps, because some restores it cannot see (below). Keep the order of the runbook: the token delete comes before anything reaches the store, and the revocations are re-issued before any broker starts.

docs.title: What each shape must keep
docs.text:
All three shapes (systemd, container, Helm) keep the same things. Only the paths differ.

What Why it is in the backup systemd container (compose) Helm The etcd data of every cluster: the directory store, and each region's session store The revocation marks, second factors, pins and sessions. A snapshot holds the plaintext index (principal, device, username, certificate, sid): guard it as the store itself. the hourly port49-etcd-snapshot timer, from an etcd host each etcd-N-data volume the port49-etcd-snapshot CronJob (examples/backup-cronjob.yaml) broker.state_dir of every broker: marks.json, witness.json, and issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key when the broker issues certificates marks.json is the copy that puts back revocations a restore lost. witness.json is how a broker tells a restore. The CA is the private key your devices trust: whoever reads the backup can issue certificates. /var/lib/port49-broker the broker-state volume one PVC per broker replica, state/ inside it port49d's accounting spool and the file beside it, <accounting.spool_path>.restore.json restore.json is port49d's record of the restore witness, so a restart still knows the store was restored. Two port49d with spools in one directory each keep their own. /var/spool/port49d the port49d-spool volume the port49d PVC (/var/spool/port49d/data) On the memory store only: the directory holding broker.revocations_file The memory store runs the broker inside port49d, which refuses broker.state_dir; the broker keeps its state beside the revocations file. That directory holds the revocations file (the marks), enrollments.json (the sealed enrollment store), the CRLs the broker verified, and, when the broker issues certificates, issuing-ca.pem and issuing-ca.key (with -next or -previous copies during a CA rotation): whoever reads the backup can issue certificates. On etcd the store keeps the marks and none of this applies. the directory of broker.revocations_file same same The enrollment store of a directory_password verifier Second factors. On etcd it is sealed records in the directory store; on the memory store it is the sealed file enrollments.json, in the directory above. the daily port49-enrollments-export timer, on a broker host no job is shipped: run port49-broker export-enrollments --out FILE from your scheduler the chart's backup.enrollments CronJob (off by default)

The configuration, the policy and the secrets are not on this list: they are in your configuration management and your secrets manager. Two cautions:

  • A backup is only restorable while every key that sealed its records is kept. Every record inside an etcd snapshot, a Velero backup or an enrollments export stays sealed under the encryption: key that was current when the record was written. An enrollments export keeps each record's own seal and seals only its envelope under the key current at export time.

    Keep every old key file, offline, as long as any backup holding its records is kept. Velero also stores the encryption Secret in its bucket, so the bucket is as sensitive as the key. Key rotation has the rule and what a missing key costs.

  • Back up broker.state_dir with the broker's host, not from a different moment. A broker whose state_dir survived the restore is the one that puts back the revocations the store lost, so the runbook starts it first.

docs.title: The enrollments export
docs.text:
port49-broker export-enrollments --out FILE writes the sealed enrollment store to a new file (mode 0600, never replacing one). The unit and the CronJob run it on a schedule, keep 14 days, and write a temporary file that is renamed, so a failed run changes nothing. On Helm a stale-check init container fails the Job when a .new file is left from a run that did not finish; remove it, and the next run goes.

A new deployment that uses directory password sign-in runs port49-broker init-enrollments once, before the first start (on Helm, examples/init-enrollments-job.yaml). It creates the store the export reads, and a second run is refused (the enrollment store is already there). Until it has run, sign-ins answer enrollment_store_lost.

To restore from an export, as an admin with a key press:

port49 directory import < enrollments-<date>.json

The import refuses when the store holds a second factor enrolled or reset after the export was taken, because it would undo it. --replace replaces the store anyway. An export sealed under a key the broker does not hold is refused, and the message tells you to set that key as encryption.previous.

Unmeasured

The Helm export has been run only against a freshly initialised store, which holds the creation mark and no enrolled person. An export that holds enrolled people has not been measured. The systemd timer has not been run on a real host: run it once by hand before you rely on it.

docs.title: The restore floor
docs.text:
An etcd restore can bring back a token that was redeemed after the snapshot. port49 refuses such a token in three places, and the runbook adds a fourth, the delete, for the cases where the first two cannot tell.

  1. port49d's restore floor. Every token records the store revision it was created at. port49d reads meta/witness once a second. When the witness or the store's revision is lower than its own record (<accounting.spool_path>.restore.json), the store was restored. The revision of that read becomes the floor: a token at or below it is refused FAIL with reason token_spent, once, and the user mints again. A token minted after the read is served. Each refusal adds one to port49_redemption_restored_refused_total.
  2. The runner's purge. The broker that holds the keyspace compares meta/witness with its own broker.state_dir/witness.json. A store below the record, or no record at all, makes it purge every unspent token and every once-only record (sign-in challenges, proofs, nonces).
  3. The mint gate. While a purge is owed, that broker mints nothing, so a token is not minted into a purge that would delete it.
  4. The delete, step 3 of the runbook, before any port49d or broker reaches the restored store.

docs.title: When port49 cannot tell
docs.text:
port49d tells a restore only from a record that is newer than the restored store. So it does not see one when:

  • the restore also restored the spool directory or broker.state_dir (Velero, a volume snapshot), so restore.json and witness.json came back with the store. They are newer than the store only when the store had writes in the backup window, which is usual on a busy store and not on an idle one;
  • port49d's spool directory is new or was lost. It has no restore.json and takes the restored witness as its first record. It logs port49d: store: no restore record at <path>: a restore made before this port49d's first read of the store cannot be told; after a restore, delete the unspent tokens before this port49d reaches the store (step 3 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot).

Either way a restored token is redeemed a second time with no line saying so. The delete is required in both cases. A broker with no witness.json (an empty or new broker.state_dir) purges once at its first takeover, which costs every user one new token and is expected on a cold start of a whole fleet on new volumes.

A record that cannot be read or decoded is moved aside (<path>.bad-<time>), and the first read is taken as a restore: every token in the store is refused token_spent once.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see It means You do port49d's stderr: port49d: store: the session store was restored from a snapshot: meta/witness is … and the tail Revocations and marks made after the snapshot are lost: follow the restore runbook, Restoring etcd from a snapshot port49d found the restore and set its floor. The line names the floor revision. After a restore without --bump-revision it also names the band (below). Follow the runbook from the revocations step if you have not. The line is a report, not a recovery. port49_store_restore_detected_timestamp_seconds above 0, and the alert port49_store_restore_detected (ticket, for a day after) Same event, as a metric. The same. A user's login fails and port49_redemption_restored_refused_total rises Their token is from before the restore. They mint a new token (port49 token). Nothing else. A broker's stderr: port49-broker: runner: <why>; every unspent token is purged and must be minted again (port49 token): N purged; M once-only records (sign-in challenges, proofs, nonces) deleted The runner purged. <why> is the store's meta/witness is … below the … this replica saw: the store was restored from a snapshot, or no witness record in broker.state_dir; …. Nothing. Every user mints again. A broker's stderr: port49-broker: runner: N revocation(s) in broker.state_dir/marks.json were missing from the store (an etcd restore, …) and are put back: <marks>; lift any that were lifted on purpose with port49 revoke --lift The runner put back the revocations its copy held. Lift again, with port49 revoke --lift, any of them that were lifted on purpose before the snapshot. A broker's stderr: broker.state_dir had no marks.json at this start; a revocation a store restore lost is put back only if this copy saw it This broker had no copy, so it put back nothing. If no broker's state_dir survived, re-issue every revocation made since the snapshot (step 4 of the runbook). port49_broker_mint_gate_closed at 1 and POST /v1/token answering 503 store_unavailable with Retry-After: 5 A broker owes the purge and mints nothing until it is done. Wait. If it stays at 1 for more than a minute (ticket port49_broker_mint_gate_closed), no runner is purging: check that one broker holds the keyspace, and read its stderr for a purge that failed. A purge cut short is made again by the next takeover. port49_redemption_restore_unjudged at 1, and port49d: store: reading meta/witness, to tell whether the store was restored: …; token redemptions are refused (store_unavailable) until a read answers; tried again every 1s port49d cannot read meta/witness, so it cannot tell whether the store was restored and refuses every token login. Page after 2 minutes: port49_redemption_restore_unjudged. Fix the store, or the daemon role's read of meta/witness. A device whose authentication ERROR is final (IOS XE, and Junos under tacplus alone) refuses break-glass until the read answers or port49d is stopped; stopping port49d lets those devices fall to break-glass. Do not delete restore.json to clear it: without the record port49d cannot tell a restore.

docs.title: The revision bump and the 5-minute band
docs.text:
Restore an etcd snapshot with --bump-revision. It raises the restored store's revision by a billion (eleven days of writes at a thousand a second), so etcd never reuses a revision for another write. port49d tells a restore from its witness whether or not --bump-revision was used, and with it the floor needs no band: nothing is refused but the old tokens.

Measured on vEOS with etcd 3.6.15 (L35-restore-arista_eos.md): a snapshot at revision 338 of a store at 347 restored to 1000000338, its next write was 1000000339, and a read at 347 was refused as compacted.

Without --bump-revision (a Velero restore cannot use it) the restored store climbs through the revisions the old timeline already used. port49d then also refuses, for 5 minutes after its read, every token minted at a revision up to the old high mark, token_spent. The log line names the time: a token minted until <time> (5 minutes after this read) at a revision up to <N> is refused until <time>; restore with --bump-revision (step 2 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot) to end that. Users see a failed login, and so does every retry until the window ends. A token minted inside the window keeps its mint time, so it stays refused until the band ends, 20 minutes after the read, and pasting the same token again keeps failing. Tell users to mint a new token after the window. Break-glass is unaffected.

docs.title: Restoring etcd from a snapshot
docs.text:
This is the runbook for a restore of etcd on any shape. Do the steps in order. A step marked Check is a stop: do not go on until the check passes.

  1. Stop what could reach the restored store.

    On Helm, first suspend every GitOps controller (Argo CD auto-sync or self-heal, Flux) that manages port49 or port49-etcd, with the commands in the Velero runbook below (the paragraph before its step 1). Resume it after step 6. A StatefulSet cannot serve loopback only (step 2), so on Helm the brokers held at 0 are the only guard. A controller that puts the replicas back lets a broker reach the restored store before the delete and before the revocations are re-issued, and can admit a revoked principal.

    Stop every port49-broker (systemd: systemctl stop port49-broker on every broker host; container: stop the port49-broker service; Helm: scale the broker StatefulSet to 0).

    port49d may run on: it goes dark while the store is down. Also stop every port49d in any of these cases, because port49d may then not see the restore, and the delete below must land before it reaches the store:

    • the restore also restored the spool directory or broker.state_dir;
    • a port49d's spool is new;
    • you cannot serve the restored store on loopback only (a StatefulSet cannot).

  2. Restore with --bump-revision and --mark-compacted on each member, from the same snapshot: etcdutl snapshot restore <snapshot> --data-dir <new dir> --bump-revision 1000000000 --mark-compacted, with the member flags your cluster uses (--name, --initial-cluster, --initial-advertise-peer-urls).

    Start the members serving clients on loopback only (for example --listen-client-urls https://127.0.0.1:2379 --advertise-client-urls https://127.0.0.1:2379, the TLS flags unchanged, the peer URLs as they were so quorum forms). On systemd and compose, no port49d or broker can reach the restored store yet; on Helm only the stopped StatefulSets keep them off it.

    If the store was restored without --bump-revision anyway, also restart every port49d only after step 5's first runner has said its put-back line. Two things go wrong otherwise:

    • a port49d restarted before then loads the restored marks, so it enforces none of the revocations the restore lost;
    • a port49d started after the restore seals below what a port49d that ran across it knows, so its logins are denied store_unavailable until that process writes at the key.

  3. Delete the unspent tokens and the judged records, on the loopback address, as etcd's root. Use your store prefix (stores.session.etcd.prefix, /port49/ by default):

    etcdctl --endpoints https://127.0.0.1:2379 del --prefix /port49/v1/t/
etcdctl --endpoints https://127.0.0.1:2379 del /port49/v1/meta/judged
etcdctl --endpoints https://127.0.0.1:2379 del /port49/v1/meta/judged_bundle

    Add the --cacert, --cert and --key of etcd's root identity; in a container, run etcdctl in the member's own network namespace. Check: all three returned. Only then restart the members on their usual client URLs.

    On Helm the one-shot Job restore-unspent runs these three deletes from etcd's own image, as etcd's root; the Velero runbook below uses it.

  4. Re-issue the revocations no broker's marks.json holds, while every broker is still stopped. These are:

    • those made while every broker was down, since no broker saw them;
    • if no broker's state_dir survived the restore, every revocation made since the snapshot.

    Run port49-broker revoke --offline --principal <principal> on a broker host as the broker's user (sudo -u port49-broker; as root it refuses and names the line). On Helm, deploy/helm/port49/scripts/revoke-offline.sh does the same from the repository root. It leaves the brokers at the 0 it finds.

  5. Check broker.policy_file on every broker host before any broker starts. Step 3 deleted meta/judged, so the reload guard at a broker's start has no judged bundle to check against. The first start says no bundle has been judged on this keyspace; this start is not judged against one and goes on, and a policy file the guard would have refused is not caught. Confirm each host holds the policy you mean to serve.

    Start the brokers, first a broker whose broker.state_dir survived the restore. The first runner puts back only the revocations its own marks.json holds that the store lacks, and names them. A broker on an empty or new state_dir that runs first puts back none of the revocations made since the snapshot: its line says had no marks.json at this start. If no broker's state_dir survived, step 4 had to re-issue them all.

    The first runner also applies every mark to the restored contexts and purges the unspent tokens. Check: a runner printed every unspent token is purged. If none did, delete the restored tokens again as root (step 3). Then start any port49d you stopped.

  6. Lift again, with port49 revoke --lift, any revocation that was lifted since the snapshot and that the put-back line named.

  7. Run port49 directory forget again for every pin forgotten since the snapshot: a restore brings the old pin back (Stores).

  8. If a replay fails token_not_found with the log line etcd: superseded record "<prefix>v1/meta/superseded_all" does not decode, delete that one key as etcd's root (etcdctl del <prefix>v1/meta/superseded_all); the next purge writes it again. That is availability, never an admission.

A restored snapshot also brings back every context it held. One that a revocation by principal or certificate ended is denied again at once by the marks. One that a self or key revocation ended has no mark and is live again until its idle TTL: revoke it again.

docs.title: Restoring with Velero
docs.text:
Prefer restoring etcd from an etcd snapshot (the CronJob's), as above, with --bump-revision, and use Velero for the other volumes. A Velero restore that includes port49-etcd is a store restore: it cannot use --bump-revision, so the 5-minute band applies, and the spool and broker.state_dir come back with the store, so the delete of step 3 is required, not belt and braces. The runbook below is the repository's own file, deploy/helm/port49/examples/velero/README.md, so it matches the chart you run. It restores etcd alone first, runs the restore-unspent Job (the delete of step 3), holds etcd down, restores port49 with its pods running so Velero can copy their volumes, then holds both StatefulSets at 0 and brings etcd back, so the revocations are re-issued before any broker or port49d reaches the store.

Unmeasured

The Argo CD and Flux suspend and resume commands in the runbook follow those tools' documented commands, and no GitOps controller has run the restore. Restoring port49 while etcd is held down in its own namespace has not been measured either: the measurement ran against an etcd that shared the release's namespace and was never held at 0. A file-system copy of a live etcd member under load, and a CSI volume snapshot in place of file-system backup, are also unmeasured. Skipping the suspend step can admit a revoked principal until the revocations are re-issued.

What is measured is on kind, with Velero 1.18.4 and its node agent (L89-kind.md): a backup of both StatefulSets, a deleted namespace and a restore left both ready with no fence refusal, the issuing CA unchanged, and a mint and a login working; a restore with the StatefulSets at 0 replicas hung; and the restore order below, with the pods running and then scaled to 0, completed with marks.json, the CA and the spool intact.

Everything from here to the end of the page is that README verbatim: what the backup holds, its requirements, how to pin the plugin, then the restore.

docs.title: What the backup holds
docs.text:
The backup holds issuing-ca.key, the issuing CA's private key, in each broker's state/ directory, the broker state, and the accounting spool of each port49d. Whoever reads the bucket and the repository key can issue certificates your devices trust.

The bucket alone holds more. Velero encrypts only the volume data, under the repository key. It stores the namespaces' Secrets as it reads them, unencrypted: the TACACS+ keys, the store's encryption key, the etcd CA and client identities, and the TLS key. Read access to the bucket is enough to take them. The repository key protects the volumes and nothing else. Protect the bucket like the CA key.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. The repository key is yours, from a Secret, created BEFORE Velero is installed and before the first backup. Velero's default repository password is a well-known static value, and Velero writes that Secret itself when it starts and finds none. A repository made under the default key keeps it, so a backup made first is encrypted with a key everyone knows. Generate the key and create the Secret from a file, never from a value on the command line:

    umask 077
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 > repository-password
kubectl create namespace velero
kubectl -n velero create secret generic velero-repo-credentials --from-file=repository-password=./repository-password
velero install ...

    Keep a copy outside the cluster: a restore into a new cluster needs it. If Velero already runs and has made no backup, delete the Secret Velero made, create yours, and restart the Velero deployment.

  2. Apply schedule.yaml only after step 1.

  3. The bucket must be encrypted at rest (server-side encryption in the object store).
  4. Access to the bucket is limited to the backup's own credentials: no other principal, no public access, no credentials shared with another workload.

docs.title: Pinning the plugin
docs.text: velero install --plugins cannot take an image by digest: Velero names the plugin's init container after the reference, and a digest makes that name invalid. Give it the tag, then check the running pod's imageID (kubectl -n velero get pods -o jsonpath='{..initContainerStatuses[*].imageID}') against the digest you reviewed, or mirror the plugin by tag into a registry you control.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
A Velero restore that includes port49-etcd is a store restore, and a store restore rolls the revocation marks back too. It loses every revocation and lift made since the backup, so a revoked principal or certificate is admitted again until it is re-issued, and it brings back every token redeemed since, redeemable again while it has not expired. The backup also restores port49d's <accounting.spool_path>.restore.json and the brokers' witness.json with the store (two port49d with spools in one directory each keep their own record). port49d can then tell the restore only if <accounting.spool_path>.restore.json is newer than the etcd copy, which is usual on a store with writes in the backup window and not so on an idle one, and a broker tells it on the same terms (its witness.json is then newer than the restored witness), and purges once more and says so at its first takeover: the token delete (step 3 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot) is required, and it must land before port49d or a broker reaches the restored store. A Velero restore cannot use --bump-revision, so when port49d does tell the restore it also arms the 5-minute band: see "What you see after step 9" below. So the restore is made in this order, with nothing reaching the store until the end.

Run step 2 in this directory (deploy/helm/port49/examples/velero/), which holds restore-unspent.yaml; step 8 from the repository root. <release> is your Helm release name, <backup> the Velero backup, <brokers> and <port49d> the broker.replicas and port49d.replicas you run, <prefix> the store prefix (/port49/ by default), and <restore> a name for the restore of port49, new each time you make one (port49-restore-1, then port49-restore-2).

Do not restore port49 with its StatefulSets at 0 replicas (a resource modifier setting /spec/replicas to 0, as the restore-scale-zero.yaml of earlier versions of this page did). Velero's file-system restore copies a volume through the pod that mounts it, and at 0 replicas there is none: measured on kind in L89 cell (c), run 42053716808, the restore stayed InProgress past 8 minutes with every pod volume restore at New and its pod absent. It does not finish. If you started one, see "Recovering from a restore at 0 replicas" below.

So the pods run for the restore, and etcd is held down while they do, so none of them reaches the store.

First, silence the alerts for the restore's window. This order keeps port49d away from the store for longer than 5 minutes, so port49_target_absent (page, 5m) fires, and port49_target_down (page, 2m) fires if step 4's pods crash-loop while etcd is held down. Silence both, and the etcd rules, in Alertmanager for the length you expect the restore to take, and remove the silence after step 11. Expect port49_store_restore_detected (ticket) afterwards; step 9 says why.

Then, if a GitOps controller manages the release, suspend it for both namespaces. These follow Argo CD's and Flux's documented commands and are not measured in port49's lab (L89 runs no GitOps controller). Argo CD with auto-sync or self-heal, or Flux, puts back what this order takes away: it re-creates the HorizontalPodAutoscaler that step 4 leaves out and reverts step 6's scale to 0, so brokers and port49d start before etcd is back or before step 8 re-issues the revocations. Skipping this can admit a revoked principal until step 8 runs.

For each Argo CD Application that manages port49 or port49-etcd, first note its sync policy: copy the .spec.syncPolicy.automated object of argocd app get <app> -o json as it is (its prune, selfHeal, allowEmpty and enabled), so step 11 restores exactly that. Suspend the parent too when the app is managed by another (app-of-apps, or generated by an ApplicationSet): the parent's next sync turns the child's sync back on. For a parent Application, suspend it the same way, first. For an ApplicationSet, first suspend the Application that syncs the ApplicationSet itself, if one does (or it puts the ApplicationSet back as Git has it), then keep the ApplicationSet from overwriting the child's sync policy: add .spec.syncPolicy to its spec.ignoreApplicationDifferences (- jqPathExpressions: [.spec.syncPolicy]), and remove that again after step 11 (first, check your Argo CD version supports ignoreApplicationDifferences). Then:

argocd app set <app> --sync-policy none

Under Flux, suspend every HelmRelease and every Kustomization that applies port49 or port49-etcd (the etcd example is plain manifests, reconciled by a Kustomization):

flux suspend helmrelease <name> -n <namespace>
flux suspend kustomization <name> -n <namespace>

Then:

kubectl delete namespace port49 port49-etcd

  1. etcd alone. No port49d or broker exists yet, so nothing reaches the store.

    velero restore create --from-backup <backup> --include-namespaces port49-etcd --wait
kubectl -n port49-etcd wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=etcd --timeout=5m

  2. The token delete (step 3 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot), from a one-shot pod holding etcd's root client certificate (the Secret port49-etcd-root, as etcd-init-job.yaml uses it). Edit PREFIX in the file if your prefix is not /port49/.

    kubectl apply -f restore-unspent.yaml
state=
for i in $(seq 120); do
  state=$(kubectl -n port49-etcd get job/restore-unspent -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.status=="True")].type}')
  case "$state" in *Complete*|*Failed*) break ;; esac
  sleep 2
done
kubectl -n port49-etcd logs job/restore-unspent --all-containers || true
case "$state" in
  *Complete*) kubectl -n port49-etcd delete job/restore-unspent ;;
  *) echo "restore-unspent did not complete ($state): read its log above, and do not go on to step 3" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

    This ends when the Job completes or fails, and prints its log either way. If it did not complete, do not go on: the log says why. Each delete is its own container (unspent, judged, judged-bundle), so kubectl -n port49-etcd logs job/restore-unspent -c unspent shows one, and kubectl -n port49-etcd describe job/restore-unspent has its pods. Delete the Job before applying it again. The deletes need a quorum of etcd, not every member: one member not yet answering after the restore is fine as long as the Job completes. context deadline exceeded from every container means no quorum: bring etcd's members back before trying again. The Job runs etcdctl from etcd's own image, so it needs no egress.

  3. Hold etcd down: kubectl -n port49-etcd scale statefulset/etcd --replicas=0.

  4. Restore port49, without the HorizontalPodAutoscaler (the chart's autoscaling.enabled): a pod it added while the pods run would have a claim with no backup, and step 5 would find a pod with no line. Step 11 brings it back. Its pods start, so the node agent can restore their volumes, and with etcd down they cannot reach the store. The lab cannot hold its etcd down apart from the release (one namespace), so L89 (d) runs this command with its etcd up.

    velero restore create <restore> --from-backup <backup> --include-namespaces port49 \
  --exclude-resources horizontalpodautoscalers.autoscaling --wait

  5. Check that the volumes came back, by the restore's name. This prints the restore's phase, then one line per pod volume restore:

    kubectl -n velero get restore <restore> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n velero get podvolumerestores -l velero.io/restore-name=<restore> -o custom-columns=PHASE:.status.phase,POD:.spec.pod.name,VOLUME:.spec.volume

    The phase must be Completed, and there must be a Completed line with volume data for every broker pod (<release>-broker-0, -1, ...) and every port49d pod (<release>-port49d-0, ...). A pod with no line did not have its volume restored. A line still New or InProgress is still copying: run the check again. Never go on to step 7 while the restore or any of these lines is not Completed. A broker that starts on an empty state_dir puts back none of the revocations the store restore lost. If one is missing or Failed, stop: no broker or port49d has reached the store, so start over from the first command with a new <restore>.

  6. Scale both StatefulSets to 0, and wait until no port49 pod is left.

    kubectl -n port49 scale statefulset/<release>-broker statefulset/<release>-port49d --replicas=0
kubectl -n port49 wait --for=delete pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=port49 --timeout=3m

  7. Bring etcd back: kubectl -n port49-etcd scale statefulset/etcd --replicas=3, and wait for it as step 1 does.

  8. Then, with no broker and no port49d running, re-issue the revocations made since the backup (step 4 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot). The script leaves the brokers at the 0 it finds. Run it from the repository root.

    deploy/helm/port49/scripts/revoke-offline.sh port49 <release> -- --principal user:bob@example.com

  9. The brokers first, a broker whose broker.state_dir survived the restore first (the check in step 5 showed every broker's volume restored, so any of them does); then port49d.

    kubectl -n port49 scale statefulset/<release>-broker --replicas=<brokers>
kubectl -n port49 rollout status statefulset/<release>-broker --timeout=10m
kubectl -n port49 scale statefulset/<release>-port49d --replicas=<port49d>
kubectl -n port49 rollout status statefulset/<release>-port49d --timeout=10m

    What you see after step 9. port49d usually logs the session store was restored from a snapshot (its <accounting.spool_path>.restore.json is newer than the etcd copy) and port49_store_restore_detected fires. This restore did not use --bump-revision, so for the 5 minutes after port49d's read every token a user mints is refused token_spent (FAIL): the new timeline's revisions sit below the old high_header. Users see a failed login, and so does every retry until the window ends. The log line names the time (a token minted until <time> (5 minutes after this read)). Tell users to mint a new token after it: a token minted inside the window keeps its mint time, so it stays refused until the band ends (20 minutes after the read), and a user who pastes the same token again keeps failing. A fresh mint after the window is served. No restored token is accepted at any point. Break-glass is unaffected. The band itself lasts 20 minutes, but only tokens minted in its first 5 are refused.

  10. Lift again what was lifted since (step 6 of Restoring etcd from a snapshot).

  11. Bring back what step 4 left out, and resume what you suspended first. With a GitOps controller, resuming it does both (unmeasured, as above). Under Argo CD, put back the automated object you noted, exactly, children first, then any parent and the Application that syncs an ApplicationSet:

    argocd app patch <app> --type merge -p '{"spec":{"syncPolicy":{"automated":<noted JSON>}}}'

    Under Flux, resume each one you suspended:

    flux resume helmrelease <name> -n <namespace>
flux resume kustomization <name> -n <namespace>

    Without one, upgrade the release to the chart version it runs, which re-creates the HorizontalPodAutoscaler and changes nothing else:

    helm upgrade <release> <chart> --version <version> -n port49 --reuse-values

With the chart's autoscaling.enabled, the HPA is not restored (step 4) until step 11.

docs.title: Recovering from a restore at 0 replicas
docs.text:
A restore made with the StatefulSets at 0 replicas waits for pods that never start, and Velero restores one at a time, so it holds up every restore after it. No broker or port49d ran, so nothing reached the store. Restart Velero, delete that restore (<restore> here is its name), then start over from the first command above with a new <restore>. Measured on kind in L89 cell (d), run 42058930263, on (c)'s hung restore: after these commands the restore was gone and no restore was New or InProgress.

kubectl -n velero rollout restart deployment/velero
kubectl -n velero rollout status deployment/velero --timeout=5m
velero restore delete <restore> --confirm
kubectl -n velero wait --for=delete restore/<restore> --timeout=5m

Prefer restoring etcd from the etcdctl snapshot CronJob (backup-cronjob.yaml) with --bump-revision, as Restoring etcd from a snapshot gives it, and use Velero for the other volumes. A file-system copy of a live etcd member is crash-consistent at best, and the three members are copied at different moments; whether a busy member's database survives that is unmeasured. L89 measured one restore on an idle cluster.

The data-directory init containers refuse a volume whose files are not owned by uid 65532 (see the chart README), so what a restore does to ownership, group and mode matters. L89 (a) measured it on kind: owner, group and mode of state/, issuing-ca.key and the spool directory were unchanged, and both StatefulSets became ready with no fence refusal.

docs.title: Broker and agent
docs.text:
Two long-running pieces sit between a person and a device, and they run in different places. The broker runs on your servers. The agent runs on the person's own machine. When a sign-in goes wrong, the first question is which of the two you are looking at.

Broker Agent Binary port49-broker port49, started by port49 login Runs on your servers, next to port49d and the stores the machine where the person works One per deployment (run several for availability) person, per machine Holds the issuing key, the revocation marks, the policy one mutual-TLS connection to the broker, and the key that proves it Listens on HTTPS, with the TLS certificate you gave it a Unix socket that only that person can reach Goes away when you stop it the session ends, or the person stops it

docs.title: The broker
docs.text:
The broker is the HTTPS service that checks who a person is and decides what they may reach. It:

  • resolves group membership from the directory at the moment of each request
  • evaluates policy
  • mints the tokens port49d later redeems

It also issues the short-lived certificates for OIDC and directory sign-ins. Concepts follows one login through it. Identities covers the three ways a person proves who they are.

You install it with the rest of the server, in the shape you chose: see Install. Its certificate and the CA the clients trust are on the TLS page.

Its state directory, broker.state_dir, holds the revocation marks and must survive a restart. The install page says what else must.

What an operator sees when the broker is down:

  • A person who is not logged in cannot log in. For an OIDC or directory sign-in, port49 login says the broker at <broker> did not answer, and until when the certificate it holds is valid. Trying again when the broker answers is the whole remedy; a new sign-in would fail at the same place. A certificate login that cannot reach the broker ends by printing the end of agent.log.
  • A person who is logged in cannot mint. port49 token fails because the broker is unavailable: the broker_unavailable code of port49 token --json (see Signing in).
  • A device login already in progress carries on. port49d answers it from the store, not the broker. How long it carries on is session.staleness_ceiling, on the port49d reference.

docs.title: The agent
docs.text:
port49 login proves the person's identity to the broker once, and starts the agent to keep what that produced. The agent holds the mutual-TLS connection open. If the key lives on a hardware token, it also holds the token's unlocked session.

Every other port49 command (token, ssh, refresh, identity, revoke) asks the agent over its socket. None of them signs in again, so a second terminal needs no second login.

  • Where it is. The socket is $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/port49/agent.sock. With XDG_RUNTIME_DIR unset it is port49-<uid>/agent.sock under the system's temporary directory. The directory is created 0700. The agent refuses to use one that is not that user's alone, because whoever can reach the socket can mint as that person.
  • Its log. agent.log, in the same directory. port49 login prints its path and, when the agent exits at start, the last lines of it.
  • No flag moves it. A command that says no agent at <path> is looking where its own XDG_RUNTIME_DIR points. If you logged in from a shell with a different XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (a sudo, a cron job, a container), the agent is somewhere else. Run port49 login in the shell that needs it, or give both shells the same XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
  • It does not dump core. The agent marks itself non-dumpable where the platform allows, so a crash does not write the key to disk. It says so on its log if it could not, and runs on.

docs.title: How long it lives
docs.text:
The agent ends itself. It exits at whichever comes first:

  • the session's end, which is the broker's max_session_age counted from the sign-in (the log says the session reached max_session_age);
  • the end of its certificate, after which the broker takes no request. For a certificate port49 issued, the next port49 login signs the person in again;
  • the broker ending the session, for a revocation or a certificate it no longer trusts (see Revocation);
  • SIGTERM or SIGINT.
