port49 refresh asks the agent to do two things: re-authenticate its session, and extend each live device session that the policy in force still grants. It prints this login lasts until <time>, which is when the agent will exit next, and one line per device.

When the agent is gone, every command says no agent at <path> and names port49 login as the next step. That is the whole recovery. A token already minted is single use and short-lived whether or not an agent is running.

docs.title: One agent, one identity
docs.text:
A second port49 login to a running agent does not start another. It refreshes the running one, and only when the broker and the certificate are the same ones.

A login for another broker, or with another certificate, is refused with already holds the agent. Refreshing would extend one identity's device sessions while the person believed they had switched. To switch, stop the first agent, or let its session end.

A hardware key adds one more case: Hardware keys covers what a locked or absent key looks like and how to put the PIN back.

docs.title: Which side owns what
docs.text: Question Look at Can this person sign in at all? the broker: its log, the decision log, Identities Was the token refused? the broker's decision log, with a code from Reason codes no agent at ... the person's machine: XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, then port49 login The agent exited agent.log on the person's machine The device refused a token it was given port49d's decision log, not the broker's

docs.title: Hardware keys
docs.text:
A person's session key can live on a YubiKey instead of in a file, and a device's policy can require a touch on that key at login. This page is "set up your key": what the key is for, how port49 hwkey setup and port49 hwkey status check it, and what can go wrong.

Only the client build of port49 reads a YubiKey or a smartcard. The static build, which the server package and the container image carry, cannot: port49 hwkey exits 2 there with a message saying it was built without PKCS#11 support. Install the clients says which build you have and where to get the other, and how to find the PKCS#11 module (libykcs11) on Linux and macOS.

docs.title: Two keys on one token
docs.text:
A device that accepts hardware_key_touch needs two keys on the same YubiKey:

Key Slot Policy Config key The session key, which signs the login and each refresh 9a, or 9e where a site keeps it PIN once, touch never issued_key The touch key, which signs a challenge from the broker for each device that asks 9c touch always touch_key

The broker checks that both attestations chain to Yubico's roots and name the same device. A session key in a file or in the TPM cannot satisfy it, and a policy that accepts only hardware_key_touch locks that person out. The policy side is in the port49d reference under broker.identity.per_login_mfa; the keys on the person's side are in the client reference.

docs.title: Check the key: port49 hwkey status
docs.text:
status reads the token and reports; it opens no key with the PIN and writes nothing to the token.

port49 hwkey status                 # human lines
port49 hwkey status --json          # one JSON object, for a script
port49 hwkey status --module <path-to>/libykcs11.so --token 1

Its first line says which attestation roots it will check against:

roots: from broker broker.example.com:8443
module: <path-to>/libykcs11.so.2 (found)
token: <masked label>
ok    session_slot
...
ready

The roots are the broker's own, fetched over TLS and checked against the broker_ca in the person's config, because a copy held by every user would drift from what the broker applies. They are public certificates. The line is roots: from broker <host>, or roots: --roots <file> when --roots FILE names a file instead; that is for offline use, and it wins over the broker. There is no config key for roots. --broker URL names a different broker to ask.

Each line after is a check, ok or FAIL with a reason. The names are a closed set: session_slot, touch_slot, attestation_roots, session_attested, touch_attested, touch_policy, same_token, and, for status alone, config_issued_key, config_touch_key, issued_certificate, certificate_expiry and agent. The attestation checks are the broker's own code, so a key that passes here passes the broker's. A serial is never printed: every line, error lines and --json reasons included, shows it masked.

status exits 0 when every check passes, 1 when something needs doing, and 2 on an error. The exit-code table has the full list.

docs.title: Set it up: port49 hwkey setup
docs.text:
setup runs the same checks, and when all pass it writes issued_key and touch_key into the person's own config file, and nothing else.

port49 hwkey setup
  • It changes only a file you own. If issued_key or touch_key already names another key, it shows the old and new values and asks, at a terminal. With no terminal it changes nothing and exits 1. A key supplied by /etc/port49/config.yaml is reported, not edited: ask the administrator, or set the key in your own file.
  • When a check fails, it prints the commands to run. The key is made with ykman, which asks for the management key; port49 never does, and never runs ykman itself:
# if 9a already holds a key, add its certificate (this replaces nothing):
ykman piv certificates generate --subject "CN=port49 9a" 9a port49-9a.pub.pem
# only if 9a holds no key, make one (this replaces any key already there):
ykman piv keys generate --algorithm ECCP256 --pin-policy ONCE --touch-policy NEVER 9a port49-9a.pub.pem

That is what an empty session slot prints; slot 9c prints the same with --touch-policy ALWAYS. port49 cannot tell an empty slot from a key that has no certificate, because libykcs11 lists a slot's key only with a certificate in it, so it prints both lines, certificate first. Run the keys generate line only if the slot holds no key. No line names a serial, PIN, PUK or management key.

  • Which token and which module. The module is found by --module, then the module-path of a key already in your config, then a probe of the system paths (not on macOS: pass --module). With more than one token present it lists them by number, model and masked label, exits 2, and wants --token N. A session key in the TPM, a file or the Secure Enclave is reported as not on a token.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 ready; for setup, the keys were written or already name this token 1 action needed: a check failed, no token is inserted, the session key is not on a token, or setup would replace a key and did not 2 an error, with a message: a bad flag, a config file that is refused, no roots, no module, a module that is refused, several tokens and no --token, a config write that fails

The roots have their own messages, all exit 2, and each names the way out:

  • the broker <host> is unreachable, so the attestation roots could not be fetched: retry, or pass --roots FILE: the broker did not answer. It is not a statement about the key.
  • the broker <host> did not present a certificate from the configured broker CA ...: check broker_ca, or pass --roots FILE: a trust failure, not an outage. Do not work around it by pointing --roots at whatever file is to hand; find out why the certificate is not the broker's.
  • no attestation roots: the broker <host> serves none ...: the broker does not verify hardware_key_touch at all, because attestation_roots_file is not set there.

docs.title: Logging in with the key
docs.text:
port49 login asks the key's PIN once, on the terminal, with echo off. The PIN goes to the agent on a file descriptor and is zeroed after use. It is never on a command line, in the environment, or in a log. A wrong PIN is sent once and never retried. The message says fewer tries are left after the first wrong PIN and one try is left before the key locks after the second: the YubiKey measured for this page reports the first as the token's low-tries flag and the second as its final-try flag. A blocked PIN is unblocked with the PUK: ykman piv access unblock-pin.

When a device asks for a touch, port49 token and port49 ssh say touch your key now. The token blinks. Touch it, or run the command again. On that YubiKey an untouched request ended after 14.4 seconds with no touch within 15s; touch the key when it blinks and try again, the key stayed unlocked, no PIN try was spent, and a touch right after the timeout signed with no PIN.

docs.title: A wrong PIN typed anywhere on the machine logs the agent off the key
docs.text:
This is intended behaviour, not a fault to report. A mistyped PIN in another process, such as a second terminal's port49 login, makes the token log the running agent's session off. The agent's next refresh then says your key needs its PIN: run port49 login, and its status reads locked. This was seen with one wrong PIN at a second port49 login on one YubiKey.

The instruction is to log in again with port49 login, which asks the PIN. A correct PIN typed in another process did not do this. Until you have a reason to do otherwise, give each token to one user at a time, and never let a script try a PIN on a token that an agent holds. A script that guesses a wrong PIN on a timer logs the agent off every time and spends the token's tries. The second box under "What has not been measured" lists what is still unknown about it.

docs.title: Two risks
docs.text:
A lent key plus its PIN is the person's login. The PIN is the only thing between whoever holds the key and port49 login as that person, and the touch only proves that someone was at the key. A key that was lent, lost or taken is the person's identity until it is revoked. Revoke the certificate or the principal: see Revocation and the runbook in Administer: revocation. Do not wait for the certificate to expire.

A wrong attestation root checks the wrong thing. port49 hwkey reports a key as ready against the roots it was given, and --roots FILE replaces the broker's. A file with a root the broker does not hold, or without one it does, makes status say ready for a key that the broker will refuse, or the reverse. The broker applies its own roots whatever status said, so a wrong file cannot grant anything; it can only waste an afternoon at the console. Use the broker's roots unless you are offline, and when you are, take the file from the broker's administrator, not from the key.

docs.title: What has not been measured
docs.text:
Unmeasured

port49 hwkey status and port49 hwkey setup have not been run against a real YubiKey for this register entry: how they behave there, and whether libykcs11 lists a slot's key when the slot holds no certificate, are unknown (L91, open). The ykman lines above are what the commands print; treat them as a starting point and read ykman piv info before and after.

Unmeasured

The touch timeout, the low-tries flags and the wrong-PIN behaviour above were measured on one YubiKey 5C Nano FIPS, firmware 5.4.3, with libykcs11 2.7.2 (the lab note). Other tokens, other firmware and other libykcs11 versions are unknown (L60, open). Also unknown: whether a port49 login to the running agent puts it back on the key after a wrong PIN typed in another process; whether port49 token still mints on the connection the agent already holds after it; and what other processes using the token do to the agent. Whether parallel forks, such as several Ansible workers sharing one agent, are asked for one touch or for several when a device requires hardware_key_touch is a question for L60's next session. The agent serializes token requests, but what the key does is not measured. A person runs port49 ssh <device> once for one such device before a play, as the Ansible collection's README says.

Unmeasured

On macOS, port49 accepts a PKCS#11 module that the admin group can write, and no other group, because Homebrew's prefix is group-writable by admin. That exception's evidence is a CI run in which Homebrew's libykcs11.dylib was refused without the rule, and its hardware claims were measured on Linux. No register entry covers a YubiKey on a Mac, so whether a Homebrew Mac loads the module and signs in end to end is unknown.

Unmeasured

How the macOS Secure Enclave key store behaves on a Mac is unknown (L63, open). It is experimental and opt-in.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text: A person signs in once with port49 login, then asks for a token for each device with port49 token or lets port49 ssh do both steps. This page is for the operator who has to explain what those commands do, and what they return to a script. The pieces they talk to are on Broker and agent.

docs.title: port49 login
docs.text:
port49 login proves who the person is to the broker and starts the agent that keeps the result. It takes one of three methods, each the same command with a different flag.

Instead of a flag, the person can set the method once in their config file with method:. A flag always overrides its config key. The keys are in the client configuration reference.

# A client certificate and key the person already holds
port49 login --broker https://broker.example.com:8443 --broker-ca <broker-ca.pem> \
  --cert <client-cert.pem> --key <client-key.pem>

# A sign-in at the identity provider; the broker issues the certificate
port49 login --oidc

# A directory name, password and authenticator code, asked at the terminal
port49 login --directory

A successful login prints port49: logged in to <broker>; the session ends at <time>, with the agent's process id and the path of its log.

A second port49 login while the agent runs refreshes that agent instead of starting another one. It says already logged in to <broker>; refreshing.

  • --oidc and --directory hold the certificate the broker issues. They sign in again only when that certificate has under a quarter of its life left, or when you pass --sign-in.
  • --cert and --key belong to the certificate method. Combining them with --oidc or --directory is refused, as is naming both of those two together.
  • The key may be on a hardware token. A key that starts pkcs11: is asked for its PIN once, on the terminal. See Hardware keys.
  • Where the broker and its CA come from. Flags first, then the person's own config file, then /etc/port49/config.yaml key by key. The broker's CA is required; the system's roots are never trusted for the broker.

docs.title: port49 token
docs.text:
port49 token core-sw01            # prints the login token, and nothing else, on stdout
port49 token --ttl 30s core-sw01  # shorten the token's life below your token_ttl; never lengthens it
port49 token --json core-sw01     # the broker's whole answer as one JSON object

A token's life is set by policy, not by you. Each subject's token_ttl (30s to 900s, on the policy reference) is how long its token stays usable before its one login. --ttl can only ask for less: a value above token_ttl gets token_ttl. How long the session on the device then lasts is the role's max_session_age, a separate setting (The token).

Flags come before the device name.

The token is the one secret that port49 ever writes to standard output. Give it to the device where the device asks for a password. It is single use and short-lived by design: see Tokens, receipts and contexts.

A store that is not ready is retried; nothing else is. If the broker's store is not ready, port49 token tries again by itself for up to 30 seconds, waiting the broker's own hint between tries. After that it fails with the last answer.

A second factor comes first. When a device's policy requires one, port49 token asks for it before the mint: a touch on the person's security key, or a sign-in at the identity provider. It prints which one, and what to do.

docs.title: --json
docs.text:
With --json, standard output is exactly one JSON object whether the mint worked or not, so a script reads one thing. Standard error carries the human words.

On success it is the broker's answer for that device. These are its keys:

Key Meaning device the device as the inventory names it verdict permit address, platform, username where to connect and as whom login the login token: <token> enable the enable token, present only with --enable expires_at when the token stops being redeemable session_expires_at when a login made with it stops being authorized; absent when the roles say never

The object holds the tokens, so treat it as a secret: do not log it.

The --enable flag mints an enable token beside the login token. Without --json, only the login token is printed.

On a failure the command exits 1 and the object has device and one of these shapes:

  • A refusal by policy. verdict is deny, and detail says why in words. reason is a code from Reason codes, the same closed vocabulary the decision log uses. It is never a code that table does not list.
  • A failure of the client or the broker. error is one of the codes below, and detail says more. These codes belong to the command and are never reason codes. The one exception is a device the broker could not decide: then error is the broker's code for it.
  • A requirement to prove. error is per_login_mfa_required and per_login_mfa lists accept (the methods that satisfy it), reuse_for_seconds, and where the reuse comes from. A challenge is never printed.
error What it means, and what to do no_agent nothing listens at the agent's socket: run port49 login, or check XDG_RUNTIME_DIR agent_too_old the agent was started by an older port49: run port49 login again session_over the session has ended: run port49 login credential_revoked the broker refuses this credential or session; a revocation is in force revocation_running a revocation of yours is still running on the broker; run the command again when it reports per_login_mfa_required prove the second factor, then run it again connection_changed the connection changed during a touch; nothing was sent: run it again broker_refused the broker refused the request or a proof, or its certificate was refused by the CRL check broker_unavailable the broker did not answer; try again when it does key_locked the hardware key needs its PIN: run port49 login (Hardware keys) key_absent the hardware key is not inserted touch_timeout no touch arrived in time; run it again and touch when the key blinks no_token the broker said permit and gave no token; tell the broker's operator agent_error any other fault of the agent or the broker; the detail has the words

A token near the end of the session's ceiling also prints a warning. The warning goes to standard error, never to standard output, so --json stays one object.

docs.title: port49 ssh
docs.text:
port49 ssh does the mint and the connection together. It asks the agent for a token, runs your own OpenSSH (8.5 or later) with the token ready for the device's password prompt, and exits with ssh's status.

port49 ssh core-sw01                       # a shell
port49 ssh core-sw01 -- show version       # one command
port49 ssh --port 2222 --ttl 30s core-sw01   # --ttl shortens the token's life; never lengthens it

Its flags:

  • --ttl, shorter than your token_ttl only, as for port49 token
  • --port
  • --ssh PATH, for another OpenSSH
  • --ssh-config FILE, for another ssh_config
  • -v

The device name may hold only letters, digits, ., _ and -. For any other name, use port49 token and your own ssh.

A login costs one attempt. The options port49 ssh passes to ssh are fixed: no public-key offers, one password prompt, no connection sharing, no agent forwarding.

The token goes only to the device it was minted for. A prompt from anything else on the way, such as a jump host that asks for its own password, is not answered with it. If the device asks for the password a second time, port49 ssh ends the connection, so no second or empty password is sent.

docs.title: Host keys
docs.text:
OpenSSH owns the device's host key. port49 does not pin one, keep a list, or add a trust step of its own.

port49 ssh runs ssh with StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new:

  • A device met for the first time is accepted and filed in your known_hosts.
  • A device whose key has changed is refused.
  • If your own ssh_config says StrictHostKeyChecking yes, that stands, and the key must already be in known_hosts.

The keys are filed under the device's name, lowercased, unless your ssh_config sets a HostKeyAlias.

Two consequences an operator should know:

  • If ssh says Host key verification failed, the key filed under the device's name is not the one it presented. Verify the new key on the device's console, then remove the old one with ssh-keygen -R <device> (the failure message prints the exact command for your known_hosts) and connect again. Do not remove it first and accept whatever answers.
  • Under accept-new, if your ssh_config points UserKnownHostsFile somewhere that cannot keep a key, such as /dev/null, port49 ssh refuses before sending anything, because every connection would be a first contact. With your own StrictHostKeyChecking yes that refusal does not apply.

docs.title: Telling port49's refusals from ssh's
docs.text:
A remote command can exit 1, and so can port49 ssh. Look for a line that starts port49 ssh: on standard error to tell them apart.

  • port49 refused. It says so under the port49 ssh: prefix, and it sent nothing to the device.
  • ssh or the device failed. ssh's own messages have no such prefix. When ssh exits 255 after the device was sent the token, port49 ssh: adds a line saying so, with port49 explain --device <device> as the next step.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
These codes are taken from the commands' code.

Command Code Meaning port49 login 0 logged in, or an agent already running was refreshed port49 login 1 the agent did not start, or did not answer within 15 seconds (the end of agent.log is printed); another broker's or another certificate's agent holds the socket, or --sign-in was given while one runs; refreshing the running agent failed; the agent socket's directory is not private; the sign-in failed at the identity provider or the directory; the broker did not answer; the broker refused the certificate it issued; a hardware key is absent, blocked or refused its PIN port49 login 2 the command line or the config is refused: an unknown flag, flags that contradict each other, a config file that cannot be read or that others can write, a missing --broker or --broker-ca, or a key file that is readable by others port49 ssh 0 ssh ended with 0 port49 ssh 1 port49 refused before ssh ran: no OpenSSH, one older than 8.5, a mint that failed, no agent, a socket directory that is not private, an ssh_config that keeps no host keys under accept-new, or a config file refused while proving an idp_mfa device's sign-in. Also ssh's own status when the remote command exits 1. Read the port49 ssh: line port49 ssh 2 a flag it does not accept, no device named, or a device name it does not accept port49 ssh 255 ssh's own failure (connection, host key, authentication), or port49 ended ssh: the asker could not be verified, the token was asked for after it expired, or the device asked for the password again port49 revoke 0 done; --list printed port49 revoke 1 refused or unreachable: no agent, the right missing, the touch refused or not given, a declined confirmation (nothing was revoked), an unreadable --cert file. Also when the broker did not answer, or answered without naming a revocation, and the revocation may be in force (it may be in force, it may have run): run port49 revoke --list before you retry port49 revoke 2 the flags are wrong: no target, two targets, or a flag that does not go with the form port49 revoke 3 the revocation is in force but incomplete or not saved, or a lift step did not finish: run the same command again port49 hwkey 0 ready; for setup, the keys are written, or already name this token port49 hwkey 1 action needed: a check failed, no token is inserted, the session key is not on a token, or setup would change a key and was not allowed to port49 hwkey 2 an error: a bad flag, no attestation roots, an unreachable or untrusted broker, a config file that is refused or cannot be written, no module found or one refused, several tokens with no --token, or the build has no hardware-key support

port49 token and port49 refresh exit 0 when they worked, 1 when they did not, and 2 for a usage error. Under --json, port49 token writes its failure object before it exits 1.

One refused config file gives different codes. A config file that others can write is refused, but not at the same moment by every command:

  • port49 login reads it first and exits 2.
  • port49 ssh and port49 token read it only when a device asks for an idp_mfa sign-in. There the refusal ends the mint with exit 1.

A script that reads the cause from the exit code alone will get this case wrong.

A script should check the code, not the text. A command run by cron or a script reads the exit code. The words are meant for a person and may change.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: port49 is watched through three things: Prometheus metrics, a shipped set of alert rules, and the logs. When an alert has fired or a log line worries you, go to the 3am index; this page is what to set up before that.

docs.title: Scraping
docs.text:
Every process serves /metrics on its metrics_listen address. The defaults:

Process Port job the alert rules expect port49d 9049 port49d port49-broker 9050 port49-broker

The job name is not cosmetic. Three rules read Prometheus's own up series by it (up{job="port49d"} and up{job="port49-broker"}): port49_target_down, port49_target_absent and port49_broker_target_absent. Give the jobs these names, or edit the rules.

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: port49d
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["<port49d-host>:9049"]
  - job_name: port49-broker
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["<broker-host>:9050"]

On Helm, prometheusRule.enabled: true renders the rules as a PrometheusRule, and a PodMonitor for each workload with job set to port49d and port49-broker.

  • It needs the Prometheus Operator's CRDs.
  • prometheusRule.labels must be the labels your Prometheus selects on. The same labels go on the monitors.
  • If your Prometheus selects PodMonitors on other labels, set them on the monitors yourself.

The metrics ports listen on every address of the host or pod and need no credential. Restrict them to your Prometheus (and, on Kubernetes, the kubelet, whose probes use the same port). The chart renders no NetworkPolicy.

port49_target_absent fires when Prometheus has no up series for port49d at all, which means no port49d is being scraped. That rule is fleet-wide: use one Prometheus per port49 fleet, or add a namespace matcher to the two absent rules.

No metric carries a device name or address. "Which device" is answered by the decision log, not by a label.

docs.title: The alerts
docs.text:
deploy/alerts/port49.rules.yaml holds the rules. Load it with rule_files:, or take the Helm chart's copy. There are two severities, and you route on the severity label:

  • page: port49 is refusing devices or losing records now.
  • ticket: it costs nothing yet, or a person fixes it in working hours.

Every alert carries a runbook_url that opens its section of the alerts reference, which gives its expression and why the threshold is what it is. The 3am index gives a do and a don't for each family.

The rules assume the defaults of the settings they watch (close_after, refresh_interval, staleness_ceiling and so on). If you change one, edit the matching rule; the reference lists them.

docs.title: The disk etcd and the spool need
docs.text:
etcd needs a disk with sustained WAL fsync p99 under 10 ms. Datacenter NVMe and cloud SSD volumes qualify; a consumer QLC drive does not.

A drive that stalls pushes port49's store calls past the 500 ms call timeout in bursts. A store call that times out is a token login answered store_unavailable.

Two alerts watch for it:

  • etcd_disk_slow (reference) fires after 10 minutes when the p99 of etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds is over 10 ms, or the p99 of etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds is over 25 ms. It reads etcd's own metrics, so scrape etcd.
  • port49_accounting_spool_disk_slow (reference) fires after 10 minutes when the p99 of port49_accounting_spool_sync_seconds is over 10 ms. The 10 ms is port49's own threshold, not an etcd figure.

It matters because port49d acknowledges an accounting record only after the record is synced to the spool. A slow disk under accounting.spool_path slows every accounting reply, and a device may see accounting fail.

The sizing defaults were measured on a cloud SSD volume that passed every load cell. The same run on a consumer QLC drive failed. The figures and the gates applied to them are in tests/lab/results/load-beehive-gates.md. Put the session etcd and the accounting spool on disks that meet the 10 ms line before you rely on either.

docs.title: Accounting is delivered at least once
docs.text:
port49d writes each accounting record to its spool and forwards it to the decision log. The log can hold the same account record twice, in two ways:

  • A crash between forwarding a record and removing it from the spool forwards that record again at the next start.
  • A record the log refuses is offered again.

Dedupe on task_id together with device.nas, flags and record.raw. The log carries task_id for exactly this, and on Junos it is the only per-record counter the device sends. It is not unique alone: a device numbers its tasks within one login, so the next login starts again at 1. The other three keys keep records apart that share a task_id. record.raw holds the arguments the device sent, so a start, a stop and a watchdog update of one task stay distinct.

Never drop a record because its task_id was seen once before.

port49_accounting_spool_drops_total is different: it counts records port49d discarded, and the stage label says where. Any rise pages (port49_accounting_spool_drops).

docs.title: Shedding
docs.text:
port49d holds one pool of connection slots across both TACACS+ listeners, limits.max_connections. Left unset, it is sized from the open-file limit at start.

When the pool is full, a new connection is reset at once. The device then moves to its next server now, instead of waiting out its own timeout. That is meant, and it is never silent. port49d says so on its log when shedding begins:

port49d: shedding: all <N> TACACS+ connection slots (limits.max_connections) are in use; each new connection is reset at Accept and the device tries its next server

and, while it goes on, once a minute:

port49d: still shedding: <N> connections reset at Accept in the last minute; <N> of <N> slots in use

Each shed adds one to port49_connections_shed_total{reason="global_cap"}. The page alert port49_global_cap_shedding fires on any rise of it over five minutes. Its warning, the ticket port49_connections_near_cap, fires when a port49d holds more than 80% of port49_connections_max open for ten minutes.

A shed device tries its next server, and with none left it falls to local authentication. Raise limits.max_connections or add replicas before the near-cap ticket becomes the page.

The pool counts only accepted connections. The per-source limits are checked first, and they count in port49_connection_events_total, not here.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Process logs go to stderr (journald under systemd, docker compose logs, kubectl logs). They hold operational lines, never a token, password, challenge or response. The decision log is separate and structured: one record per decision, with the fields in the reference.

The log lines worth knowing at 3am are in the 3am index.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
port49 holds three kinds of secret:

  • the shared keys it shares with devices
  • the key that seals its stored records
  • the keys it uses for etcd and TLS

No secret is ever written in a configuration file, the policy, or a container's environment listing. A file that CI and every operator read carries only a name for the secret. The secret itself is a file that a mount, a package or a secret agent puts on disk.

This page says what the names look like, which files port49 will agree to read, and which mounting mechanisms were measured.

Rotation is on Key rotation.

docs.title: The secret reference
docs.text:
A key version in the policy names its secret with secret_ref. There are two forms:

Form Example Meaning env:NAME env:PORT49_KEY_CORE_V1 The environment variable NAME, read once, exactly as set. file:/absolute/path file:/etc/port49/keys/core-v1 A file, with one trailing newline removed. The path must be absolute and already clean (no .., no doubled /). 
keys:
  core:
    current: {version: 2, secret_ref: "file:/etc/port49/keys/core-v2"}
    accept:
      - {version: 1, secret_ref: "file:/etc/port49/keys/core-v1", retire_after: "2027-01-31"}

Two rules apply to both forms.

  • A reference that does not parse is refused without being printed. The likeliest cause is the secret itself, pasted where its name goes. Rotate that secret.
  • An empty secret is refused.

encryption.current.secret_ref and encryption.previous.secret_ref take the same two forms and must come to exactly 32 bytes. They are listed in the encryption reference.

docs.title: Where a policy may point: key_secret_refs
docs.text:
The policy file is written by the people who edit policy, and it is committed and reviewed. It must not be able to choose which of the host's secrets becomes a device key. So port49d.yaml carries an allowance, key_secret_refs. A device key's secret_ref outside it is refused before anything is read.

Key Default Allows key_secret_refs.env_prefix PORT49_KEY_ env: variables that start with it and are longer than it. At least 4 characters, ending in _. key_secret_refs.file_dir /run/port49/keys file: paths below this directory. Absolute, clean, never /.

Both need a restart. The full entries are in the reference.

  • port49-broker refuses the key_secret_refs key, because it never holds a device key.
  • In CI, port49 policy test --config port49d.yaml checks a policy against your allowance. Without --config it checks the defaults and says so.

The three deployment shapes set it like this:

Shape key_secret_refs Key files systemd file_dir: /etc/port49/keys (the shipped port49d.yaml) The directory is root:port49d mode 0750 and each file root:port49d 0440. /run is cleared at reboot, so the keys are not kept there. Container (Compose) the default, /run/port49/keys A port49d-keys volume mounted read-only: directory root:65532 0750, files root:65532 0440. Helm the default, /run/port49/keys One Secret mounted whole, one Secret key per version, in port49d's pod only.

The encryption key is never under the key directory. A policy may name any file below file_dir, so a sealing key kept there could be named as a device key. A port49d configuration that names key material inside file_dir is refused at start.

  • port49d's encryption key lives at /etc/port49/secrets/encryption.key on all three shapes.
  • On systemd, the broker's copy, the same 32 bytes, is /etc/port49/secrets/broker-encryption.key.

Prefer file:. A file can be added while port49d runs. An env: variable is read once and never again, and a new one cannot be added to a running process. So a version that needs an env: name needs a restart.

docs.title: The secret-file rule
docs.text:
Whoever can write a file decides who gets access to what it grants, so port49 reads a secret file only when the file and everything above it are fenced. For a file: reference, port49d requires:

  • Owner. The user port49 runs as, or root. Any other owner is refused with the uid named.
  • Mode. No world bit, and no write bit for anyone but the owner. 0440 and 0600 pass. 0644, 0660 and 0666 do not.
  • Group read needs a group port49 is in. A group-readable file is accepted only when its group is the process's own group or one of its supplementary groups, such as Kubernetes' fsGroup. A file readable by a group the process is not in, such as Debian's ssl-cert, is refused: its members could read the secret too. chgrp it to the service's group.
  • ACLs. A POSIX ACL is judged by its entries, not the mode. An entry naming any user but the process's or root, a group the process is not in, anyone with write, or other with anything, is refused.
  • Stay inside the allowed directory. A link is followed (a Kubernetes Secret volume is made of links), but the file it comes to must lie inside file_dir. A link out to the TLS key is refused.
  • The directory holding the file. Owned by the service user or root, and writable by nobody else. A read-only mount does not excuse it. The one excuse is a sticky directory (mode with the t bit, such as the Vault injector's 1777 volume) that the service user or root owns, and then only for a file with a single hard link.
  • The directories above it, and the directories that hold a link on the way. Each is owned by the service user or root. An ancestor that others can write passes only if it is sticky or on a read-only mount; a directory holding a link passes on a read-only mount. A read-only mount trusts whoever writes its source, so bind only a directory that root or the service user alone can write.

Every refusal names the file and the fix, and none prints a byte of the secret. The text you will see is like these:

  • A group the process is not in: ... is group-readable by gid N, which this process is not in (gid M) ... chgrp it to the service's group
  • A wrong owner: ... must belong to the user this process runs as ... or to root - chown it

docs.title: When a key file is not there yet
docs.text:
Put the key file in place first, and add the policy line second. To remove a key, take the policy line out first. The order matters because a running port49d and a starting one treat a missing file differently.

While port49d runs, a missing file is retried. A key version's file may not be readable yet: a Secret volume or an agent has not rendered it, or its mode is wrong. A new policy that names such a file is not put in force, and the policy already serving stays. port49d tries again every 30 seconds until the file reads or the policy file changes. It says so on the first refusal, then at most every ten minutes. A SIGHUP makes it say so again at once.

At a start, a missing file is not retried. A policy that names a file that is not there makes the start refuse. The unit or pod crash-loops until the file is back or the policy line is out.

Once read, a file is never read as a key again. If a held file is later rewritten in place, or can no longer be read, port49d keeps the secret it already holds. It counts the version in port49_key_secret_files_changed (alert). A restart would take the new bytes on that replica alone, which is how a fleet ends up with two replicas holding two secrets. The cure is a new file under a new version, never an edit (Key rotation).

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
The chart mounts the device keys from one Secret, whole, at /run/port49/keys in port49d's pod only.

  • The pod sets fsGroup: 65532 with fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch.
  • The volume's defaultMode is 0440.

So the files are owned by root, group 65532 (the process's own group), mode 0440. Measured on kind (L82, kind v0.29.0 with node image v1.33.1):

  • With defaultMode: 0440 and fsGroup: 65532 the key file is root 0440 and port49d starts with it.
  • A key added to the Secret appeared in a whole volume mount, and a login keyed with the new version passed with no container restart through External Secrets.
  • A subPath mount of the same Secret did not change after three minutes while the whole mount did. Never mount device keys with subPath; the kubelet updates only a whole mount in place.

The broker's pod loads no device key. Each etcd client identity is its own Secret, so neither pod holds the other's etcd key.

docs.title: Secret agents
docs.text:
port49 holds no client for any secret store. A store reaches it as a file that its own agent renders, and the file has to pass the secret-file rule. Two agents were measured on kind (L83):

Mechanism Device keys Encryption key Why External Secrets syncing into a Secret volume Supported Supported Measured in L82: a new version reaches a running process. Vault Agent injector No Yes, with vault.hashicorp.com/agent-run-as-same-user: "true" By default the agent is uid 100 and owns the rendered file, and port49d crash-loops on the owner rule. With agent-run-as-same-user: "true" the file is port49d's own and it starts. But a new version is a pod rollout, not a reload, so it fails the "no restart" requirement for a device key. Secrets Store CSI driver No No Its files are root mode 0644 (a world bit: refused), or 0440 with the provider's file permission set, which the process's user cannot read; the driver sets no group for fsGroup to act on.

A device key must reach a running process with no restart, which is why only a mechanism that passes that test is offered for one. The encryption key changes rarely, and a rollout is acceptable for it.

docs.title: systemd and containers
docs.text:
Both were measured in L84 (systemd 255 and Docker Compose).

  • systemd. LoadCredential= renders a file that passes the rule and may carry the encryption key for port49d. It cannot add a credential to a running unit, so device keys stay in /etc/port49/keys.
  • Compose secrets:. The file must be root:65532 mode 0440 on the host. Compose does not apply the long syntax's uid, gid or mode, and a 0444 file is refused. Adding a secret recreates port49d, so it is not used for device keys.
  • Never leave a secret in docker inspect output or a unit's Environment= line.

The install pages hold the exact commands for each shape: systemd, container, Helm.

docs.title: Stores
docs.text: port49 keeps its state in two stores, each with a job. This page says what each holds, how to lay them out for one site or several regions, and what you see and do when one is cut off. The part to read before you need it is a cut region at 3am.

docs.title: The two roles
docs.text:
Role Config key Holds Directory stores.directory The records every region must agree on: revocation marks, second factors (including the TOTP step a code was last used at), the enrollment mark, unlocks, directory membership pins and back-channel logouts. Also the key window the directory was last written under. Session stores.session Everything else: tokens, receipts, contexts, OIDC owner records, attempt counts, and the sealed snapshots each process keeps of its directory cache.

Each has a backend: memory (the default, in one process, lost when it stops) or etcd. The keys of both blocks are in the port49d reference; this page does not repeat them.

Every process loads the revocation marks from the directory before it serves and follows them as they change. A login, a mint and a command are all answered from that copy, so none of them waits on a region far away. That is why a cut region keeps serving.

docs.title: Single site
docs.text:
Leave stores.session out. The session store is then the directory store, one etcd and one keyspace:

stores:
  directory:
    backend: etcd
    etcd:
      endpoints:
        - https://etcd-1.example.net:2379
        - https://etcd-2.example.net:2379
        - https://etcd-3.example.net:2379
      ca_file: /etc/port49/etcd-ca.pem
      daemon:
        cert_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon.pem
        key_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon-key.pem

etcd in port49d.yaml needs a policy: block and no broker: block; port49-broker.yaml uses etcd too. If you do name stores.session, it must reach a different cluster, or the same one with the same keys in both blocks. Two blocks that reach one etcd cluster and one prefix under different names (an IP address and a DNS name) are refused at start, and so are two blocks that name one store and set etcd.call_timeout differently.

docs.title: Several regions
docs.text:
Stretch one directory etcd across the regions, one member in each, and give each region a session etcd of its own. Each region runs its own port49d and port49-broker.

stores:
  directory:
    backend: etcd
    etcd:
      endpoints: [https://etcd-dir-a.example.net:2379, https://etcd-dir-b.example.net:2379, https://etcd-dir-c.example.net:2379]
      ca_file: /etc/port49/etcd-ca.pem
      daemon: {cert_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon.pem, key_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon-key.pem}
  session:
    backend: etcd
    etcd:
      endpoints: [https://etcd-sess-a.example.net:2379]
      ca_file: /etc/port49/etcd-ca.pem
      prefix: /port49/
      daemon: {cert_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon.pem, key_file: /etc/port49/etcd-daemon-key.pem}

Never mix backends: memory for one store and etcd for the other is refused, and so is a nest of keyspaces on one cluster. The directory's etcd block takes endpoints, ca_file, prefix, daemon, broker, roles, call_timeout, bulk_timeout and start_timeout only.

A split starts on fresh stores. There is no migration from one store to two. Stand the new stores up empty, and let people sign in again and the brokers re-mint.

docs.title: One set of encryption keys everywhere
docs.text:
Every region holds the same encryption: keys. The directory records, in meta/seal_keys, the key ids it was last written under, and every broker start writes it. A process whose keys do not include the current id there refuses to start and exits 1, naming the directory store and the key id. That is the rule for a directory store of its own (a split); on a single shared store the start goes on, says it, and port49_crypt_store_key_unknown is 1 (alert port49_crypt_store_key_unknown). A running runner on a split rechecks the directory every hour and says the same on stderr once; that recheck sets no gauge.

Rotate in three steps. Finish a step in every region before you begin the next, and restart the processes at each (encryption needs a restart):

  1. Add the new key as encryption.previous everywhere. Nothing is sealed under it yet, but every region can now open what is.
  2. Make the new key encryption.current and the old one encryption.previous, everywhere.
  3. Remove the old key from encryption.previous, everywhere, once Key rotation's waits are over; on a split that includes port49_directory_pins_sealed_previous at 0 on the keyspace holder, from a pass that ended after the last step-2 restart.

The ids must differ, because the id labels every record the key seals.

docs.title: A cut region at 3am
docs.text:
"Cut" means a region cannot reach the directory etcd. Its session store still answers. The table is what you see, and what to do.

What happened What you see What to do A region's link to the directory is cut Devices notice nothing: logins and commands are answered from the session store and the cached marks. The line directory store: not answering (...): serving from the cache confirmed <age> ago; revocations, lifts, enrollments, unlocks and second-factor resets are refused until it answers. port49_store_directory_reachable is 0 and time() - port49_store_directory_confirmed_timestamp_seconds climbs. port49 store status prints the directory unreachable and exits 3. Alerts port49_store_directory_unreachable, then port49_store_directory_stale. Restore the link. On the heal the line directory store: answering again; the cache was <age> old appears and the marks catch up. Someone is revoked in region A while region C is cut A and B deny the person's next command. C does not: open sessions keep working, and tokens minted before the cut still log in. To cut C off now without the directory, remove the person's grants from the policy file C's hosts load (live within two watch intervals), or stop C's port49d. On the heal, C's runner says a revocation of <principal> made elsewhere reached N token key(s) and M context(s) here. A lift made in A during a long cut comes back when C heals C's runner says N revocation(s) in broker.state_dir/marks.json were missing from the store (...) and are put back. Lift it again in any region once the cut has healed (port49 revoke --lift). A person signs in with a password and a TOTP code in the cut region 503 store_unavailable, "the broker could not reach its store, so it signed no one in; try again shortly" (the first directory read of a sign-in, the person's unlock record, is what fails). The broker says sign-in: the unlock store did not answer: ..., at most once every 10 seconds. The log records an issue denial with reason store_unavailable. Use a certificate, OIDC or a hardware key, or break-glass. Password sign-in returns when the cut heals. It fails closed so that one code never signs in twice across regions. port49 revoke, port49 directory unlock, reset-second-factor, init-enrollments or import in the cut region The command fails in about stores.directory.etcd.call_timeout with "the directory store did not answer, so nothing changed". A revocation says the record may not have been made and names the fallback. Run it from a region that reaches the directory. port49d or port49-broker restarts during the cut (a deploy, an OOM kill) It serves from a snapshot, up to the ceiling (below). port49 store status shows cache <age> (snapshot). Nothing while the cut is shorter than the ceiling. The cut outlasts the ceiling on a process that started from a snapshot port49d: the line directory store: the snapshot this run serves from is <age> old, past session.staleness_ceiling (4h0m0s): the listeners close until the directory answers. port49-broker: every mint and sign-in is 503 store_unavailable. Processes that never restarted keep serving. Restore the link. Or raise session.staleness_ceiling and restart, if you know the copy is current. A process restarts in the cut and finds no snapshot younger than the ceiling (a new region, or every writer gone longer) Its listeners stay closed; port49d says no snapshot in the session store is younger than session.staleness_ceiling. A cold start exits 1 after start_timeout. The region's other processes keep serving. Wait for the heal, then start it again.

docs.title: A restart during a cut: the snapshot and its ceiling
docs.text:
Every 60 seconds, while its copy is confirmed, each process writes a sealed snapshot of its directory cache to its session store. A process that restarts while the directory does not answer serves the union of the marks in every snapshot younger than session.staleness_ceiling (4 hours by default), never the newest alone, so a deleted or replayed snapshot cannot lift a mark.

Only a load of the directory that succeeds clears the ceiling and the (snapshot) tag. At the ceiling the process fails closed: port49d closes its listeners and port49-broker refuses every mint and sign-in. A key or cluster fault found at the heal ends the process, exit 1, and its listeners do not reopen. The fix is in the process's encryption: or stores: block, not in the directory.

docs.title: When the session store is the one that is down
docs.text:
A session store port49d cannot use is a different failure. port49d checks it every etcd.health.interval (1 second by default) through its token and context pools, and after etcd.health.close_after failed checks in a row (5 by default) it closes every listener, so that devices use their local method. It opens them again after open_after passes in a row (3). The page alert is port49_store_health_failures_close; port49_store_health_failures counts the failed checks, and port49_store_circuit_open says which pool's circuit opened.

A token or context pool whose circuit stays open for etcd.hold_ttl (15 seconds by default) closes the listeners too, without waiting for the checks.

port49-broker never closes anything: it keeps answering 503 store_unavailable while its store is down, and /readyz says it is serving.

Two things stay true while this happens:

  • Only the token and context pools close the listeners. A slow or refused bulk scan opens a circuit and raises an alarm, but it is not a store gone, and it does not close anything.
  • /readyz does not report store health. It answers whether the process is serving, so a store outage does not take every replica out of a load balancer at once. Alert on the metrics above, not on /readyz.

A call whose caller's deadline had already passed when it reached the store is counted as outcome="deadline_on_entry" on port49_store_calls_total, and it does not count toward opening a circuit: the time was spent before the store was asked, so it says nothing about the store. A call that the store was too slow to answer within its deadline still counts as a failure. A rising count of this outcome is therefore not a sign that the store is unhealthy; the store alerts above are.

Some devices do not fall back to their local method when the server answers an error. See IOS XE and a down store before you rely on break-glass.

docs.title: port49 store status
docs.text:
Run it on a host that reaches the process's metrics_listen:

port49 store status --metrics 127.0.0.1:9049

It asks port49d or port49-broker what each store is. One line per role: the backend, how many of the etcd members answer out of those listed, whether the store is reachable, and for the directory the age of the cache. Examples:

directory  etcd    3/3 members  reachable  cache 0.4s
session    etcd    1/1 members  reachable

directory  etcd    ?/? members  unreachable  cache 41.2s  1 logouts pending
           <why the store did not answer, on a line of its own>

The indented second line is the reason, printed only when a store does not answer; it is not an error of its own.

cache <age> (snapshot) means the process started from a snapshot, not a live load. feeds down: lists a feed whose watch has stopped. A session store that is the directory store prints shares the directory store, and the memory backend prints in process. The exit code is 0 when every store answers, 3 when one does not (the lines are still printed), and 1 when the listener does not answer or another status is already running. --metrics defaults to 127.0.0.1:9049.

docs.title: Forgetting a directory membership
docs.text:
A person's directory entry (an LDAP entry, for example) is pinned to the principal the first time it is verified. If an entry is deleted and re-created, the principal is refused, directory: user:... is pinned to entry ... and is now claimed by ..., until an operator forgets the pin:

port49 directory forget <principal>

Confirm that the re-created entry is the same person first. One forget reaches every region: each reads the pin forgotten at its next verification. In a cut region the forget is refused (store_unavailable); run it from a region that reaches the directory. A region cut off when you forget keeps refusing the re-created entry until the heal. While the directory is cut, a member who is already pinned is served from the cached pin, and a first bind or a refusal's record fails closed.

An etcd restore from a backup older than a forget brings the old pin back. Run port49 directory forget again once the restore is done. port49d judges a restore from its own witness record whether or not the restore used etcd's --bump-revision, and says so in the alert port49_store_restore_detected; the restore steps are on backup and restore.

A cut region says, at most once per principal per 10 minutes, directory store: not answering: serving <principal>'s cached directory membership (its pin as this region last read it); a forget made elsewhere reaches this region when the directory answers. The table that remembers who was told holds 65,536 principals. When it is full it drops entries older than the window, then the oldest, so a fleet larger than that can see the line repeat for a principal.

docs.title: Back-channel logouts
docs.text:
An identity provider's back-channel logout that reaches any region refuses that session's mints and refreshes in every region, once each region's logout feed delivers the record. Each region's runner says a logout made elsewhere (...) reached N token key(s) and M context(s) here.

If the region that received the logout is cut from the directory:

  • The provider still gets 200, and the region applies the logout at once.
  • The logout is kept pending. port49_store_logouts_pending and port49 store status (N logouts pending) count it; the alert is port49_store_logouts_pending.
  • On the heal the runner forwards it, and the other regions refuse that session from then on.
  • To cut the session off in the other regions before the heal, run port49 revoke --principal <principal> from a region that reaches the directory.

The cut region's runner does not repeat itself while this lasts. It says N back-channel logout(s) pending until the directory store answers once for a run of forwarding passes that fail, and then says nothing more until a pass forwards them.

The retry lines come from the other regions, the ones following a logout made elsewhere. If such a region cannot finish reaching the logout in its own session store, its a logout made elsewhere (...) reached line carries not every step finished (...). The logout is then tried again after a wait that doubles from 1 second to at most 64 seconds, and the logged-out person's mints and refreshes are refused meanwhile.

Look for the first line of the run, not the latest. The first failure's line carries the port49 revoke remedy for ending the person's live sessions at once. The lines after it read still not reached after N tries (...); tried again in <wait> (the remedy was said with the first failure).

A logout the broker can never reach is not tried again. Its line ends not every step finished (...) with no wait and no remedy, and the next takeover of that keyspace reaches it once more.

docs.title: A person who signs in again during a cut
docs.text: A logout that reaches a region late still ends the logins made after the logout was sent. A person who signs in again in a region that has not yet followed the logout may therefore be logged out again when it arrives. This is deliberate: cutting logins off by time would fail open under clock skew between regions.

docs.title: What the lab measured
docs.text: The three-region runs are in the notes L74 and L75. With one region cut: its open session's command was permitted, and port49 store status exited 3; a revocation in another region reached the cut region's session 11 seconds after the heal; a logout posted to the cut region was refused there at once, shown pending, and refused by another region 5 seconds after the heal. Password sign-in in the cut region answered 503 store_unavailable.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text: RFC 9887 puts TACACS+ inside a TLS 1.3 connection with mutual authentication. A device proves who it is with a certificate, not a shared key, so there is no key to rotate on the fleet. port49 serves it on a second listener beside the RFC 8907 one. A device speaks one or the other, as its inventory record says.

docs.title: The two listeners
docs.text:
Listener Config key Default Device record RFC 8907 (obfuscated under a shared key) listen :49 transport: tcp (the default) RFC 9887 (TLS 1.3, mutual) tls_listener.listen :300 transport: tls

Run both at once while you migrate, or only one. To serve TLS alone, set listen: none and add a tls_listener: block; a file with neither listener is refused. They may not bind the same address.

listen: none
tls_listener:
  listen: ":300"
  cert_file: /etc/port49/tls/server.pem
  key_file: /etc/port49/tls/server-key.pem
  client_ca_file: /etc/port49/tls/device-ca.pem
  intermediates_file: /etc/port49/tls/device-intermediates.pem
  state_dir: /var/lib/port49
  certificate_status:
    crls:
      - name: device_ca
        url: https://pki.example.net/device-ca.crl
        issuer_file: /etc/port49/tls/device-ca.pem
Key What it is for cert_file, key_file The server certificate chain (leaf first) and its key. The key must be owned by port49's user or root, with no group or other mode bit. client_ca_file The device CA certificates: the anchors a device certificate must chain to. intermediates_file Optional. Issuing CAs held here, so a device that sends only its leaf still verifies. device_identity Which certificate names identify a device (below). server_names When set, the SNI names a ClientHello may ask for. state_dir Absolute directory where the verified CRLs are kept so a restart keeps them. Required when certificate_status.crls names any. certificate_status Required. Revocation: CRLs, OCSP, or disabled: true, always a written choice. handshake_timeout, session_ticket_lifetime, reload_interval, expiry_warning_fraction Timing. Defaults and limits are in the reference.

A device that connects to the wrong listener is reset: a tcp device on 300 before any TLS byte, a tls device on 49 after its first header (transport_mismatch).

docs.title: How a device is identified
docs.text:
A device is the inventory record its source address belongs to. Its certificate must then name that device, by one of two rules (tls_listener.device_identity.match, both on by default):

  • By name. A dns_name in the certificate equal to the device's inventory name, or to the name under a suffix in device_identity.dns_suffixes, ignoring case and a trailing dot. A wildcard never names a device, and neither does a name with non-ASCII characters.
  • By address. An ip_address in the certificate that is one of the device's addresses.

The common name is never read. A certificate that names another device is refused identity_mismatch, and the detail says what the certificate named and what was wanted. The values of the reason are in the tls_outcome table.

docs.title: Two names that cannot be told apart
docs.text:
• tls_name_clash. Two tls devices whose names are equal under ASCII case folding are both refused admission, and the start names them (inventory: device "<name>" is refused (tls_name_clash): ...). The rest of the fleet loads. Rename one of them.
  • Unidentifiable devices. A dns_suffixes clash, or a non-ASCII name with no ip_address match, means a certificate cannot be told from another's. Such a device is declined at Accept as identity_mismatch, with no handshake and no strike, and named once at start or reload: tls_listener: device <name> cannot be identified: .... Rename it, or give it an ip_address the certificate carries.

docs.title: The server certificate's names
docs.text:
Do not count on the device to check the names: the server certificate must come from a CA the device trusts for nothing else. A certificate from a CA your devices also trust for web sites is a certificate anyone who can get one issued can use against them.

A device configured with a DNS name or an address may or may not check that port49's certificate carries it. In the lab:

  • IOS XE 17.18.02 accepted a server certificate that named only a DNS name, and one that named another address, though it was configured by address (the lab note).
  • EOS and XRd 26.1.1 refused the one naming another address (EOS, XRd), and EOS refused the DNS-only one too.

If you want a wildcard in the server certificate, confine it to a subdomain only TACACS+ servers use (RFC 9887 section 5.1.6).

Unmeasured

Whether Junos, NX-OS and XRd check the server certificate's DNS name or address is unknown. In the lab Junos and NX-OS failed the logins with a certificate naming only a DNS name and one naming another address, and XRd failed the DNS-only one, but the cause was not proven. Give them a certificate that carries every name and address the device might be configured with, and do not rely on either result.

docs.title: Junos
docs.text:
Junos makes the client certificate optional for TLS, and port49 requires it. Without it a login is refused no_client_certificate (port49's own refusal, measured with the lab's reference client in L72). Tell the device to send its certificate on each server and on accounting:

set system tacplus-server <server-address> tls mutual-authentication certificate-id <id>
set system accounting destination tacplus server <server-address> tls mutual-authentication certificate-id <id>

The lab configured exactly this on vJunos-router 26.2R1.7 (the lab note), beside a tls trusted-ca-group line. The whole stanza is in deploy/device-aaa/juniper_junos-tls.set. Junos also sends the server's IP address as the SNI name, so if you set server_names, list every address the device may dial, or leave it unset. The device sees an internal_error alert and port49d logs tls_refused with sni_mismatch.

Unmeasured

Which Junos releases accept this line, and whether SRX does, is unknown; the line was run on one image only. Whether a Junos device whose authentication-order lists tacplus alone falls to anything over TLS when port49 answers ERROR was not measured. The lab placed the client certificate through a lab-only root shell, so the documented enrolment on Junos is also unmeasured, and which of two certificates the device sent is not recorded.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
certificate_status is required, so skipping the check is a choice you wrote down. With CRLs, port49d fetches or re-reads each list every refresh_interval (10 minutes by default), keeps what it verified in state_dir so a restart does not lose them, and checks OCSP if you configure it. A revoked certificate completes the handshake and is then reset with no alert, certificate_revoked.

When the status of a certificate cannot be established (a CRL source down past the list's nextUpdate), on_unavailable: refuse (the default) completes the handshake and resets the connection, recorded status_unavailable. This is a decline, not a strike: the next connection inside the decline window is reset at Accept with no new record, and a device falls to its local method at once. on_unavailable: allow admits the connection and says so; it is the reviewed escape, not the default.

docs.title: Migrating a device from tcp to tls
docs.text:
1. Issue the device a client certificate (clientAuth) from a CA in client_ca_file, naming the device by its inventory name or address. If the device sends only its leaf, put the issuing CA in intermediates_file. In the lab, EOS sent its leaf alone (EOS); Junos, IOS XE, NX-OS and XRd sent the leaf and the intermediate (Junos, IOS XE, NX-OS, XRd).
  2. Start the TLS listener beside the RFC 8907 one, and check port49_tls_server_certificate_lifetime_left_ratio.
  3. On the device, add the TLS server at port 300. With no port configured the lab found Junos and NX-OS dial 49, IOS XE dials 6049, XRd dials 49 and EOS dials 300, so configure the port explicitly (the same five notes).
  4. Change the device's inventory transport to tls. From then on the device is declined on 49 and served on 300.
  5. Remove the shared-key server from the device.

Keep the window in which the device lists both the TLS server and a plain one as short as you can (RFC 9887 section 6.1). In the lab, XRd sent plain TACACS+ headers to the plain server in a mixed list (XRd). IOS XE, Junos and EOS opened a connection to it that was reset before any header, and NX-OS opened none (IOS XE, Junos, EOS, NX-OS). Whether those three would have sent a header had the server stayed up is not measured. port49 refuses a tls device's packet on the RFC 8907 listener (transport_mismatch), so a device that does fall back is not served, but it is a header on the wire.

A sync that flips a device from tls to tcp is recorded transport_changed, and port49 does not block it. The alert is port49_inventory_transport_changed.

docs.title: What you see at 3am
docs.text:
What happened What port49d says Fix A device's certificate expired Record tls_refused with certificate_expired, naming the device and the certificate's NotAfter; the counter port49_tls_handshakes_total{outcome="certificate_expired"}. Before it expired, the expiry_warning_fraction line and port49_tls_device_certificate_lifetime_left_ratio below 0.33. Renew it on the device. A device stopped renewing a short-lived certificate One line a day naming it, once it is in the last third of its own life. Fix its enrolment before the certificate expires. The device CA rotated unknown_ca per device once client_ca_file lost the old CA; a reload line names the anchors in force. Open connections close at their next packet. Keep both CAs in client_ca_file until every device has re-enrolled; read outcome="unknown_ca" at zero before you remove the old one. The CRL is unreachable After nextUpdate: tls_listener: certificate status: CRL ... lines and status_unavailable records, and then one line every 10 minutes counting the declined devices. port49_cert_status_unavailable_total{component="tls_listener"}. Restore the CRL source. A failed source is retried from 30 seconds, doubling up to refresh_interval, so a file: source copied in by hand is read at the next retry, at most refresh_interval later. A device speaks TLS 1.2 only Record version_refused: "offered 303; RFC 9887 requires TLS 1.3". Upgrade the device, or set it back to transport: tcp. A device on the wrong port or transport Record transport_mismatch naming the device and its record's transport. Correct the device's server port, or the record's transport. SNI mismatch Record sni_mismatch, "asked for server name X". A decline, no strike. Correct the device's server name, or server_names. The certificate names another device Record identity_mismatch, e.g. "the certificate names dns_name [leaf-02.example.net]; device leaf-01 is dns_name leaf-01 or leaf-01.example.net, or ip_address 10.0.1.5". Reissue the certificate, or fix the inventory name or address. port49d's own certificate expired The start or reload line "server certificate ... expired"; port49_tls_server_certificate_lifetime_left_ratio below 0. Every device's handshake is recorded handshake_failed and struck, with a detail that begins "the device aborted the handshake (it may refuse port49's certificate)". Replace cert_file; it is picked up within reload_interval. The strikes lapse on their own.

The alerts for these are port49_tls_handshake_failures, port49_tls_device_certificate_renewal_late, port49_tls_server_certificate_renewal_late, port49_tls_server_certificate_expired, port49_tls_cert_status_unavailable and port49_crl_next_update_passed.

docs.title: IOS XE and a down store
docs.text:
When port49's store is down and port49 answers ERROR (store_unavailable), IOS XE 17.18.02 over TLS does not fall to its local method, so break-glass fails: the lab login failed in 4.1 seconds (the lab note). XRd 26.1.1 behaved the same way (the lab note). Junos (with password after tacplus in authentication-order, as the lab configured it), EOS and NX-OS fell to local in the same test (Junos, EOS, NX-OS).

A down store and IOS XE

On IOS XE and XRd over TLS, a store outage that makes port49 answer ERROR locks out the local break-glass account too. Keep an out-of-band way in (the console), and read stores for when port49d closes its listeners instead, which is what lets a device use its local method.

docs.title: The component label
docs.text:
port49_cert_status_checks_total, port49_crl_loads_total, port49_crl_next_update_timestamp_seconds and port49_cert_status_unavailable_total carry component: tls_listener for this listener and broker for the broker's own CRLs. A CRL of the same name in both has a series in each. A rule that divides or compares two of them one-to-one fails to match across components, so aggregate first or ignore the label:

sum by (component) (rate(port49_cert_status_unavailable_total[5m]))
  / sum by (component) (rate(port49_cert_status_checks_total[5m]))

Or match with ignoring(component) where only that label differs. The shipped rules each name their component (component="tls_listener"), so they need neither; see the alerts notes.

docs.title: Which edits need a restart
docs.text:
An edit to any tls_listener: key needs a restart. port49d says this once, at the first SIGHUP: tls_listener: config changes take effect at restart; files reload now. Only the first SIGHUP says it; a later SIGHUP of an edited restart-only key says nothing and changes nothing, so do not read silence as applied.

The files reload by themselves. cert_file, key_file, client_ca_file and intermediates_file are re-read every reload_interval (1 minute by default, 10 seconds to 1 hour) and at SIGHUP. A CA rotation needs no restart: the anchors in force are named in the reload line, and a connection whose chain no longer verifies ends at its next packet. A file that does not load leaves the set in force serving, and the failure is said once.

A change to the inventory or the policy (a device's transport, its addresses) is picked up by the watch and SIGHUP, with no restart. Everything else in port49d.yaml, listen included, is read at start; the reference marks the few other keys that SIGHUP re-reads.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
port49 uses Semantic Versioning.

Version What it means v0.1.0 The beta. 0.x Configuration may break between releases. Every such change is called out loudly in the release notes. Read them before you upgrade. 1.0.0 The compatibility promise. Before it, configuration may break between releases, always with a release note; from it, the SemVer rules hold.

Release tags look like v0.1.0. A tag carries no pre-release suffix, unless the suffix maps to a valid Python (PEP 440) version, because the Python package is released from the same tag.

docs.title: Which version of these docs you are reading
docs.text:
The site keeps one copy of the docs per release line, so a page matches the port49 you run:

Address What it is /latest/ The newest release. The site root redirects here, and a link to /latest/<page> stays valid across releases. Before the first release, it is the same copy as dev. /0.1/, /0.2/, ... The docs of one release line, rebuilt from the highest patch release of that line (v0.1.2 replaces v0.1.1). /dev/ main, ahead of any release. It describes behavior no release has yet.

The version selector in the page header lists these, and keeps you on the same page when you switch, if that page exists in the other version. The banner at the top of the page says which one you are reading: "This site describes port49 v0.1.2." for a release, or that the site describes main, not a release. If your binary says port49d 0.1.0 (see below), read /0.1/.

docs.title: One version across every artifact
docs.text:
A release has one version, and every artifact carries it:

  • the port49-server and port49 packages
  • the archives
  • the container image
  • the Helm chart and app versions
  • the Python package
  • the Ansible collection

They are set to the same number before the tag is pushed, and a check refuses the release if they differ. So you never have to guess which client goes with which server: the same number means the same release.

docs.title: Read the version of a binary
docs.text:
Every binary prints its own version:

port49 --version
port49d --version
port49-broker --version
port49-inventory --version

The line is the binary's name and the version, such as port49d 0.1.0. port49 version prints the same line as port49 --version. Quote that line in a bug report.

What the version part says depends on how the binary was built:

  • A release build prints the version without the tag's leading v. The container image prints the same string as the package.
  • make build from source prints what git describe gives for the checkout, without the v. It is marked -dirty when the tree has changes.
  • A plain go build stamps nothing, and prints the word dev in place of the version.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Before a 0.x upgrade, read the release notes for config changes.
  • After an upgrade that changes the etcd roles, apply them again by hand. It is never done for you (see Stores).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
port49 runs in three shapes. They are peers: each runs the same two processes, port49d and port49-broker, on the same etcd, and nothing in port49 requires any one of them. Choose the one your team already operates.

Shape You get Page systemd the port49-server package (.deb or .rpm) with two units Install with systemd Containers port49d, port49-broker and a three-member etcd under Compose Install with containers Helm two StatefulSets and a PVC per replica Install with Helm

The people who sign in need the clients, which are installed on their own machines and not on the server.

docs.title: What every shape needs
docs.text:
Each shape page states the first four again, in its own terms.

  1. The device's source address reaches port49d unrewritten. port49d admits a device by the address it sees, so a NAT or a proxy in front of port 49 breaks admission.
    • On a host, this is the default.
    • In a container, follow the network notes on the container page.
    • In Kubernetes, a LoadBalancer Service needs externalTrafficPolicy: Local (the chart's default); the Helm page has the measurement.
  2. etcd, with two processes. port49d and port49-broker run apart, each with its own etcd identity. The memory store is one process and is for a trial only.
  3. broker.state_dir survives a restart. It holds the revocation marks, the witness and the issuing CA. Put it on a volume that is kept, and back it up with the host.
  4. etcd is port49's own cluster, on a disk that keeps up. etcd needs sustained WAL fsync p99 under 10 ms, and a member at etcd 3.4.24, 3.5.8 or 3.6 or later: port49d refuses an older one and says which. A slow disk pushes port49's store calls past their timeout in bursts, and the etcd_disk_slow alert fires after ten minutes of it.
  5. Every broker host and every port49d host keeps its clock on NTP. A token's expiry is the broker's clock plus the TTL, read against port49d's clock, and a subject's token_ttl may be 30 seconds. A broker 30 seconds behind a port49d mints tokens that are dead on arrival: every login with one fails token_not_found, the same as a typo, and nothing else points at the clock. A broker that runs ahead lengthens every token by the skew, until its lease reclaims it (at most lease_grace, 5 minutes, plus two minutes past token_ttl), and port49d says so (clock: a token was minted ... ahead of this host's clock, port49_token_minted_ahead_total, the port49_token_clock_skew ticket). A session ceiling follows the broker's own auth_time for a certificate login, and for OIDC the provider's, capped at the broker's now, so skew moves it by the skew; a broker behind makes a context look staler (context_stale sooner), while one ahead cannot push a refresh time into the future. In Kubernetes this is the nodes' clocks; in a container, the host's. Alert on the hosts' own NTP sync, because port49 cannot see a broker that is behind: with node_exporter, node_timex_sync_status == 0 and abs(node_timex_offset_seconds) > 1.

docs.title: Install the binaries with mode 0755
docs.text:
Install port49 with mode 0755, owned by root, with no setgid bit and no file capabilities. The packages and the image already do. If you copy the binary by hand, do the same.

The reason is port49 ssh. It tells ssh to run port49 itself as SSH_ASKPASS, by the path /proc/<pid>/exe. A setgid or capability-bearing binary makes that path unexecutable for the ssh process, and ssh then sends the device an empty password, so the login fails.

port49d needs no file capability to bind port 49. The systemd unit grants CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE as an ambient capability instead.

docs.title: First-install steps
docs.text:
On etcd (every shape in the table above), run these once, in this order. The shape pages give the details for each in that shape.

  1. port49d store-roles prints the etcdctl commands that create port49's two etcd roles. Run them as etcd's root, once per cluster. After a port49 upgrade that changes the roles, apply them again by hand; it is never done for you. The Compose stack runs this for you on its trial PKI.
